sections.label: Measures 4–5
sections.titre: Back to the tonic, then to its substitute
sections.texte: The neighbour resolves: the B in the bass climbs back to C (m. 4), while the F and D of the upper voices fall back to E and C — the tonic chord is recovered note for note as in m. 1. Measure 5 changes colour WITHOUT changing the bass: the held C becomes the third of an A minor chord (vi6), the most direct substitute for the tonic — it shares two notes with it (C and E).

sections.label: Measure 6
sections.titre: The only accidental in the excerpt
sections.texte: The first real harmonic shift since the opening: the bass stays on C (which now becomes the seventh rather than the root), but the harmony above turns into a complete D7 (D–F♯–A–C). The F♯, the only note foreign to the key signature in the whole excerpt, is an ARTIFICIAL leading tone pulling towards G: Bach is now aiming at the dominant (V), not yet at the tonic.

sections.label: Measures 7–8
sections.titre: The dominant, then a tonic that does not quite close
sections.texte: The bass at last steps down to B — the leading tone of the key — and stays there for the last two measures: first under a G major chord (V6), then under the arrival of the tonic (m. 8). But this tonic is not in its most stable state: its major seventh (B itself, since the bass does not move) tints it with a suspended tension that calls for the rest of the piece rather than closing it.

synthese.titre: Two pedals, a single gesture
synthese.texte: The entire harmony of the excerpt rests on two bass notes: C (mm. 1 to 6, with a brief detour to its neighbour B in m. 3), then B (mm. 7–8). The musical motion does not come from the bass, which barely moves — it comes from the upper voices, which redraw the chord above it.

synthese.titre: The two diatonic semitones
synthese.texte: E–F (in the Dm7 of m. 2 and its surroundings) and B–C (the leading tone, mm. 3 and 7–8) are the only two natural semitones in C major — they generate all the tension of the piece, without a single accidental until m. 6.

synthese.titre: Colour follows function, not shape
synthese.texte: Measure 3 has the SHAPE of a dominant (G7) but the FUNCTION of a prolonged tonic — hence its blue colour despite the figure “V6/5”. In tonal harmony, function always outweighs surface appearance.

cours2.title: Chords
cours2.subtitle: Build a triad, enrich with a seventh, master inversions.

quiz.perfect: Perfect — you've mastered chords and their structures.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few nuances to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep exploring — listen to the chords again and retry.

narrative.triadesBody: A chord is born from a simple idea: stacking thirds. Start from a root, move up by a third, then another. Two stacked thirds produce three pitches — a triad. What differentiates the four types is the size of each third.
narrative.gammeTitle: The 7 chords of the major scale
narrative.gammeBody: By building a triad on each scale degree — using only the notes of that scale — we get 7 chords, each with a distinct color and function.
narrative.gammeClickHint: Click a degree to see and hear the chord:
narrative.gammeInfoBox:
Fixed sequence in major scale:
I=Maj · II=min · III=min · IV=Maj · V=Maj · VI=min · VII=dim
narrative.tetradsBody: We enrich a triad by adding an extra third above the fifth. This 4th note — the seventh — deepens the chord's color without breaking its structure.
narrative.tetradsWarnBox: The V degree (G7) is the only dominant 7 chord (X7) in the scale. It contains the full tritone B–F.
narrative.gammeTetradesTitle: The 7 seventh chords of the major scale
narrative.gammeTetradesBody: Stacking a fourth third on top of each triad of the scale gives 7 seventh chords — each inheriting the function of its degree, but with a richer color.
narrative.gammeTetradesClickHint: Click a degree to see and hear the seventh chord:
narrative.gammeTetradesInfoBox:
Fixed sequence in a major scale:
I=Maj7 · II=m7 · III=m7 · IV=Maj7 · V=7 · VI=m7 · VII=m7♭5
narrative.renversementsBody: A chord always contains the same notes — but which note is placed in the bass changes the color. The lowest note determines the inversion. The notation uses a slash: C/E = C major with E in the bass.
narrative.renversementsInfoBox: Slash notation: C/E = C major chord with E in the bass. Always: chord name / bass note. Root position has no slash.
narrative.renversementsTetNote: The “+” isn't generic: it only appears when the chord carries the key's leading tone — the case of the V degree (V7), as here. Another four-note chord without a leading tone (ii7, IVΔ7…) is figured WITHOUT +: 7, 6/5, 4/3, 2.
narrative.quizScoreGood: Very good! A few points left to consolidate.
narrative.quizScoreKeepGoing: Keep practising — re-read the sections and try again.
narrative.maitreAnecdote: It is said that Bach would get up at night to resolve on the piano a tritone left unresolved by his sons. The dissonant chord created such tension in his ear that he could not sleep without resolving it. For him, a chord was never a static note — it was a force in motion.
narrative.maitreLesson: A chord is not merely a stack of notes — it is a force seeking rest.
narrative.invDesc0: The root is in the bass. The chord sounds full, stable, grounded.
narrative.invDesc1: The third is in the bass. The chord sounds lighter, more open — smooths the bass line.
narrative.invDesc2: The fifth is in the bass. More unstable, often used as a passing chord.
narrative.invDesc3: The seventh is in the bass. Very suspended colour — pushes strongly toward resolution.

conservatoire.intuition: A chord is not a stack of notes but a tension between them — understanding intervals means hearing harmony before reading it.

reference.citation: Every chord has a personality determined by the intervals it contains.

voix: The dominant chord (V) contains the tritone B–F that resolves to the tonic chord
Parallel fifths and octaves between voices are forbidden
Double the root in root position, the third in first inversion

pieges.erreur: Doubling the third of the dominant chord (leading tone)
pieges.correction: Double the root or the fifth, never the leading tone

resume: Triad = root + third + fifth
Major triad: major third + perfect fifth
Inversions: 1st (third in bass), 2nd (fifth in bass)

analyseNarrative.tonalite: A♭ major (four flats in the key signature: B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭).
analyseNarrative.forme: Two four-measure phrases. The first (mm. 1–4) asserts the tonic in its three guises (root position, first inversion, root position) and then reaches the dominant. The second (mm. 5–8) opens with a rare move — the dominant slides DIRECTLY to the subdominant, without passing through the tonic — before closing the phrase with a full return to I.

sections.label: Measures 1–3
sections.titre: Three guises of the tonic
sections.texte: Measure 1 states the tonic chord in root position: the root (A♭) is doubled between the bass and the accompaniment, while the melody sings the third (C). Measure 2 inverts the same chord — the bass now carries the third (C) and no longer the root: this is the first inversion (I6), which lightens the bass without changing the function (still blue, still tonic). Measure 3 returns to root position, the bass dropping back to A♭.

sections.label: Measures 4–5
sections.titre: The dominant, then a “retrogression” to the subdominant
sections.texte: The first change of function in the excerpt: the chord E♭–G–B♭ (V), in root position, turns everything red. It is a plain triad, WITHOUT a seventh — the G (the leading tone of the key) is indeed present, ready to pull towards the tonic. But instead of resolving to I as the ear expects, the harmony steps back to the subdominant (m. 5, D♭ major): a genuine retrogression, not a shortcut in the writing — the repose on the tonic will have to wait three more measures.

sections.label: Measures 6–7
sections.titre: A passing chord, then the only minor triad in the excerpt
sections.texte: The bass descends by step (D♭ → C → B♭), linking the subdominant of m. 5 to the ii of m. 7 by way of a brief return to the tonic in first inversion (m. 6 — a PASSING chord, not a real point of rest). Measure 7 introduces B♭ minor (ii), the only minor triad in the whole excerpt: orange, like IV — the two degrees of the subdominant family.

sections.label: Measure 8
sections.titre: Return and closure
sections.texte: The bass completes its descent on A♭, doubled at the octave in the low register: the phrase closes on the tonic. The melody ends with a complete arpeggio of the chord (A♭–C–E♭–A♭), after a brief appoggiatura.

synthese.titre: The colour code always follows the function
synthese.texte: Blue = tonic (I, I6), orange = subdominant (IV, ii), red = dominant (V) — the same convention as in the other conservatory scores. Here, unlike in the Bach Prelude (lesson 1), no colour contradicts its own figure: each shade corresponds exactly to the shape of the chord.

synthese.titre: The V→IV retrogression
synthese.texte: Resolving a dominant is not a mechanical obligation: here it slides to the subdominant before the tonic returns, only in m. 8 — worth noticing precisely by contrast with the V→I expectation set up by the general rule.

synthese.titre: A single minor triad
synthese.texte: Across the eight measures only one chord is minor: the ii (B♭ minor) of m. 7 — the overall colour remains resolutely major, in the image of the key itself (A♭ major).

cours3.title: Tonal Functions and Voice Leading
cours3.subtitle: The tritone as tension engine, T/SD/D functions, and the rules of 4-voice counterpoint.

quiz.perfect: Perfect — the tritone and tonal functions hold no more secrets.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few nuances to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep exploring — listen to the progressions again and retry.

narrative.tritonH2: The tritone — engine of harmonic tension
narrative.tritonP1: The tritone is the interval of 3 whole tones (6 semitones) that forms naturally between the 4th and 7th degrees of a major scale. In C major: F and B. Its acoustic instability is the engine of all tonal harmonic tension.
narrative.tritonInfoBox: In C major: the tritone forms between F (4th degree, subdominant) and B (7th degree, leading tone). Both notes appear in G7 — which is why G7 is the perfect dominant.
narrative.tritonAudioLabel: Listen to the tritone F–B in C major
narrative.tritonAudioDesc: In G7 → C: B rises to C (+½ tone, leading tone→tonic) and F falls to E (-½ tone, seventh→third). This double contrary motion is the tritone resolution.
narrative.tritonH3Why: Why does the tritone create tension?
narrative.tritonP2: The tritone divides the octave into two equal halves (6+6 semitones). This perfect symmetry deprives it of natural direction — it does not know where to go. The ear perceives this ambiguity as tension that must resolve.
narrative.tritonWarnBox: The tritone in C major is the functional key: the presence of both notes F and B in a chord determines its function. It organises all harmonic tension.
narrative.tritonH3Classification: Chord classification relative to the tritone
narrative.fonctionsP1: Every chord in a major scale fulfils a functional role determined by its relationship to the tritone. That role defines its behaviour in the progression — whether it creates rest, preparation, or tension.
narrative.fonctionsTipBox: Quick memo: F and B? → Dominant. F alone? → Subdominant. Neither? → Tonic.
narrative.fonctionsClickHint: Click a degree to hear it and see its analysis.
narrative.fonctionsInfoBox: Diatonic substitutions: two chords of the same function can replace each other. Am ↔ C (two tonics), Dm ↔ F (two subdominants). This flexibility allows harmonic variety without changing the functional logic.
narrative.fonctionsWarnBox: Em (3rd degree): a 'bastard' chord — it contains B (leading tone) but not F. Its function is ambiguous. Composers disagree on its role, and it is rarely used alone in a simple progression.
narrative.progressionsP1: The sequence SD → D → T is the backbone of tonal harmony. All progressions are variants or extensions of it. Cadences punctuate the musical discourse like punctuation marks.
narrative.progressionsClickHint: Click a progression to listen and see its analysis.
narrative.voixP1: Four-voice harmony (Soprano, Alto, Tenor, Bass) is not a stack of chords — it is a controlled polyphony where each voice has its own melodic logic. Voice leading is the art of moving these 4 lines simultaneously in a fluid and logical way.
narrative.voixClickHint: Click a rule to see its details.
narrative.voixTipBox: Key principle: good voice leading relies not on multiplying movements, but on their necessity. Keep common tones, move by step, and only move a voice when musically required.
narrative.voixH3Minimaliste: The minimalist model: II – V – I
narrative.voixRowSopranoMouvement: D holds, then rises to E (+whole tone)
narrative.voixRowAltoMouvement: F holds (7th of G7), falls to E (-½)
narrative.voixRowTenorMouvement: A falls to G (-whole tone), holds
narrative.voixRowBasseMouvement: D rises to G (+4th), falls to C (-5th)
narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Brahms was obsessed with the purity of four-voice writing. He hunted parallel fifths and octaves as absolute offences against taste, marking his students' scores in red. He said that two voices moving together in fifths cease to exist as independent voices — they become one and the same colour.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Voice leading is the art of making each melodic line independent and fluid.

conservatoire.intuition: Harmonic function is the dramaturgical role of each chord in the musical discourse — tonic rests, dominant tensions, subdominant prepares.

reference.citation: Harmony is not an end in itself, but a means of expression.

voix: The authentic progression V–I is the cadence par excellence
The plagal cadence IV–I concludes gently (amen cadence)
Avoid bass movements by unresolved tritone

pieges.erreur: Chaining IV–V–IV (functional regression)
pieges.correction: Respect tonal direction: T → S → D → T

resume: Functions: Tonic (I, III, VI), Dominant (V, VII), Subdominant (II, IV)
Authentic cadence V–I = strong closure
The tritone in V7 resolves: B→C, F→E

analyseNarrative.tonalite: G minor (i) — two flats in the key signature (B♭, E♭). The minor mode is INFERRED by tonal-profile correlation (there is no <mode> tag in the MuseScore export): it is confirmed by the omnipresence of the I pole (Gm) and by the dominant D7 with its leading tone F♯, the only note foreign to the key signature in the whole excerpt.
analyseNarrative.metrique: C (4/4, alla breve).
analyseNarrative.forme: The famous opening theme rests on a pedal — the fifth of the tonic (D), held in the bass for four measures — then slides by a single semitone to an enriched subdominant (IIø7, mm. 5–6), before the cadential progression IIø7–V7–I that this lesson teaches (mm. 7 to 9, m. 9 being a half measure so as to reach the resolution).

sections.label: Measures 1–4
sections.titre: The theme, over the fifth of the tonic held in the bass
sections.texte: The left hand spins out a steady motif in eighth notes (G–D–G–B♭: the root, the fifth, the root and the third of G minor). It is a TONIC chord throughout, but with its own FIFTH (D) in the bass — not an independent dominant pedal, merely one of the notes of the tonic itself. Above it, the famous anacrustic motif (E♭–D–D) launches the theme, unfolded across the four measures.

sections.label: Measures 5–6
sections.titre: The enriched subdominant, reached by step
sections.texte: The bass moves from D to E♭ by a single semitone — without the slightest leap — to reach a half-diminished seventh chord (A–C–E♭–G, the half-diminished second degree), this time with its OWN fifth (E♭) in the bass. This is the orange colour: the enriched subdominant moves decisively away from the tonic.

sections.label: Measures 7–8
sections.titre: The dominant and its tension
sections.texte: The leading tone of the key (F♯, the only accidental in the whole excerpt) appears at last in m. 7: together with the C (the seventh of the chord) it forms the tritone that carries the entire tension of the dominant. In m. 8 the bass stays close by (D, A, F♯): the same dominant chord, first heard as a triad in second inversion (V6/4), then enriched by its seventh (V7, still in second inversion, hence the “+6”).

sections.label: Measure 9
sections.titre: Return — not yet a closed cadence
sections.texte: The tension subsides onto the tonic — but still in second inversion (i6/4), exactly the texture that opened the excerpt. This is not an authentic cadence in the strict sense (which would require the root in the bass): rather a return to the opening idea, the loop that rounds off the phrase in order to launch the theme again.

synthese.titre: One note, two functions
synthese.texte: The D carries the whole harmony of the first four measures (the fifth of the tonic); then, a semitone higher in the bass (E♭), it slides the harmony towards the subdominant — a shift of a single semitone is enough to change the function completely.

synthese.titre: The tritone, engine of the dominant
synthese.texte: F♯ (the leading tone) and C (the seventh) form the interval that pushes everything towards resolution — the only accidental foreign to the key signature in the whole excerpt, reserved for the two measures of dominant harmony.

synthese.titre: A cadence that does not quite close
synthese.texte: IIø7–V7–I is indeed the cadential progression this lesson teaches, but here it loops back onto a I in second inversion (as at the start), not onto a root in the bass — the tension subsides without the phrase closing completely.

cours10.title: Modes of the Major Scale
cours10.subtitle: Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian — seven colors, one scale.

quiz.perfect: Perfect — you've mastered the modes!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more listens and you'll have it.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep listening actively — the ear learns with practice!

narrative.modesH2: The 7 modes of the major scale
narrative.modesIntro: A mode is simply the major scale played from a different degree. In C major (C D E F G A B), if we start on D and play the same notes up to D, we get the Dorian mode. Each starting degree creates a unique harmonic color.
narrative.modesInfoBox: Fundamental principle: all modes share the same notes — it is the starting note (the tonic) that changes everything. By shifting the tonic, we change the intervals and therefore the emotional color.
narrative.modesClickHint: Click on a mode to hear it and see its details.
narrative.harmonieIntro: Each mode generates its own diatonic chords. The harmonic color of a mode comes as much from its chords as from its scale — it is the relationship between the tonic and the surrounding chords that creates the modal identity.
narrative.harmonieInfoBox: Modal vs tonal thinking: in tonal music, chords create tension and call for resolution (SD → D → T). In modal music, chords establish a color — they do not necessarily call for resolution. The Im → IV movement in Dorian is not a cadence, it is a colorful oscillation.
narrative.harmonieWarnBox: Modal vs Tonal: in tonal music, V7 → I is the fundamental resolution. In modal music, this resolution is avoided — progressions that maintain the modal color are preferred rather than resolving it. This is why modal music sometimes seems to "float" or "go in circles" — it is intentional.
narrative.quizFeedbackExcellent: Excellent — the modes hold no more secrets!
narrative.quizFeedbackGood: Good — a few more listening sessions and it will be perfect.
narrative.quizFeedbackKeepGoing: Keep listening to the modes actively — the ear learns!
narrative.maitreAnecdote: In 1959, Miles Davis recorded Kind of Blue — the best-selling jazz album of all time. Instead of chaining complex chords, he built each piece on a single mode. So What is entirely in D Dorian. Davis said: 'I wanted the musicians to think of a color, not a chord sequence.'
narrative.maitreLesson: A mode is not a scale with one different note — it is a harmonic color, a way of hearing the world.

conservatoire.intuition: A mode is the same major scale seen from a different degree — the landscape doesn't change, only the listening point does, and with it the entire color of the music.

reference.citation: Each mode carries its own tonal gravity, independent of any classical harmonic function.

voix: The Dorian (2nd degree) is the brightest minor mode: its major 6th sets it apart from the natural minor scale
A modal piece can stay on a single chord for measures on end — color replaces harmonic motion
Without a dominant or a cadence, it's the mode's characteristic degree (here the Dorian's 6th) that carries its whole identity

pieges.erreur: Looking for a V–I cadence in a modal piece like "So What"
pieges.correction: Modal music doesn't cadence: it colors a fixed tonal center, never moving away from it or returning to it via a dominant

resume: 7 modes = 7 rotations of the same scale, each with its own tonic
The Dorian colors the minor with a major 6th: the most used mode in modal jazz
"So What" (Miles Davis, 1959): a vamp in D Dorian, with no functional harmony

analyseNarrative.tonalite: D dorian — no key signature, but this is neither C major nor A minor: the modal centre is D (the second degree of C major, taken as the point of departure).
analyseNarrative.forme: A two-bar modal vamp (a call from the bass alone, then an answer in chords), repeated four times in succession (measures 1-2, 3-4, 5-6, 7-8) before the pick-up into the repeat (measure 9, which also carries the first ending written into the score). Not one of the nine measures contains a dominant: the piece never cadences, it colours a single tonal centre from beginning to end — the exact counter-example to the nine preceding pieces of this conservatory course, all of them built on functional progressions.

sections.label: Measure 1
sections.titre: The call: the bass alone
sections.texte: The double bass states the tune's riff entirely on its own — an eighth-note pick-up, then a rising line (D-A-B-C-D-E) that closes back onto C. No vertical chord is written (N.C., “no chord”): only the label “I” beneath the bass staff tells us that D remains the modal centre, even with no harmony laid down.

sections.label: Measure 2
sections.titre: The answer: two rootless chords
sections.texte: The piano answers with two brief chords, each without its root written out: D-G-B (the 3rd, 5th and 7th of Em7, without the E) on beat 3, then C-F-A (the same degrees of Dm7, without the D) on the offbeat that follows. In this modal context, II7 prepares no dominant at all: it is a colour that falls straight back onto the modal tonic, without ever passing through a classical tension chord.

sections.label: Measures 3-6
sections.titre: The cycle repeats
sections.chiffrage: Dm7 | Em7 – Dm7  ·  Dm7 | Em7 – Dm7
sections.fonctions: I | II7 – I7  ·  I | II7 – I7
sections.texte: Measures 3 and 5 take up the bass riff of measure 1 note for note. Measures 4 and 6 give the same chordal answer as measure 2 — only the bass varies discreetly (a D-A round trip in measure 4, a single D in measure 6). Nothing moves harmonically: it is repetition that builds this tune, not a progression.

sections.label: Measure 7
sections.titre: A different breath
sections.texte: The only real variation in the whole excerpt: instead of the rising riff, the bass repeats the same note three times (E), in a syncopated rhythm (one note held across beat 2). No label accompanies this measure — it is the only one in the entire excerpt to carry none at all, not even a “I”: the tension of the call stays open longer here than anywhere else before the answer returns.

sections.label: Measure 8
sections.titre: Last answer before the repeat
sections.texte: The cycle closes as in measures 2, 4 and 6: the same answer in two rootless chords. Nothing yet signals the end of the section — it is the following measure that carries the repeat mark.

sections.label: Measure 9
sections.titre: Pick-up and first ending
sections.texte: The bass riff of measure 1 returns unchanged. It is also on this measure, and on this one alone, that the score carries the first ending of the repeat (the repeat barline begins at measure 2): after this measure the cycle starts again from measure 2, before a second ending (outside this excerpt) carries the tune onward.

synthese.titre: One colour, never a cadence
synthese.texte: No dominant chord appears in these nine measures. The II7 (Em7) is never a predominant preparing a resolution: it is a simple colouring that drops straight back onto the modal tonic — the opposite of everything the first nine pieces of this conservatory course teach.

synthese.titre: Repetition as the engine
synthese.texte: The tune does not develop through a chain of chords but through the almost exact repetition of a single two-bar module — only measure 7 departs from it, by a simple change of rhythm in the bass, without ever introducing a new chord.

synthese.titre: “Rootless” chords
synthese.texte: The two chords of the answer (Em7, Dm7) are written without their root: a voicing technique highly characteristic of jazz piano, where the bass already supplies the root and the right hand concentrates on colour (3rd, 5th, 7th).

cours12.title: Tritone Substitution
cours12.subtitle: Replace V7 with the chord a tritone away — same tension, chromatic bass line.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — tritone substitution holds no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more progressions to practice.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep comparing both resolutions by ear — that's how it clicks!

narrative.principeP1: In C major, G7 is the natural dominant — it resolves to C by a descending fifth. Tritone substitution replaces G7 with D♭7, located exactly a tritone lower (6 semitones). D♭7 resolves to C just as well, but the bass descends by a semitone (D♭→C) instead of a fifth leap.
narrative.principeInfo: Definition: tritone substitution (or "tri-sub") replaces any dominant V7 chord with the dominant a tritone lower. G7 → D♭7, D7 → A♭7, A7 → E♭7, E7 → B♭7, etc.
narrative.compCardStandardFeel: Strong, assertive — the classic authentic cadence
narrative.pourquoiH3: Why it works — the shared tritone
narrative.pourquoiP: G7 and D♭7 share exactly the same two guide tones (3rd and 7th), but their roles are reversed. It is this common tritone that allows both to resolve to C.
narrative.enharmoniqueNote: B = C♭ (enharmonic) · F = F — the 2 notes remain, the roles are swapped
narrative.tritonTip: The tritone resolution: B→C (ascending semitone) and F→E (descending semitone). These two movements converge toward the tonic and its 3rd — it is the attraction of the tritone toward the major third of the tonic, whether the bass is G or D♭.
narrative.applicationP1: Tritone substitution applies to any dominant 7th chord, whether it is the main V7 or a secondary dominant. Its most sought-after effect is the descending chromatic bass line.
narrative.ii251H3: II – V – I: standard vs substitution
narrative.bassLineInfo: The bass line D → D♭ → C is one of the most characteristic progressions in jazz. The pianist or bassist can build this chromatic descent in the bass voice, independently of the upper voices.
narrative.secondaryDomP: Any dominant 7th chord (including secondary dominants V7/X) can be substituted. In a progression with several dominants, a continuous chromatic descent can be created in the bass.
narrative.jazzExample1Title: Autumn Leaves — Miles Davis / Bill Evans
narrative.jazzExample1Body: The Am7♭5–D7–Gm progression is one of the most well-known in the jazz repertoire. With tritone sub: Am7♭5–A♭7–Gm. The bass descends A–A♭–G chromatically. Bill Evans and Miles Davis use this substitution in their iconic versions of Autumn Leaves.
narrative.jazzExample2Body: Monk, inventor of many substitutions, uses tritone subs in Round Midnight to enrich his own composition. Miles Davis and Gil Evans develop these ideas in their version with orchestral arrangement (1957). The chromatic richness of this piece owes much to substitutions.
narrative.jazzExample3Body: Giant Steps (1960) pushes the logic of substitution beyond the tritone: Coltrane divides the octave into 3 equal parts by major thirds (B → G → E♭), creating harmonic changes at an incredible speed. It is the ultimate extension of the substitution concept — no longer by tritone, but by major third.
narrative.limitWarn: Limitation of substitution: tritone substitution applies to dominant 7th chords only (unstable internal tritone). It does not apply to Maj7, minor 7 or half-diminished chords — these chords do not have the same type of tension to resolve.
narrative.maitreAnecdote: In 1959, Coltrane began composing Giant Steps. He showed his scores to his musicians during the recording session. Tommy Flanagan, a seasoned session pianist, had never seen it before. The result is audible on the album: Flanagan improvises cautiously, stunned by the speed of the harmonic changes — a modulation every two beats, by major thirds. Giant Steps was released in 1960 and redefined the limits of jazz harmony.
narrative.maitreLesson: Tritone substitution is discovering that a chord can resolve to two different tonics by sharing the same tritone. It is not magic — it is symmetry.
narrative.quizFeedbackExcellent: Excellent — tritone substitution holds no more secrets!
narrative.quizFeedbackGood: Good — a few more progressions to practice and it will be perfect.
narrative.quizFeedbackKeepGoing: Keep listening to both resolutions — the ear is trained through comparison!

conservatoire.intuition: Two dominant chords a tritone apart share the exact same tritone — their tension is identical, only the direction the bass resolves in changes.

reference.badge: Mulholland & Hojnacki · The Berklee Book of Jazz Harmony
reference.citation: Any dominant chord can be replaced by the one built a tritone away: the two share the same 3rd and 7th, simply swapped.

voix: V7 and bII7 (subV7) share the same tritone (3rd and 7th swapped) — the resolution tension is identical
Tritone substitution creates a descending chromatic bass motion into the resolution chord
It's especially effective right before a tonic chord

pieges.erreur: Using tritone substitution on a chord that isn't a genuine functional V7
pieges.correction: Reserve subV7 for dominants (V7 or secondary dominants), never for a tonic or subdominant chord

resume: subV7 = a dominant chord built a tritone above (or below) V7
Both chords share the 3rd and 7th (simply swapped): same tension, different resolution
"Satin Doll" (Ellington): Db7 replaces G7 (subV7) right before the return to C major

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C major (no key signature) — but never asserted directly before measure 7: the whole phrase is nothing but a chain of ii-V pairs that settles onto the tonic only at the very end.
analyseNarrative.forme: 8 measures = the A phrase of the standard: a sequence of ii-V pairs (or their substitutes) rising step by step before resolving onto C major at measure 7, then immediately relaunching the cycle towards a repeat of the section.

sections.label: Measures 1-2
sections.titre: ii7-V7, the basic pattern
sections.texte: The excerpt opens on the most classic progression in jazz: ii7-V7 in C major. The bass slides chromatically (E♭) right at the end of measure 1 — a passing note descending a semitone to the root (D) that opens measure 2.

sections.label: Measures 3-4
sections.titre: iii7-V7/II, the sequence rises
sections.texte: The same ii-V pair moves up a third: Em7 (iii7, a chord of the tonic family), then A7, the secondary dominant of degree ii (V7/II) — a colour that prepares a return to Dm7 which never arrives within this excerpt. The bass resumes its chromatic slide at the end of the measure, this time towards E.

sections.label: Measure 5
sections.titre: vi7-V7/V, a well-dressed dominant of the dominant
sections.texte: Another ii-V pair, transposed once more. The voicings grow markedly richer here: Am7 sounds with neither root nor third — only 5th, 7th and 11th (E-G-D). D7 (V7/V) adds the 9th (E) and the 11th (G) to its minor 7th (C) — a far richer chord than a textbook D7.

sections.label: Measure 6
sections.titre: bVI7-subV7, the tritone substitution
sections.texte: The key moment of the lesson: instead of the expected ii7-V7 (Dm7-G7), the score gives Abm7-Db7. Db7 (subV7) replaces G7 by tritone substitution — in theory the two chords share the same tritone (F-B), which this particular realisation sounds only through the B (the 7th of Db7). On the last offbeat of the measure, the right hand already anticipates the chord of resolution (Cmaj9) and holds it tied across the barline.

sections.label: Measure 7
sections.titre: Resolution — already under way before it arrives
sections.texte: Resolution at last onto the tonic — prepared from the end of the previous measure: Cmaj9 (major 7th B, 9th D) occupies the first two beats without even being re-struck, before the bass slides towards Dm9 to set the cycle going again.

sections.label: Measure 8
sections.titre: A chromatic passage towards the relaunch
sections.texte: A complete diminished seventh chord (E♭-F♯-A-C, checked note by note) serves as a chromatic passing sonority, extending the rising bass line begun in measure 7 (C-D-E♭-E) up to Em7 (iii7), which closes this phrase and relaunches the cycle towards a repeat of the A section.

synthese.titre: One sequence, transposed three times
synthese.texte: ii7-V7 (measures 1-2), iii7-V7/II (measures 3-4), vi7-V7/V (measure 5): the same harmonic gesture, replayed at three different pitch levels, before the tritone substitution (measure 6) replaces it one last time to bring the tonic back at last.

synthese.titre: The substitution, simply a movement of the bass
synthese.texte: Replacing G7 with Db7 changes almost nothing to the ear (same tritone, same tension) — but it turns the resolution of the bass from a leap of a fourth (G→C) into a plain descending semitone (D♭→C): the real reason jazz musicians use it so much.

synthese.titre: The resolution is there before it even arrives
synthese.texte: The tonic chord (Cmaj9) is already sounding, tied over from the previous measure, when measure 7 officially begins — a rhythmic give-and-take typical of jazz that blurs the border between tension and resolution.

cours14.title: Modal Harmonisation
cours14.subtitle: Colouring each mode with its characteristic chords — no mandatory tonal resolution.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — modal harmonisation holds no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more progressions to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep comparing the modes by ear — it comes with practice!

narrative.principesP1: In tonal harmony, chords have functions: Tonic (T), Subdominant (SD), Dominant (D). The progression SD→D→T creates tension and resolution. In modal harmony, chords have colours: they oscillate around the tonic and sustain the colour of the mode — with no mandatory resolution.
narrative.infoBoxGoldenRule: Golden rule: to maintain the modal colour, regularly use the characteristic chord of the mode (the one containing the distinctive note) and avoid V7→I (which introduces the leading tone absent from the mode and creates a tonal resolution).
narrative.tonalDesc: I – IV – V7 – I: tension on G7, resolution to C.
narrative.modalDesc: Im – IV – Im – IV: coloured oscillation, no resolution.
narrative.warnBoxCommonTrap: Common pitfall: harmonising a modal melody with V7→I "by reflex". E.g. in D dorian, playing A7→Dm introduces C# (the leading tone absent from dorian) and immediately transforms the modal colour into classical harmonic minor.
narrative.modesP1: Each mode has its characteristic progression. Click on a mode to see its chords, hear the progression and understand what to avoid.
narrative.warnBoxLocrien: The Locrian mode: its tonic chord is diminished — almost impossible to use as a stable tonal centre. It is used instead as a punctual colour within a broader modal context.
narrative.maitreAnecdote: Debussy broke with tonal harmony by using medieval modes, pentatonic scales and parallel chords. In La Cathédrale engloutie (1910), blocks of chords move together without functional resolution. He would say: 'I hear colours, not functions.'
narrative.maitreLesson: Chords are not functions (T, SD, D) — they are colours. In modal music, we paint with chords rather than chaining them in a directed progression.

conservatoire.intuition: Modal harmony doesn't build tension to resolve — it sets a color and holds it, carefully avoiding the move to the dominant that would break the spell.

reference.badge: Messiaen · The Technique of My Musical Language
reference.citation: The charm of impossibilities lies above all in this very impossibility of escaping the mode without turning back: this is what gives these harmonies their very particular atmosphere.

voix: Modal harmony oscillates around the tonic through color, not through tension to resolve
Avoid V7→I: this progression introduces the leading tone missing from the mode and breaks the modal atmosphere
A single "characteristic" chord (containing the mode's distinctive note) is enough to set the color

pieges.erreur: Looking for a dominant or a tonal resolution in a progression that has none
pieges.correction: Recognize a coloristic oscillation (e.g. IV-I with no V at all) and analyze it as such, not as an "incomplete" tonality

resume: Modal harmony = a color held in place, not tension followed by resolution (unlike tonal harmony)
The V7→I motion is avoided: it would introduce the leading tone and break the mode's atmosphere
"First Gymnopédie" (Satie): IVmaj7-Imaj7 looping over 9 measures, never a dominant

analyseNarrative.tonalite: D major (two sharps) — but the excerpt never once lets the D chord be heard as a point of firm arrival: it begins and ends on G (IV), which occupies 5 of its 9 measures. A reading in G Lydian (with C# as the #4) is just as defensible on the strength of this excerpt alone — the two readings share exactly the same two sharps. The remainder of the piece (outside this excerpt) will settle the matter in favour of D major.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 3/4. No tempo or character marking in this file (the original carries “Lent et douloureux”, not reproduced here) — quarter note = 60 added as an editorial choice, for synchronised playback.
analyseNarrative.forme: 9 measures = a strict harmonic pendulum between two major-seventh chords, IVmaj7 (G) and Imaj7 (D), without the dominant (A) ever being sounded: measures 1-4, the accompaniment alone sets the rocking in place; measures 5-9, the melody enters and descends an octave (F#5 to F#4), systematically crossing the “coloured” degrees of each chord (7th, 9th, 11th, #11) rather than its stable notes.

sections.label: Measures 1-4
sections.titre: The harmonic pendulum, with no melody
sections.texte: The texture is frozen for the first four measures: a deep bass note held right through the measure (G2, then D2), a quarter rest, then a three-note chord struck on the second beat and held to the end (B3-D4-F#4 over G; A3-C#4-F#4 over D) — the celebrated rocking of a sarabande stripped bare. F#4 is the only note that remains at exactly the same pitch in both voicings: a pivot, without which the two chords would have nothing left in common to the ear. No dominant (A) ever appears: with no V there can be no cadence — the IV-I alternation is a static plagal oscillation, suspending tonal direction rather than building it. Tellingly, the excerpt opens directly on the subdominant, not on the tonic.

sections.label: Measure 5
sections.titre: The melody enters: seventh, then ninth
sections.texte: After a rest, the melody enters on F#5 — the major seventh of G, exactly two octaves above the F#4 of the accompaniment — then leaps up to A5, the ninth. The score explicitly figures this chord as “Gmaj9” (not simply “maj7”): the melody touches precisely the extension the figuring announces. From the very first breath, two “dissonant” notes set down as self-evident, with no preparation whatsoever.

sections.label: Measure 6
sections.titre: The one “resolved” gesture in the excerpt
sections.texte: G5 on the first beat is an 11th over the tonic chord (D) — the only melodic dissonance in the whole excerpt that steps back down, to F#5 (the third), yet on a weak beat and without preparation. The line then drops a fourth to C#5, the seventh of D.

sections.label: Measure 7
sections.titre: The climb towards the #11
sections.texte: A stepwise ascent B4-C#5-D5 (third to fifth, by way of C#). Here again the figuring announces the colour precisely: this is the ONLY measure in the entire excerpt where a “(#11)” is added to the G chord, and it is exactly the note the melody touches in passing.

sections.label: Measures 8-9
sections.titre: The stable fifth, then the major seventh left hanging
sections.texte: A4, held through the whole of measure 8: the fifth of D, the only fully consonant and stable note in the entire melodic phrase. Then F#4, held through the whole of measure 9: the major seventh of G, one octave below the F#5 that opened the melody in measure 5. The excerpt closes in complete suspension, without the slightest cadence — a descending arc of exactly one octave, from the high F# to the low one.

synthese.titre: Only one genuinely common note: F#
synthese.texte: G-B-D-F# and D-F#-A-C# share two notes in theory (D and F#), but in the actual voicings of the accompaniment only F#4 stays at exactly the same pitch — the D changes octave each time (bass, or middle of the chord). It is this slender thread that holds the two colours together.

synthese.titre: The major seventh as colour, not as dissonance
synthese.texte: Neither the F# of G nor the C# of D is prepared or resolved — a treatment unthinkable in strict tonal harmony (that of the Bach Invention analysed in the previous lesson), where a major seventh is a dissonance to be directed somewhere. Here it is a stable state, constitutive of the chord: the most radical gesture in the piece.

synthese.titre: G Lydian or D major? Nothing decides
synthese.texte: Over these nine measures alone the two tonal readings remain equally valid — which is precisely the effect sought. In Bach, every chord justifies itself through the voice leading; in Satie, harmony is a repeated sonic object with no voice leading at all (block chords, no lines answering one another): the same reading exercise, two opposing grammars.

cours13.title: Two-Voice Counterpoint
cours13.subtitle: Fux's 5 species — note against note, passing notes, suspensions, florid counterpoint — the rules of two-voice motion.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — two-voice counterpoint holds no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few rules still to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep listening to the species — the ear learns with practice!

narrative.especesIntro: Fux organises the study of counterpoint into 5 progressive species. Each species introduces a new difficulty: first pure consonances, then passing notes, then suspensions, and finally free combination.
narrative.especesInfoBox: General principle: two-voice counterpoint is written above a cantus firmus — a reference melody in long notes. The counterpoint voice must be melodically interesting and harmonically correct with respect to the CF.
narrative.especesClickHint: Click on a species to hear it and see its rules.
narrative.especesRow3Fig: Neighbor notes, escape tones, passing notes
narrative.reglesIntro: Strict counterpoint rests on three pillars: the quality of intervals (consonances vs. dissonances), the type of motion between voices, and the rigorous treatment of each dissonance.
narrative.reglesWarnBox: Hidden fifths and octaves: even when voices reach a fifth or octave by direct motion (not parallel), this "hidden fifth" is forbidden between outer voices (soprano and bass) in the strict style. The two voices must not approach a perfect fifth or octave while moving in the same direction.
narrative.reglesSuspensionsIntro: A suspension unfolds in 3 mandatory steps: preparation → dissonance → resolution.
narrative.reglesSuspensionsInfoBox: Suspension cycle: 1. Preparation — the note is present as a consonance on the weak beat. 2. Dissonance — the note is held by a tie on the strong beat (the CF has moved, creating a dissonance). 3. Resolution — the dissonance descends by a conjunct step to a consonance.
narrative.reglesMelo1Detail: The line should be primarily stepwise — naturally singable. Leaps should remain rare and justified.
narrative.reglesMelo2Rule: After a large leap, return in the opposite direction
narrative.reglesMelo2Detail: A leap of a sixth, seventh, or octave should be followed by a gradual melodic return in the opposite direction.
narrative.reglesMelo3Detail: The highest point of the line should appear only once. Repeating it dilutes the dramatic effect.
narrative.reglesMelo4Rule: Avoid leaps of augmented or diminished intervals
narrative.reglesMelo4Detail: The augmented second, diminished fifth, and tritone are difficult to sing and create tonal ambiguities.
narrative.reglesMelo5Rule: Avoid prolonged repetitions of the same note
narrative.reglesMelo5Detail: A note repeated several times in a row stagnates the line and harms its melodic independence.
narrative.reglesMelo6Detail: When the upper voice drops below the lower voice (or vice versa), the melodic identities become entangled.
narrative.reglesTipBox: Fux's method: always start by mastering the 1st species in all modes before moving to the 2nd. Fux insists: each species is an indispensable tool. Florid counterpoint (5th species) is only accessible once the first 4 have been internalised intuitively.
narrative.quizFeedbackGreat: Excellent — Fux would be proud of you!
narrative.quizFeedbackGood: Good — a few more species to practise.
narrative.quizFeedbackKeepGoing: Keep practising the species one by one — the order matters!
narrative.maitreAnecdote: In 1725, Fux publishes the Gradus ad Parnassum ('Steps to Parnassus') in Vienna. He is 65 and suffering from gout. He writes it as a dialogue: Aloysius (his ideal, Palestrina) teaches Josephus (himself). This book would span the centuries: the young Haydn would study it alone in his room in Vienna. Mozart would use it to teach. Beethoven would copy entire passages into his notebooks.
narrative.maitreLesson: Writing two independent voices is harder than writing one complex voice. Each voice must have its own life — and yet, together, they must form a coherent harmony.

conservatoire.intuition: Counterpoint means writing a second voice with a melodic life of its own that still agrees with the first at every instant — two lines answering each other, never just doubled harmony.

reference.citation: Counterpoint is the art of combining voices or parts so that they agree with one another according to certain fixed laws.

voix: Note against note (1st species): perfect consonances (octave, 5th) are best approached by contrary or oblique motion
Contrary motion between the two voices is the surest way to avoid parallel fifths and octaves
Each voice keeps its melodic independence — no crossing, no prolonged unison

pieges.erreur: Moving both voices in the same direction into a fifth or an octave
pieges.correction: Prefer contrary or oblique motion when approaching perfect consonances

resume: Counterpoint = two melodically independent voices that agree vertically
Fux's 5 species: note against note, 2 against 1, syncopations/suspensions, florid figures, florid counterpoint
Invention No. 1 BWV 772 (Bach): subject and answer traded between the two hands, modulating to the dominant

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C major (no key signature) at the outset — but the pivot chord in measure 4 tips the piece towards its dominant, G major, where it settles for good through to the end of the excerpt (measures 7-8).
analyseNarrative.forme: 8 measures = the opening phrase of the Invention: the subject stated in the soprano, then in the bass an octave lower (measure 1), the end of the subject and a touch of dominant colour (measure 2), a diatonic sequence by way of transition (measure 3), pivot chord and modulation to G major (measure 4), the dominant prepared and then resolved by a detour (measures 5-6), the subject restated in the bass at its transposition and a half cadence on the new dominant (measures 7-8).

sections.label: Measure 1
sections.titre: The subject, stated then imitated at the octave
sections.texte: The subject appears first in the soprano: C-D-E-F-D-E-C (beats 1-2), a pure tonic arpeggio threaded through with stepwise motion. On beats 3-4 it migrates to the bass, an octave lower, while the soprano holds a countersubject within the tonic chord (G-C-B-C). The F3 that falls on the downbeat of beat 4 in the bass belongs to that melodic line of the subject, not to the harmony: there is no call to figure a subdominant chord here — the whole measure is nothing but a prolonged tonic.

sections.label: Measure 2
sections.titre: The answer, and a touch of dominant seventh
sections.texte: The bass completes the subject by descending an octave (G3-G2), then sets out again on G (G-A-B-C-A-B-G) while the soprano answers above. On the last beat, a lower neighbour in the soprano (G-F♮-G) sounds the F natural that colours G into G7 (V7) — exactly the figure written at that precise point in the score.

sections.label: Measure 3
sections.titre: Ascending diatonic sequence
sections.texte: Four chords in sequence over a stepwise ascending bass (C-D-E-F-G-A-B). Right at the end of the measure, an unfigured passing chord forms between the two voices — B (bass) - D - F (soprano), a complete diminished vii° — and presses naturally towards the C of the following measure: a fine point of analysis that the roman-numeral figuring, holding “vi” to the very end of the measure, does not show, but which the actual pitches confirm.

sections.label: Measure 4
sections.titre: The pivot chord and the tip into G major
sections.fonctions: IV – V6/5 – V4/3 – V4/2 (already in G major)
sections.texte: The hinge of the whole excerpt: the C that opens the measure is at once I of C major and IV of G major — a pivot chord in the strictest sense. The three beats that follow lay out the dominant of the new key as a fully arpeggiated bass line (F#-A-C), passing through all three of its inversions (V6/5, V4/3, V4/2); the F# arrives in the bass precisely on the third eighth note of the measure, the leading note of G that confirms the colour of the new tonic. The C (the seventh of D7) held in the bass at the end of the measure is tied across the bar line: its resolution is deferred to measure 5.

sections.label: Measures 5-6
sections.titre: The deferred resolution, then the real tonic
sections.chiffrage: D7/C (V4/2) – G (I) – G (I) – C (IV) | Em (vi) – G (I) – G/B (I6) – D (V)
sections.fonctions: D (V4/2, prolonged) – T – T – SD | T (vi) – T – T (I6) – D
sections.texte: The held seventh (C) does not resolve down to B as expected: the bass escapes from it by an ascending scale (D-E-F#) and reaches the tonic directly in root position (G), an evaded resolution. The dotted C5 that follows in the soprano is an accented dissonance which rises to D5 instead of falling — an unusual treatment that stretches the tension out one beat further. In measure 6 the bass hesitates for a moment between G (I) and a fleeting return to E (vi) before settling on B (I6, a held note); a passing C3 then links B to D, which opens the cadence: a genuine 6-5 suspension (B4 to A4) carried over the bass D3-D2, with no seventh whatsoever (there is no C anywhere in the rest of the measure) — a plain D major chord, not D7.

sections.label: Measures 7-8
sections.titre: The subject returns in the bass, half cadence
sections.texte: The subject reappears, this time wholly in the bass and on G (G-A-B-C-A-B-G): a restatement a fifth above its original entry in measure 1, in the key now firmly in place. After a brief passage through six-four position (I6/4) and then the inverted dominant (V6/5, F#3 beneath C5), the bass comes to rest on G on the upbeat to the final beat. Measure 8 launches the subject again on D while the soprano holds an F#4; the notes A-B-C that follow in the soprano sound a C natural — the seventh that installs D7 (V7), confirmed in the bass by the motion D-C-D. The excerpt breaks off on this open dominant, at full tension, just before the Invention goes on.

synthese.titre: One subject, two voices, a single idea
synthese.texte: The whole excerpt rests on a single melodic motif (C-D-E-F-D-E-C, or its transpositions) that migrates ceaselessly between soprano and bass — stated in the soprano (measure 1), imitated in the bass an octave lower (still measure 1), then restated in the bass on the new degree (measures 7-8): the very principle of invention counterpoint, in which one line alone generates the entire two-part discourse.

synthese.titre: A modulation through the nearest door
synthese.texte: C major tips over into G major, its dominant — the most natural modulation there is, set in motion by a pivot chord (C = I/IV, measure 4) and then confirmed by a secondary dominant arpeggiated in full in the bass (D7 through all three of its inversions). From that moment on, the figuring reasons in the key of arrival.

synthese.titre: Resolutions delayed, never fudged
synthese.texte: Twice in this excerpt a prepared dissonance is denied its most expected resolution: the seventh of measure 4 escapes by way of a scale instead of falling (measure 5), and the accented C5 in the soprano rises to D5 rather than the reverse — two detours that stretch the tension without ever betraying it.

cours16.title: Reharmonisation
cours16.subtitle: Diatonic substitution, tritone substitution, modal borrowing, parallel harmonisation — transforming chords under an intact melody.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — reharmonisation holds no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more techniques to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep comparing before/after versions by ear — that's how it clicks!

narrative.principleP1: Reharmonizing a progression means replacing some or all chords with others — while keeping the melody intact. The fundamental condition: each melodic note must be compatible with the new chord (root, third, fifth, seventh or extension).
narrative.principleInfoBox: Golden rule: before validating a substituted chord, verify that each melodic note is 1, 3, 5, 7 or an extension (9th, 11th, 13th) of that chord. If a note 'floats in the void', choose a different chord or technique.
narrative.principleWarnBox: Voice leading: a technically correct reharmonization can sound abrupt if inner voices make large leaps. Always prefer stepwise motion (half-step, whole step) for inner voices — a quality criterion as important as melodic compatibility.
narrative.techniqueDiatoniqueDescription: Two chords sharing at least two common notes can replace each other. In C: CMaj7 (C E G B) and Am7 (A C E G) share C, E and G. The melody stays compatible because its notes are present in both chords.
narrative.techniqueDiatoniqueTip: Replacing I with VI creates a 'soft deceptive resolution' — V7→VIm instead of V7→I. Less definitive, more expressive. Ubiquitous in Bill Evans and Keith Jarrett.
narrative.techniqueTritoniqueDescription: V7 is replaced by the chord a tritone (6 half-steps) away. G7 and Db7 share the same tritone (B–F / F–Cb) — same tension notes, inverted roles. The bass descends a half-step to I instead of a fifth.
narrative.techniqueTritoniqueTip: Bass Db→C (half-step) vs G→C (fifth). The chromatic motion is the acoustic signature of this substitution: same resolution tension, radically different sound.
narrative.techniqueModalDescription: A chord is borrowed from the parallel minor scale. In C major, Fm (IVm), AbMaj7 (bVI) or Bb7 (bVII) come from C minor. These unexpected flats momentarily darken the color — a poignant, introspective effect.
narrative.techniqueModalTip: FMaj7 → Fm is the most common borrowing. Ab (3rd of Fm) flattens the color. Evans uses it on Waltz for Debby to create expressive contrast within a bright section.
narrative.techniqueParalleleDescription: The same chord type moves chromatically under the melody. Inner voices all move in parallel by the same interval. An impressionist technique (Debussy, Ravel) adopted by jazz — Evans, Mehldau.
narrative.techniqueParalleleTip: Parallel chords are 'neutral' in themselves. It's the melody that creates harmonic interest and logic. Three consecutive chromatic Maj7 chords create an immediate impressionist effect.
narrative.applicationP1: Reharmonization can be applied block by block (changing one chord at a time) or completely (rebuilding the entire chord chart under the melody). Great jazz pianists combine all four techniques to create personal progressions.
narrative.compTritonsubNote: Bass D–Db–C: descending chromatic motion, bebop signature
narrative.compModalborrowNote: Fm introduces Ab — dark, poignant color very characteristic of Bill Evans
narrative.compExtensionsNote: Same function, richer color — Bill Evans' sonic signature
narrative.compDiatonicNote: Am7 shares C, E, G with CMaj7 — soft deceptive resolution
narrative.pianistEvansWorks: Waltz for Debby, Autumn Leaves, My Foolish Heart
narrative.pianistEvansStyle: Modal borrowings, extensions, discrete substitutions — 'signing' a standard without betraying it
narrative.pianistJarrettStyle: Free reharmonizations, parallel harmonization, expressive chromaticism
narrative.pianistMehldauStyle: Cross-genre reharmonization — pop melody, complex jazz changes with substitutions
narrative.pianistColtraneWorks: My Favorite Things, Body and Soul
narrative.pianistColtraneStyle: Complete reharmonization — entire chart replaced (modal or Coltrane cycle)
narrative.applicationBlocText: Change one chord at a time. Safer — you control the impact of each substitution. Bill Evans often works this way: a IVm here, a Db7 there.
narrative.applicationCompleteText: Rebuild the entire chart. More radical and creative. Coltrane transforms My Favorite Things into a completely new modal chart — melody intact.
narrative.applicationTipBox: Bill Evans' principle: 'never sacrifice voice leading'. Each chord change must allow inner voices to move by half-steps or whole steps. Great jazz progressions sound fluid precisely because inner voices move little — the melody does the expressive work.
narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Evans plays Autumn Leaves on his first solo album (1956) and the listener recognizes the familiar melody — but the chords have changed. FMaj7 became Fm, G7 became Db7. Without altering a single note of Joseph Kosma's melody, Evans transformed a springtime standard into a melancholy nocturne.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Reharmonization is not virtuosity — it's listening. Before substituting a chord, ask yourself: can the melody still be heard? Does the new chord say something the original could not?

conservatoire.intuition: Reharmonizing isn't about replacing a melody — it's about finding it new traveling companions: every substituted chord must still carry the melody note without betraying it.

reference.citation: A good reharmonization doesn't change what the melody plays — it changes what it says.

voix: Before validating a substituted chord, check that each melody note is still the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, or an extension of the new chord
A secondary dominant can replace a diatonic chord with its own V7 (e.g. V/IV instead of a borrowed chord)
Favor stepwise motion in the inner voices — a technically correct but jarring reharmonization always sounds wrong

pieges.erreur: Introducing a secondary dominant whose extension contradicts a note already present in the melody
pieges.correction: Always check the new chord color against the actual melody note before validating it

resume: Reharmonizing = replacing the chords under an untouched melody, keeping every melody note compatible with its new chord
Secondary dominants (V/V, V/IV) and tritone substitutes are the most common tools
"My Funny Valentine" (Bill Evans): minor cadence iiø7-V7alt-i preceded by a subdominant excursion (IV9-IV13sus)

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C minor (three flats). The standard changes of the A section are famous for their line cliché: Cm-Cm(maj7)-Cm7-Cm6, the descending line C-B-B♭-A over a tonic pedal, before Abmaj7-Fm7-Dø7-G7. This transcription does not play the line: it compresses it and replaces it.
analyseNarrative.forme: 9 measures = the first A section of the standard. The model's horizontal line cliché is verticalised in the very first chord (measure 1); the two measures thus freed up (2-3) are filled with altered turnarounds and with a reharmonisation of the same melody; two chords of the changes (Abmaj7/Fm7) are merged into one (measure 5); and the arrival of the iiø7 (measures 7-8) itself becomes a formal gesture — an arching wave, not simply a chord.

sections.label: Measure 1
sections.titre: The line cliché already summed up in a single chord
sections.texte: Bass C3, and above it A♮3-D4-E♭4-G4: root, major sixth, ninth, third, fifth — a complete Cm6/9. The A♮, the point of arrival of the standard line cliché (C-B-B♭-A), is thereby integrated vertically from the very first chord: four measures of horizontal harmony summed up in one voicing. The friction between D4 and E♭4 (a minor second at the heart of the chord) is the cluster signature of the whole transcription. The melody enters as an upbeat halfway through the second beat: C5-D5-E♭5, the generative cell of the theme, marked p.

sections.label: Measure 2
sections.titre: The substituted turnaround, entirely altered
sections.texte: In place of measures 2-3 of the standard cliché, a fully altered II7-V7 turnaround. D7: a 3-7 shell in the bass (F♯3-C4), F♮4 (= E♯, the ♯9), B♭4 (♭13) and the root in the soprano. G7 (placed as an anticipation, an eighth note then a dotted quarter): a 7-3 shell (F♮3-B♮3) — the voice leading between the shells is exact, F♯→F♮, C→B, each voice falling by a semitone — capped by E♭ (♭13), A♭ (♭9), and the fifth on top. These ♭9/♭13 over G7 are the notes of C harmonic minor: the alteration is no exoticism, it is the key itself.

sections.label: Measure 3
sections.titre: The same melody, an adverse harmonisation
sections.texte: The voicing of measure 1 returns exactly (the same four notes), and the melody launches the cell C-D-E♭ once more. But the harmony tips over on the fourth beat (the D4 of the third beat is no more than a passing note in the bass): E♮4-F♯4 light up above B♭3 — third, Lydian ♯11 and seventh of a rootless C7, functioning as V7/iv towards F minor. The same melody, the opposite harmonisation: the excerpt's first lesson in reharmonisation. Crescendo marked.

sections.label: Measure 4
sections.titre: The chromatic wave
sections.texte: The densest measure of all. Aø9 (A3 in the bass, E♭-G-B♮(the ninth)-D above, without the third, C) functions as V/iv towards F minor. Then G♭13(♯11): the tritone substitute for C7, in a complete voicing (G♭-B♭ in the bass, F♭-A♭-C-E♭ above). And then the remarkable gesture: F13(♯11) is exactly the same structure slid down a semitone (F-A / E♭-G-B♮-D) — parallel planing, every voice descending a semitone as a single block. Diminuendo marked: the wave falls back.

sections.label: Measures 5-6
sections.titre: Two chords merged, then the descent towards the iiø
sections.texte: Fm9 (bass F2-C3 in tied whole notes): three successive positions of the same chord in the right hand — G-A♭-C (9/3/5, another second-cluster), B♭-D♮ (the 11th and the Dorian 13th, not the flattened sixth of the natural minor), then A♭-C-E♭ (3/5/7). The standard changes give Abmaj7 and THEN Fm7 here — two relative chords that the transcription merges into a single spread-out Fm9 (Fm9 already contains every note of Abmaj7). Measure 6: F13sus9 (11, 13, 9, 7, no third), then the bass slides down to E♭ beneath F3 (Fm9/E♭): F→E♭→D, the obligatory passage of the changes (measures 6-7 of the standard) — the one place where this transcription follows them to the letter.

sections.label: Measures 7-8
sections.titre: The arc around the iiø: summit, then descent
sections.texte: The whole of measure 7 is a triplet arpeggio running across both hands: the bass spells out D2-D3-F3-A♭3-C4-E♭4 (the complete ø7 chord, plus a ♭9 spilling over), while the right hand piles up three-note voicings rising in parallel as far as A♭4-C5-G5 — the highest point of the entire excerpt. Measure 8 comes back down in an almost symmetrical gesture (the same three-note stacks, traversed in reverse), the bass descending E♭4-D4-A♭3-F3, before landing on the third beat on G7(♯9♭13): G2 in the bass, an F3 shell, then B♮-E♭-F-B♭ (3-♭13-7-♯9). The melody descends A♭-G-F in a triplet — the A♭ a passing ♭9: the chord thus accumulates a ♯9 and a melodic ♭9, a saturated dominant just before the resolution.

sections.label: Measure 9
sections.titre: The bare resolution
sections.texte: A deliberately stripped-down resolution after the swell that came before. Melody E♭4 (a dotted half note); in the bass, D4→C4: a 9-8 appoggiatura that resolves — the sole ornament in an otherwise empty measure. Then the triplet F4-G4 launches a fresh upbeat towards the continuation of the theme, cut off here.

synthese.titre: The tritone substitute, without even resolving
synthese.texte: G♭13(♯11) (measure 4) is the classic tritone substitute for C7 — but instead of resolving to F minor like the expected subV7, it slides down a single semitone to F13(♯11), an identical structure. Substitution becomes a purely chromatic device here (planing), detached from any idea of resolution — colour takes precedence over function.

synthese.titre: The line cliché, horizontal then vertical
synthese.texte: The standard unfurls Cm-Cm(maj7)-Cm7-Cm6 across four measures; this transcription stacks the same notes (including the A of the cliché) into a single Cm6/9 from measure 1 onwards, freeing all the remaining space for reharmonisation.

synthese.titre: The voicing as an autonomous expressive object
synthese.texte: In Bach (Invention no. 1, lesson 13), form is born of voice leading; in Satie (Gymnopédie, lesson 14), of repetition; in the bare jazz changes (Autumn Leaves, lesson 15), of functional succession. Here the texture itself — the arch of measures 7-8, the planing of measure 4 — becomes a formal event: the voicing, and not merely the chord it carries, is the subject.

cours15.title: Advanced Jazz Progressions
cours15.subtitle: Basic, extended and minor II–V–I, rhythmic harmony, turnarounds and jazz blues.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — jazz progressions hold no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more progressions to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep listening actively — jazz is learned through the ear!

narrative.maitreAnecdote: Parker ('Bird') improvised in 1945 over Ko-Ko (Cherokee changes) at a speed that astonished his contemporaries. He simultaneously used tritone substitutions, secondary dominants, and b9/#9 extensions that no one had chained together so rapidly. Dizzy Gillespie said: 'He heard things we hadn't even heard yet.'
narrative.maitreLesson: II–V–I is not a formula — it's a space for exploration. The more you master its variations (extensions, substitutions, chains), the more colours you have at your disposal.
narrative.iiviIntro: The II–V–I is the fundamental harmonic cell of jazz. IIm7 prepares, V7 creates tension, IMaj7 resolves. This same structure exists in basic form, with extensions, and in minor — three very different colours on the same architecture.
narrative.iiviInfoBox: Key principle: the tritone in V7 (B–F in G7) is the engine of resolution. B rises to C (3rd of CMaj7), F falls to E (7th of CMaj7) — an irresistible double chromatic movement that defines the jazz cadence.
narrative.iiviWarnBox: Essential practice: learn to play (or sing) the II–V–I in all 12 keys. Standards constantly modulate — knowing the progression in every key is the sine qua non for improvising freely.
narrative.rythmeIntro: Harmonic rhythm is the speed at which chords change. It is a fundamental dimension of a piece's identity — as important as the tempo or melody. Turnarounds are the end-of-chorus progressions that "turn" back to the repeat.
narrative.rythmeGiantDesc: Coltrane (1960). Keys change every 1–2 bars following a cycle of major thirds (C–E–Ab). Extremely dense harmonic rhythm.
narrative.ryhmeSoWhatDesc: Miles Davis (1959). D Dorian for 16 bars, Eb Dorian for 8 bars. Very slow modal harmonic rhythm — the colour settles and stays.
narrative.ryhmeCycleDesc: Chaining II–Vs in keys descending by fifths is the foundation of many standards. Dm7–G7 (II–V in C), then Gm7–C7 (II–V in F), then Cm7–F7 (II–V in Bb)... You'll recognise Autumn Leaves, All The Things You Are, and dozens of others.
narrative.rythmeRhythmChangesBox: Rhythm Changes: the I Got Rhythm chord changes (Gershwin, 1930) are the basis of hundreds of bebop standards — Anthropology, Oleo, Cottontail. 32-bar AABA structure: A section = I–VI–II–V repeated, B bridge = secondary dominants.

conservatoire.intuition: The II-V-I isn't a fixed formula — it's a skeleton that jazz dresses up with extensions, substitutions, and secondary dominants, link after link, without ever losing the thread back to the tonic.

reference.citation: The jazz musician doesn't play chords: they play lines that tell the story of the chords, always anticipating the one that's coming next.

voix: A secondary dominant (V7/X) briefly tonicizes degree X before resolving to it
The tritone substitute (subV7) replaces a dominant with the 7th chord a tritone away — same tension, a bass line that descends by half-step
A chain of secondary dominants forms a descending sequence of fifths, the backbone of many standards

pieges.erreur: Analyzing each chord in isolation without spotting the secondary dominant that precedes it
pieges.correction: Always check whether a dominant chord resolves a half-step or a fifth away to a degree other than the tonic — that's a secondary dominant (V7/X)

resume: A chain of secondary dominants (V7/III, subV7/VI, V7/V...) briefly tonicizes each degree before the final resolution
The tritone substitute replaces a dominant with its tritone: same tension (3rd/7th swapped), chromatic bass
"Autumn Leaves" (Kosma): descending iv-VII-III-VI-ii°/V-V-i sequence, then a V7/IV turnaround that closes the loop

analyseNarrative.tonalite: G minor, with its relative B♭ major permanently on the horizon — the very principle of the “Autumn Leaves” changes, which loop between the two poles by way of a chain of descending fifths (C→F→B♭→E♭→A→D→G). In this arrangement, almost every chord of the sequence is in fact a secondary dominant towards the degree that follows.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Tempo 120 (medium swing).
analyseNarrative.forme: 10 measures = a one-beat pickup (measure 1) + the complete A section of the standard (measures 2-9, eight measures) + the start of its repeat (measure 10) — the pickup motif in fact returns at the end of measure 9, confirming that the form loops back on itself.

sections.label: Measure 1
sections.titre: The pickup, and its bitonal ambiguity
sections.texte: Three ascending stepwise eighth notes, G-A-B♭, the left hand silent. A figure open to two readings: 1̂-2̂-3̂ in G minor (tonic, second degree, minor third) or, viewed from the relative pole, 6̂-7̂-1̂ in B♭ major (submediant, leading note, tonic) — the ambiguity of the two twin keys laid out from the upbeat, before the first chord has even sounded.

sections.label: Measures 2-3
sections.titre: Cm9, then F7: the sequence sets off, the 13th hardens
sections.texte: The chord marking in the file already reads “m9”, not “m7”: D4 (the ninth) is indeed held in the bass beneath the struck E♭4-B♭4, under the E♭5 of the melody — a complete Cm9 from the written symbol onwards; only the simplified roman numeral (“IV7”) leaves the ninth unspecified. In measure 3 the inner voice descends D4→D♭4 (13th→♭13) while the A3 (the third) is held on — an F7 that hardens as the measure unfolds, prepared by a chromatic acciaccatura (C♯4) at its head.

sections.label: Measure 4
sections.titre: IIImaj7, then the first arranger's gesture
sections.texte: B♭maj7 treats its major seventh (A) as a stable colour, exactly as in Satie (previous lesson). Then, absent from the most common changes: a rootless E7 (G♯3 = third, F♯3 = ninth, D = seventh), the tritone substitute for B♭7 (V7/VI). The bass travels B♭2-F3-E♭2-D3 across the whole measure — four distinct pitches that come to rest on D, never returning to the E♭.

sections.label: Measures 5-6
sections.titre: A Satie-like VImaj7, then the peak of tension
sections.texte: A close-voiced E♭maj9 (F3 = ninth, G3 = third, D4 = major seventh) prolongs the motionless colour. Measure 6 replaces the expected diatonic ii° (Am7♭5) with its dominantised version: a fully altered A7 — C♮5 held (♯9), F4 (♭13, after a chromatic F♯), E♭4 (♭5) inside the triplet, and G♯3→G♮3 in the bass, grinding against the seventh before falling into line with it. The peak of tension of the whole excerpt, in exactly its rightful place ahead of the principal dominant.

sections.label: Measure 7
sections.titre: V7, the 4-3 resolution crossed with the ♭9
sections.texte: Built in two stages: first a complete D9sus4 (D-G-A-C-E: fourth, fifth, seventh, ninth), then the suspension resolves (G3→F♯3, a 4-3 motion) at exactly the moment the melody sets down E♭4 — the ♭9 — held as a half note: resolution and fresh dissonance exchanged within one and the same gesture.

sections.label: Measures 8-10
sections.titre: Return, turnaround, and a truncated repeat
sections.texte: Measure 8 (Gm7→Gm6→Gm(♭6), three chords in succession) is a line cliché (F→E♮→E♭, 7th-6th-♭6th) over a static minor tonic. Measure 9 (G7(add ♭9), roman numeral “V7/IV”) sounds G-B-D-F-A♭ complete between the two hands, the secondary dominant that prepares the return of Cm7 while the melody launches the pickup motif again. Measure 10 reopens the loop: Cm7 with the 11th (F5) at the top of the voicing, an ascending arpeggiated triplet, and a bass that comes to rest on a chromatic B♮ — the excerpt is cut off before its target can reveal itself.

synthese.titre: Two substitutions, two different logics
synthese.texte: The E7 inserted in measure 4 ADDS a chord absent from the most common changes (a chromatic approach by tritone substitute). The A7 of measure 6 REPLACES a chord already there (the diatonic ii°, Am7♭5) with its dominantised version, on the same root. Two quite distinct reharmonisation techniques, brought together in this single chorus.

synthese.titre: Almost every chord is a secondary dominant
synthese.texte: V7/III, subV7/VI, V7/V, V7/IV: the descending sequence of “Autumn Leaves” strings together passing tonicisations rather than bare diatonic degrees — the very vocabulary of lesson 15.

synthese.titre: Dissonance as the default material
synthese.texte: After Bach (dissonance as contrapuntal event) and Satie (dissonance as motionless colour), this arrangement reveals a third regime: 9ths, 13ths and ♭9s are neither prepared nor resolved in the classical sense — they are the chord's norm, managed through degrees of alteration (13→♭13, sus4→♭9, fully altered) along a cycle of fifths that Bach would have recognised.

cours21.title: Analysis of Modern and Contemporary Composers
cours21.subtitle: Debussy, Ravel, Stravinsky, Messiaen, Satie, Beatles, Radiohead, Morricone — from impressionism to rock, how the 20th century reinvented harmony.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — 20th-century musical languages hold no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more composers to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep listening — modern harmony reveals itself through the ear!

narrative.composersHeading: 8 COMPOSERS — From Impressionism to Contemporary Rock
narrative.composersIntro: From Debussy breaking tonality through colour, to Radiohead fusing Messiaen with electronics — the 20th century multiplied harmonic languages. Click each card to explore the techniques, hear the progression and understand the reference work.
narrative.analyseHeading: TONAL · MODAL · BITONAL — Three ways of thinking about harmony
narrative.analyseIntro: Compare the progressions, listen to both versions and identify the style. The ear recognises before the brain — trust your first impression.
narrative.quizScoreMsg0: Perfect! The languages of the 20th century hold no more secrets.
narrative.quizScoreMsg1: Very good! A few composers to revisit.
narrative.quizScoreMsg2: Keep exploring — modern harmony reveals itself through listening.
narrative.maitreCardConcept: Chords as colours — freeing harmony from the dominant-tonic resolution
narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Debussy was expelled from the Paris Conservatoire several times for playing 'incorrect' chords. His teacher noted: 'He does as he pleases.' That was exactly his intention.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Debussy treats chords like colours on a canvas — a 9th chord need not resolve; it can float and create an atmosphere, like a brushstroke of impressionist paint.

conservatoire.intuition: A chord does not have to move in order to become an event — if it never changes again and is struck with accents that fall somewhere different each time, then rhythm alone takes charge of the entire discourse.

reference.badge: Stravinsky · on The Rite of Spring
reference.citation: I was the vessel through which Le Sacre passed.

voix: Two perfectly consonant chords (a triad, a dominant seventh) can be stacked at the smallest possible distance — a semitone — to create the most brutal collision in the whole polytonal vocabulary.

Once it has been set down, a polychord can remain completely motionless for several measures: it is then rhythm (accents that change place with every repetition) that produces the musical event, not harmony.
Dissonance has more than one role: it can be an isolated event, a drama, a suspension, a state, a vocabulary — or, as here, pure percussion.

repertoire.compositeur: After Igor Stravinsky, The Rite of Spring — The Augurs of Spring (1913)

pieges.erreur: Looking for harmonic development or resolution in the hammering of the Augurs chord
pieges.correction: There is none: the vertical sonority stays rigorously identical from the first blow to the last — only the rhythmic accents shift from one repetition to the next. The analysis must bear on rhythm, not hunt for a progression that does not exist.

pieges.erreur: Confusing this polychord with the Petrushka chord (Stravinsky, 1911) on the grounds that both superimpose two consonant objects
pieges.correction: The two sit at opposite extremes of adjacency: Petrushka stacks two triads a TRITONE apart (the maximum distance, no note rubbing against another), while the Augurs chord stacks a triad and a seventh chord a SEMITONE apart (the minimum distance, every note of the triad rubbing against a note of the seventh chord).

pieges.erreur: Analysing this teaching piece as a transcription of The Rite of Spring
pieges.correction: It is an entirely original piece, composed to illustrate the phenomenon — The Rite of Spring remains under copyright in France until 2042, and not one of its notes is reproduced here.

resume: The Augurs chord (Stravinsky, 1913) superimposes a major triad and a dominant seventh chord a semitone apart — the most brutal collision possible, since every note of the triad rubs directly against a note of the seventh chord.

Once it has been set down, the chord never changes again: the event is produced by rhythm (accents displaced at each repetition), not by harmony — dissonance treated as percussion rather than as tension.
