Compared with the Petrushka chord (two triads a tritone apart, 1911), the Augurs chord chooses the opposite extreme of adjacency — two answers from Stravinsky, two years apart, to the same question: what is to be done with tonal function?

analyseNarrative.tonalite: No single key — two consonant objects (a dominant seventh, a major triad) superimposed a semitone apart.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. No tempo indicated (demonstration piece); mm. 4-5 in eighth notes to depict the rhythmic hammering.
analyseNarrative.forme: A demonstration in six measures: the two objects separately, their collision, two measures of hammering with displaced accents, then the final held chord.

sections.label: Measures 1-2
sections.titre: The two objects, separate
sections.texte: E♭7 first: an utterly ordinary dominant seventh. Then F♭ major — spelled this way rather than “E major” so as to keep the same notational logic as the source that inspired this teaching piece — its immediate neighbour, a semitone higher. Taken separately, each of the two is entirely commonplace.

sections.label: Measure 3
sections.titre: The collision: the Augurs chord
sections.texte: The two objects sound together, each perfectly intact. But here, unlike a collision at the tritone (the Petrushka chord, where the two triads share no adjacent note), EVERY note of the upper triad is crushed a semitone away from a note of the lower seventh chord: the root of the triad against the root of the seventh chord, its third against the third of the seventh chord, its fifth against the fifth of the seventh chord. Three simultaneous frictions, at the smallest interval available.

sections.label: Measures 4-5
sections.titre: The hammering: harmony frozen, rhythm on the move
sections.texte: The chord does not change a single note for two whole measures of hammered eighth notes — but the accents do change place with every repetition. It is the complete reversal of ordinary harmonic writing: normally the chord moves over a stable rhythm; here it is the other way round. Dissonance is no longer a tension awaiting its resolution: it has become an object one strikes, exactly like a drum.

sections.label: Measure 6
sections.titre: The final held chord
sections.chiffrage: F♭ major + E♭7, under a fermata
sections.texte: The same chord, unchanged since measure 3, closes under a fermata. Nothing has been “resolved” — the object has simply stopped being struck.

synthese.titre: The sixth regime: dissonance as percussion
synthese.texte: A chord can be heard as an isolated event, as a drama that unfolds, as a tension suspended indefinitely, as a stable state one inhabits, or as the colour of a vocabulary — but there is a sixth regime, in which the vertical sonority no longer moves at all and RHYTHM alone produces the event. The Augurs chord never resolves: it is struck, with accents falling somewhere different each time, until the hammering itself becomes the subject.

synthese.titre: Two polychords, the two extremes of adjacency
synthese.texte: Compared with the Petrushka chord (two triads a tritone apart, the maximum distance between two centres), this one chooses the opposite extreme: two consonant objects pressed against each other at the semitone, the minimum distance. The result is more brutal, because every note of the upper triad rubs directly against a note of the seventh chord — the dissonance is no longer a mere neighbouring of systems, it is a crushing.

synthese.titre: A line of descent reaching all the way to rock
synthese.texte: Treating dissonance as an object to be struck rather than as a tension to be resolved became, long after 1913, a common principle of amplified music — the chord struck in a loop, with no progression, where it is rhythmic intensity that carries the discourse rather than harmonic succession.

cours20.title: Analysis of the Great Classical Composers
cours20.subtitle: Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Chopin, Liszt, Berlioz, Tchaikovsky, Rachmaninoff — the harmonic signatures that shaped Western music.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — the great masters hold no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more composers to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep exploring — each listen reveals new harmonic details!

narrative.compositeursIntro: Each composer develops a recognisable harmonic language. Click on each card to discover their techniques, listen to their signature progression and understand their reference work.
narrative.analyseIntro: Listen to the progressions, compare the versions and identify each composer's style. Ear-training analysis is the key to stylistic recognition.
narrative.quizPerfect: Perfect! You have mastered stylistic analysis.
narrative.quizGood: Very good! A few composers to review.
narrative.maitreCardConcept: Modulations by third & nascent romantic colours
narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Schubert composed over 600 lieder, several in a single day. He died at 31 without ever having conducted most of his major works in public.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Modulation by third — sliding from C major to A-flat major without a transition — creates a unique colour, like a sudden change of lighting on the same scene.

conservatoire.intuition: Harmony can stop representing a feeling in order to narrate an action: Berlioz interrupts a melody in mid-flight and replaces it with a fall of an octave — the refused resolution, pushed until it becomes a literal gesture.

reference.citation: I spent the night dreaming of death, with a frenzied enthusiasm.
reference.auteur: Hector Berlioz, on the genesis of the Symphonie fantastique

voix: One and the same melodic formula (here, a descending scale) can carry two opposite affects depending on its rhythmic context — the lament becomes a funeral march without a single note changing.
A physical interruption (a phrase cut off short, replaced by an abrupt leap) can function as a genuine narrative gesture — harmony no longer colours an emotion, it recounts a specific event.
A change of mode (minor to major) can be used as a stage direction rather than as a mere colour — here, the switch literally marks the passage from one scene to another.

repertoire.titre: Symphonie fantastique, 4th movement — March to the Scaffold (arr. string trio)

pieges.erreur: Looking for a complex or chromatic chord to explain the effect of the “blade” (m. 169)
pieges.correction: It is the opposite: the chord there is stripped to the extreme (a plain G, without a third), and the effect comes from a RHYTHMIC gesture — a fall of an octave synchronised between the outermost instruments — not from an unusual harmony.

pieges.erreur: Analysing theme 2 (m. 62, in B♭ major) as a Classical modulation prepared by a dominant
pieges.correction: There is no preparation: the relative major installs itself directly, by simple juxtaposition of contrasting blocks — the crowd's fanfare follows the funeral theme with no transition, by design.

pieges.erreur: Treating the final turn to the major (m. 170) as a merely decorative Picardy third
pieges.correction: Here the change of mode has an explicit NARRATIVE function (the crowd exulting after the execution) — the mode becomes a stage direction, not just a harmonic colour.

resume: A descending G minor scale (theme 1) takes up the old formula of the Baroque lament and turns it, by rhythmic context alone, into a funeral march — proof that musical meaning never resides in pitch alone.

The blade (m. 169) interrupts the idée fixe in mid-flight and replaces it with a fall of an octave synchronised in the two outermost instruments — the refused resolution pushed as far as the literal gesture.
The final switch to G major (m. 170) functions as a stage direction rather than a colour: harmony stops representing an affect in order to narrate an action, the crowd exulting.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: G minor from the start until the scene of the blade (m. 169) — with a long incursion into its relative major, B♭, for theme 2 — then a final and definitive switch to G MAJOR for the last nine measures.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Tempo di marcia (quarter note = 144), with a marked slowing (rit., 144→120) at measure 165, an “a tempo” at 170, then a last rit. in the very final measures up to the closing fermata.
analyseNarrative.forme: Introduction (m. 1-16) — theme 1, the march-lament (m. 17-61) — theme 2, the fanfare in B♭ (m. 62-76) — development, alternations and combinations (m. 77-163) — the idée fixe, one last time (m. 164-168) — the blade (m. 169) — triumphal G major up to the closing fermata (m. 170-178).

sections.label: Measures 1-16
sections.titre: Introduction: the march approaches, pianissimo
sections.texte: Everything begins with a simple held minor third, pianissimo, staccato: G in the viola and the violin, B♭ in the viola, doubled at the octave in the cello — no fifth yet, no real harmony yet, just a colour that settles in and repeats itself, like a footstep approaching from far off.

sections.label: Measures 17-61
sections.titre: Theme 1: the lament-scale become a march
sections.texte: Entrusted to the low strings alone, a descending scale runs through nearly two octaves of natural G minor — exactly the kind of line that, across centuries of music, has carried mourning and complaint (Purcell's descending tetrachord, the chromatic bass of so many Baroque laments). Here the same melodic formula changes meaning without changing a single note: the dotted rhythm, the marching gait turn it into a funeral cortège. That is where Berlioz's irony lies — parading the condemned man to the very formula of mourning.

sections.label: Measures 62-76
sections.titre: Theme 2: the fanfare in B♭, the crowd
sections.texte: With no preparatory dominant, the music tips into its relative major for a blazing fanfare — the cynical counterpart of the funeral theme that precedes it: the crowd coming to watch the spectacle. The contrast is total, but the kinship remains audible: the two themes share the same key signature, the same basic material; only the colour (mode, register, rhythm) sets them against each other.

sections.label: Measures 77-163
sections.titre: Development: alternations, pizzicati, a remembered horn call
sections.chiffrage: (combinations of the two themes, pizz./arco in bursts)
sections.texte: The two themes cross, relieve one another, interrupt one another — a great play of alternation between pizzicato and arco that mimes the mechanics of the cortège on the march. At the heart of this development, a brief horn call (twice, note for note identical): in the original orchestra this motive is given to distant horns — here the string trio preserves its echo, a discreet nod to the large forces from which this arrangement is drawn.

sections.label: Measures 164-169
sections.titre: The idée fixe, one last time — then the blade
sections.texte: Dolce assai e appassionato: in the violin, the melody of the beloved rises one final time, G-A-B♭-C-D climbing little by little towards B♮ and then C6 — a tender thought, almost suspended outside time. Then, at measure 165, nothing: the only entirely silent measure in the whole piece, a rit. that is not merely a slowing but a real severing of the discourse. And at measure 169, the execution: the phrase is cut off in mid-flight, replaced by a dry fall of one octave, doubled in the two outermost instruments (violin and cello) at exactly the same instant — the blade, then the head falling.

sections.label: Measures 170-178
sections.titre: Triumphal G major: the hammered third, up to the fermata
sections.texte: A tempo, the Picardy third settles in and no longer budges: B natural hammered in ostinato for seven measures, then fanfare arpeggios — the major mode as pure stagecraft, the crowd exulting while the curtain falls. The piece ends on a G major chord spread across nearly four octaves, under a fermata.

synthese.titre: The guillotined resolution
synthese.texte: The device of “the refused resolution” runs through this corpus from Bach (an evaded seventh) and Beethoven (a deceptive cadence) all the way to Wagner (a tension never untied): Berlioz, in 1830, gives the most literal version of it imaginable — a melodic phrase cut off short, in mid-flight, replaced by a physical fall of one octave. The shift from minor to major that follows is no longer merely a colour: it is a STAGE DIRECTION, harmony ceasing to represent an affect in order to narrate an action.

synthese.titre: An old formula, a new meaning
synthese.texte: The descending scale of theme 1 is, note for note, the same gesture as the lament tetrachords that have run through this corpus since the seventeenth century — only the context (the march tempo, the dotted rhythm) makes it a funeral cortège rather than an intimate complaint. The same melodic formula, two opposite affects: proof that meaning in music never resides in pitch alone.

synthese.titre: 1830, the missing decade
synthese.texte: This piece fills a gap in the corpus's genealogy of harmonic dramaturgy, between Beethoven (1808) and Chopin (1839): Haydn makes the shared code laugh (1791), Beethoven dramatises it (1798-1808), Berlioz NARRATIVISES it (1830, programme music), Chopin internalises it (1839), Wagner suspends it indefinitely (1859). Five stations, over five pieces, of a single thread that continues as far as Morricone within this same corpus.

cours19.title: Introduction to Orchestration
cours19.subtitle: The 4 instrument families, their ranges and roles — doublings, balance, registers and SATB distribution in the orchestra.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — orchestration holds no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few instrument families still to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep exploring the instrument families — the ear learns with practice!

narrative.instrIntro: The symphony orchestra is organized into 4 major families. Each family has its own acoustic characteristics, ranges, and typical roles. Knowing these characteristics is the starting point for any orchestral writing.
narrative.instrInfoBox: Golden rule: the lower you go, the more you must space the voices. A C2–E2 chord sounds muddy; C2–G2–C3 sounds clear. In the upper register, thirds and seconds are perfectly readable. This rule guides the distribution of all orchestral and piano voices.
narrative.ecritureIntro: Orchestration is the art of assigning musical voices to instruments according to their characteristics. Five principles guide the writing: doubling, dynamic balance, register management, SATB distribution, and specific constraints for piano and chamber music.
narrative.ecritureWarnBox: Classic pitfalls: (1) Brass too loud — they cover the strings and woodwinds. (2) Low register too tight — muddy sound. (3) Uncovered range — harmonic gap. (4) Piano doubled in unison with strings — the timbres don't blend. Ravel consistently avoids these pitfalls: every note, every instrument, in its rightful place.
narrative.maitreAnecdote: In 1922, Sergei Diaghilev asked Ravel to orchestrate Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition for the Ballets Russes. Ravel spent months choosing each instrument for each tableau. When a colleague asked how he decided, he replied: 'I invent nothing. I hear the colour first — the timbre of the right instrument — and then I write the note.'
narrative.maitreLesson: Orchestration is not decoration: it is an essential part of composition. Before writing for an instrument, ask yourself: in which register does it sound best? What is its natural colour? How does it interact with the others? The ideal instrument played in its ideal register produces a beauty no other can replicate.
narrative.famCordesDesc: The backbone of the orchestra. Strings play tutti (the whole ensemble) or as separate sections. Their homogeneity of timbre allows blends and progressive crescendos impossible with other families.
narrative.famCordesI3Role: Harmonic foundation, reinforcement of the bass
narrative.famBoisDesc: Woodwinds bring colour and individuality. Each instrument has such a distinct timbre that they are heard even when doubled by strings. They provide intermediate doublings, lyrical solos, and counterpoint.
narrative.famBoisI0Timbre: Airy, luminous, fast in the upper register
narrative.famBoisI2Role: Middle harmony, solos, very versatile role
narrative.famBoisI3Timbre: Low, dark, slightly comic in the upper register
narrative.famBoisI3Role: Bass of the woodwinds, counterpoint, low doubling
narrative.famCuivresDesc: Brass are the most powerful instruments in the orchestra. Used sparingly at soft dynamics, they blend into the texture; at forte, they dominate everything. Ravel and Brahms master the art of using them at full power without masking the strings.
narrative.famCuivresI0Role: Link between woodwinds and brass, middle harmony, lyrical solos
narrative.famCuivresI1Range: F#3 – C6  (sounds as written or a tone lower)
narrative.famCuivresI1Timbre: Brilliant, bright, fanfare, cutting in the upper register
narrative.famCuivresI2Timbre: Powerful, deep, majestic — only glissando possible
narrative.famCuivresI2Role: Low harmony, brass chorals, bass of the brass
narrative.famCuivresI3Role: Low foundation of the brass, harmonic bass
narrative.famPercussionsDesc: Percussion structures the rhythm, underlines climaxes, and adds colour. Pitched instruments (timpani, xylophone) play precise pitches; unpitched instruments (snare drum, cymbals) add timbre and colour.
narrative.famPercussionsI0Range: Pitched — playing range C2 to A3
narrative.famPercussionsI0Timbre: Solemn, rolling, thunderous depending on stroke
narrative.famPianoDesc: The piano is a complete harmonic instrument — it can play melody, harmony, and bass simultaneously. In the orchestra, it is often used as a soloist or a percussive colour. The guitar is more common in chamber ensembles and jazz.
narrative.famPianoI0Role: Autonomous or solo instrument, percussive colour in the orchestra
narrative.prDoubluresDesc: Doubling an instrument means giving it the same melodic or harmonic line — in unison or at the octave. Doubling reinforces the sound without changing its function.
narrative.prDoubluresRule: Strings + Woodwinds → soft blend, rounded sound. Strings + Brass → power and brilliance. Avoid doubling fortissimo brass with woodwinds: the brass will cover them.
narrative.prDoubluresExample: Beethoven 5th: the G–G–G–Eb motif is played by strings and woodwinds together from bar 1 — unison doubling for maximum impact.
narrative.prEquilibreDesc: Balance between families is one of the major challenges of orchestration. A fortissimo brass section can cover 30 violins playing forte. Dynamic proportions must be chosen with care.
narrative.prEquilibreRule: Brass fortissimo: woodwinds and strings disappear. For strings to be heard at forte, brass should play mezzo-forte. The piano in the orchestra is often in opposition or as a soloist, rarely doubling.
narrative.prEquilibreExample: Ravel's Boléro: the same melody and harmony are repeated 18 times with progressively denser orchestration — a model of cumulative balance.
narrative.prRegistresDesc: The orchestra covers a spectrum from C0 (bass/low tuba) to C8 (piccolo/high violin). The orchestrator's role is to fill this spectrum harmonically without creating 'gaps' or 'overcrowding'.
narrative.prRegistresRule: Avoid gaps: if the tenor jumps to soprano without a middle voice, the sound seems hollow. Avoid overcrowding: too many notes in the same register creates muddy sound. Space the voices: the lower the voices, the more they must be spaced.
narrative.prRegistresExample: Fundamental rule: low intervals should be wide (fifths, octaves) and high ones can be narrow (thirds, seconds). A C major triad: in the bass = C2–G2–C3; in the treble = C4–E4–G4.
narrative.prSatbDesc: The distribution of counterpoint voices (Soprano/Alto/Tenor/Bass) maps naturally onto orchestral families according to their respective ranges.
narrative.prSatbRule: Soprano (S) → Violin I, Flute, Oboe, Trumpet. Alto (A) → Violin II, Viola, Clarinet, Horn. Tenor (T) → Cello, Trombone, Bassoon. Bass (B) → Double bass, Tuba, low Bassoon.
narrative.prSatbExample: A Bach chorale transcribed for orchestra: bass in cellos/double basses, tenor in violas/low horns, alto in violins II/clarinets, soprano in violins I/oboes.
narrative.prPianoDesc: Pianistic writing follows specific constraints related to the two hands, the sustain pedal, and the instrument's ideal range.
narrative.prPianoRule: Right hand: melody + upper harmony (register C4–C6). Left hand: bass + accompaniment (register A0–C4). Sustain pedal: prolongs and connects harmonies. Avoid too many notes in the low register (muddy sound) and too many in the high register (shrill).
narrative.prPianoExample: Chopin Nocturne: lyrical melody in the right hand (register E4–G5), wide arpeggios in the left hand (register C2–G3), sustain pedal held throughout the bar.
narrative.exRavelDesc: The same snare-drum rhythmic ostinato, the same melody in C major, the same harmony — repeated 18 times with progressively denser orchestration. Each repetition adds instruments or changes combinations. A real-time study in orchestration.
narrative.exDebussyName: Debussy — Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune (1894)
narrative.exDebussyDesc: Orchestral impressionism at its finest: solo flute, harp, muted strings, stopped horns, woodwinds in half-tints. Each instrument in its most poetic register. No loud brass — everything is suggestion and colour.
narrative.exBeethovenDesc: A model of economy of means: a 4-note motif distributed across all families. The orchestration follows the intensity of the discourse — strings + woodwinds at p, tutti fortissimo at key moments. Every instrument in its rightful place.

conservatoire.intuition: A single harmony held for 84 measures, a single displacement, a single accident — Boléro pushes harmonic immobility to its breaking point, and demonstrates that all the tension of a work can be lodged somewhere other than in its chords.

reference.citation: It is orchestration without music.
reference.auteur: Maurice Ravel (as reported by his biographers)

voix: A pedal can hold up an entire work: here the bass never leaves C and G for 84 consecutive measures — all the tension one expects from harmony is delegated to the crescendo and to the thickening of the texture.

A modulation with neither preparation nor pivot (here, an ascending major third, C → E) remains legible to the ear even without any transitional chord — the displacement alone is enough to constitute an event, precisely because nothing else has moved before it.

A foreign note obstinately repeated (not a line that progresses) can create a tension as strong as any real melodic development — the “grating” of the return comes from the repetition of a single rough edge, not from its evolution.

pieges.erreur: Looking for a complex harmonic progression in the first 84 measures of Boléro
pieges.correction: There is none: the left hand plays nothing but C and G from the beginning to the end of this section, verified measure by measure without exception. The whole musical construction comes from the crescendo and the orchestration, not from the harmony.

pieges.erreur: Believing that the “chromatic line” announced at the return (m. 93-96) is a melodic line progressing step by step
pieges.correction: Note-by-note verification: these four measures repeat EXACTLY the same figure, with a single foreign note (A♭) repeated identically each time — this is not a line that advances, but a going-over. The real line that descends step by step appears only in the following measure, in the chord of the crash itself.

pieges.erreur: Analysing the crash chord (m. 97) as a seventh or altered ninth chord from the usual tonal vocabulary
pieges.correction: It is a non-functional polychord: two incompatible stacks (C-F and A♭-B-D♭) slammed down together, which cannot be reduced to a single figurable chord within the tonal system — hence the figuring “?”, not an empty box but a genuine analytical category.

resume: Boléro (Ravel, 1928) holds 84 measures over a single C-G pedal — the limiting case of immobile harmony: all the tension of the work comes from the crescendo and the texture, not from the chords.

The work's one modulation (C → E, m. 85-92) is a displacement by a major third with neither preparation nor pivot — the interval that divides the octave into three equal parts, owing nothing to the logic of fifths.

The only real harmonic disorder in the work is its last loud chord (m. 97): a non-functional polychord (C-F against A♭-B-D♭) — in a piece without harmonic tension, dissonance no longer resolves, it breaks.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C major from first bar to last — a single genuine tonicisation, in E major (m. 85-92), never confirmed by a cadence and never meant to last.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 3/4. Tempo di bolero, moderato assai (quarter note = 72). pp at the outset, the ostinato boléro rhythm in the right hand from the very first measure.
analyseNarrative.forme: One immense crescendo over a pedal (m. 1-84, 86% of the piece), a single tonicisation in E (m. 85-92), a return that grates (m. 93-96), a crash (m. 97) and a bare collapse (m. 98).

sections.label: Measures 1-84
sections.titre: The C-G pedal: one chord for 84 measures
sections.texte: Verified measure by measure, the left hand never leaves C and G — the fifth beaten out in boléro rhythm, without a single exception, for 84 consecutive measures. The work's two themes (one diatonic, the other more highly coloured) alternate above it, but both rest on exactly the same pedal: all the tension of this section comes neither from a chord nor from a cadence, but from the crescendo and from the accumulation of voices progressively added to the texture.

sections.label: Measures 85-92
sections.titre: E major: the work's one harmonic event
sections.chiffrage: III (E, with an internal I-...-V cycle on E-B)
sections.texte: After 84 immobile measures, an abrupt displacement by an ascending major third, with neither preparation nor pivot: C becomes E. Within this new colour, however, the left hand is no longer the frozen drone of the preceding pedal: each measure pulses in itself, from E (beat 1) towards B (beat 3), a miniature tonic-dominant cycle. Then, without anything in the text of the score announcing it, this “dominant” begins to slide from one measure to the next — B, then F♯-B, then G — quietly leading the ear back towards C even before the return has been consummated.

sections.label: Measures 93-96
sections.titre: The return that grates: a repeated note, not a line that progresses
sections.texte: The return to C is clear-cut. But what settles in there is not a melodic line that advances: it is EXACTLY the same figure, repeated four times identically — the C-G pedal, then a single isolated A♭ in the middle of the measure, then G. This foreign note (the lowered sixth degree, borrowed from the minor mode) never moves: it comes back, obsessively, in the same place, in the same measures, without ever resolving or developing. It is this identical repetition of a rough edge that “grates” — not a trajectory, a going-over.

sections.label: Measure 97
sections.titre: The crash: the piece's only real harmonic disorder
sections.chiffrage: C-F (right hand) against A♭-B-D♭ (left hand) — a polychord
sections.texte: After 96 measures of an utterly simple syntax, the one moment where the writing loses all functional logic: two incompatible stacks slammed down together, C-F on one side, A♭-B-D♭ on the other — five pitch classes that form no identifiable chord in the tonal vocabulary. It is only at this instant, and nowhere before, that a real line descending step by step appears: A♭-G-F-E♭-D♭ in the right hand, right through to the end of the measure.

sections.label: Measure 98
sections.titre: Final collapse: bare C-G
sections.texte: After the din, nothing but an open fifth, C-G — the same fifth that had held the whole piece up since its first measure, but alone now, stripped of everything that had accumulated above it for 97 measures. The piece does not close with a cadence: it stops, dead, on the very interval that had kept it standing.

synthese.titre: The limiting case of immobile harmony
synthese.texte: This piece takes to an industrial scale what the corpus has already encountered on a smaller one (Satie's eight-measure pedal, the sixty-four measures of Voiles): 86% of the work rests on one and the same function. All the tension expected of tonal harmony is here delegated elsewhere — to the crescendo, to the thickness of the texture, to the accumulation of voices — while the chord itself does not move.

synthese.titre: The major third, a displacement that owes nothing to the fifths
synthese.texte: The piece's only real modulation (C → E) passes through no pivot chord and no preparatory dominant: it is a displacement by a major third, the very interval that divides the octave into three equal parts — the one in Coltrane's cycle in Giant Steps, the one in the augmented triad of Voiles. When an entire work rests on a single tension, the displacement it allows itself has no reason to follow the logic of fifths.

synthese.titre: A repeated note rather than a line: the true nature of the “grating”
synthese.texte: The most instructive passage in the piece is not where you would expect it: what “grates” at measures 93-96 is not a chromatic line that advances, but a single foreign note, obstinately repeated identically. The real line that progresses step by step appears only a measure later, INSIDE the crash itself — a reminder that one must always check what the notes actually play, not merely what a structural marker announces.

cours18.title: Motivic Development
cours18.subtitle: The 5 elements of a motif, the repetition paradox, and the 4 families of techniques — from harmony (least radical) to rhythm (most radical).

quiz.perfect: Excellent — motivic development holds no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more techniques to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep listening to the transformations — the ear learns with practice!

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: In 1808, Beethoven premiered his 5th Symphony. The opening motif — G–G–G–E♭, just four notes — generates twenty minutes of music. A student asked how he could build so much from so little. Beethoven replied: “That is exactly the right question. Richness lies not in the quantity of material — it lies in the depth with which you develop it.”
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Before composing, ask yourself: is my opening motif short enough to be memorable? Distinctive enough to be recognisable? Flexible enough to be transformed? A motif that answers yes to all three can generate a symphony. One that is too complex is hard to develop; too simple, it exhausts itself quickly.
narrative.motifP1: The motif is the smallest distinct and immediately recognisable musical unit. It serves as the guiding thread of musical discourse: repeated and transformed, it gives coherence and direction to a phrase, a movement, or an entire work. Unlike support music (which accompanies an external action), discourse music develops its own ideas autonomously.
narrative.motifDemoTitle: The most famous motif: Beethoven's 5th Symphony
narrative.motifDemoDesc: Just 4 notes — 3 repeated + a descending minor third. This motif is fragmented, transposed, augmented and liquidated across all 4 movements of the symphony: 20 minutes of music from a 4-note cell.
narrative.motifH3Elements: The 5 constituent elements of a motif
narrative.elem1Desc: The characteristic melodic leaps — the distinctive melodic identity (third, fifth, tritone). Beethoven's motif: a descending minor third G→E♭.
narrative.elem2Desc: The distinctive rhythmic pattern — often more identifiable than the melody. Three short notes + one long (ta-ta-ta-TAA) in Beethoven.
narrative.elem3Desc: The chords that support and colour the motif — determining whether the expression feels tense, resolved, or ambiguous.
narrative.elem4Desc: The texture surrounding the motif: arpeggios, block chords, independent bass line, counterpoint.
narrative.elem5Desc: Nuance, articulation, attack — the physical expressive character. Forte or piano, legato or staccato.
narrative.motifWarnBox: The paradox of repetition: repetition is necessary — without it, the listener recognises nothing and the musical discourse loses all coherence. But it is dangerous if too pure: repeating identically more than twice quickly breeds monotony. The solution is to repeat while transforming — maintain recognition while renewing interest.
narrative.motifH3Rhetorique: The motif as character: 3 rhetorical stages
narrative.step1Desc: Establish the motif's identity — present it clearly and unambiguously.
narrative.step2Desc: Anchor the motif in the listener's ear — repeat (transformed) to confirm the identity.
narrative.step3Desc: Transform, develop, combine — the motif travels and matures.
narrative.ex1Desc: Just four notes. Beethoven fragments, transposes, augments and liquidates this motif throughout all four movements. Twenty minutes of symphony from a four-note cell.
narrative.ex2Motif: Motif associated with a character or idea
narrative.ex2Desc: Wagner assigns a motif to each character (Siegfried's sword, the curse of the Gold). The motif returns transformed according to the dramatic state — a motif of glory becomes sinister through harmonic change.
narrative.ex3Desc: Williams inherits directly from Wagner: each character or concept has its leitmotif. The Force theme is transformed into a military march for Darth Vader — same contour, radically different harmonic context.
narrative.motifInfoBox: The motif is not an ornament — it is the seed of all musical thought. Before composing a phrase, ask yourself: is my core idea distinctive enough to be recognisable? Flexible enough to be transformed in 10 different ways? A good idea generates a phrase; an excellent idea generates a symphony.
narrative.techP1: Development techniques are organised into 4 families, ranked from least to most radical. We begin by transforming the context (harmony, dynamics) before touching the melody, and we modify rhythm last — as it is often the most identifying element of the motif.
narrative.famAOrder: First — the least radical changes. The melodic and rhythmic identity of the motif remains intact.
narrative.famADesc: Transforming the harmonic context or the accompanying texture. The motif remains fully recognisable because its melody and rhythm are preserved — only the 'colour' changes.
narrative.famASub1Detail: Replace I with VI (diatonic substitution), or V7 with its tritone substitute. Same melody, different harmonic colour.
narrative.famASub2Detail: Transform the bass into independent counterpoint — parallel thirds or sixths, or contrary motion to the melody.
narrative.famASub3Detail: Break chords into successive ascending or descending notes. Transforms the texture without touching the melodic motif.
narrative.famASub4Detail: Add an independent voice that answers or imitates the motif. Enriches polyphonic density.
narrative.famBOrder: Second — expressive changes without altering notes or rhythm.
narrative.famBDesc: Modifying expressive parameters: dynamics, articulation, register, timbre. The motif keeps its structure intact — only its 'energy' or 'costume' changes.
narrative.famBSub1Detail: Forte → piano, crescendo, decrescendo. Same melody, radically different dramatic intensity contrast.
narrative.famBSub2Detail: Legato → staccato, accents on unexpected beats. Changes the character without touching pitches or durations.
narrative.famBSub3Detail: Transpose by an octave: going up brings brightness and urgency; going down creates gravity and depth.
narrative.famBSub4Detail: Change the instrument or register: same motif in the strings, then brass, then tutti — entirely different effects.
narrative.famCOrder: Third — the pitches change, but the rhythm often remains recognisable.
narrative.famCDesc: Modifying the melodic contour of the motif while often maintaining its rhythmic structure. The ear recognises the motif by its rhythm even when pitches change significantly.
narrative.famCSub1Detail: Each interval is inverted: an ascending third becomes a descending third. G–G–G–E♭ becomes G–G–G–B♭.
narrative.famCSub2Detail: The motif is played backwards — from the last note to the first. E♭–G–G–G (retrograde of Beethoven's motif).
narrative.famCSub3Detail: Insert passing notes, or remove a note from the motif. The contour remains recognisable, lightened or enriched.
narrative.famCSub4Detail: Pitches shift according to the scale (harmonic sequence) but the rhythmic pattern remains identical.
narrative.famDOrder: Last — the most radical changes. The motif may become unrecognisable.
narrative.famDDesc: Modifying note durations or metric structure. Rhythmic alterations are the most transformative: rhythm is often the most distinctive feature of a motif — to touch it is to risk it.
narrative.famDSub1Detail: Double (or triple) the duration of each note. The motif slows down, takes on a solemn grandeur — Beethoven uses this in sonata developments.
narrative.famDSub2Detail: Divide the duration of each note. The motif speeds up, becomes nervous or urgent — liquidation effect at the end of a phrase.
narrative.famDSub3Detail: Moving from 4/4 to 3/4 (or vice versa). The same motif in a different metre creates a feeling of imbalance or lightness.
narrative.famDSub4Detail: Transform syncopations into strong beats (regularisation) or strong beats into syncopations (deregulation). Changes rhythmic energy without touching pitches.
narrative.techArpegeFormula: C – E – G – C  (ascending broken chord)
narrative.techArpegeDesc: Accompanying with arpeggios transforms the texture without touching the melodic motif.
narrative.techContrepointDesc: Two voices in contrary motion — the bass ascends while the upper voice descends.
narrative.techTipBox: Combinations: the 4 families combine freely. A motif can simultaneously receive a harmonic substitution (A), be played pianissimo (B), and be slightly transposed (C). Combinations create the richest transformations — this is exactly what Beethoven does in his great developments.

conservatoire.intuition: An entire 36-measure strophe, played again almost identically — and checking it note by note shows that “almost” is exactly the right word: even the strictest repetition always lets a few minute discrepancies through, to anyone who knows how to look for them.

reference.citation: I admired its severity of style and the profound logic that creates an inner connection between all the motifs.
reference.auteur: Jean Sibelius, as reported by Karl Ekman

voix: Repeating material identically is never entirely neutral: the reprise of a large section can allow itself minute redistributions (a changed voicing, a substituted melodic note) that go unnoticed by the ear without ever amounting to an absolute copy-and-paste.
One and the same melodic cell (here, a descending tetrachord) can be developed by changing only its harmonic clothing — the tetrachord stays, the chords that accompany it change.
The technique of motivic development is not confined to a short motive: it can be applied on the scale of an entire strophe, including when that strophe is for the most part repeated without change.

pieges.erreur: Believing that a large-scale reprise (an entire section played again) is necessarily a 100% copy-and-paste
pieges.correction: Checking this piece note by note shows that 30 of the 36 measures of the reprise are strictly identical — but 6 are not (a redistributed voicing at the entry, 3 isolated melodic substitutions, and the closing clausula, which varies explicitly). Large-scale repetition almost always lets small discrepancies through.

pieges.erreur: Looking for a real modulation in this piece's unusual harmonic colours (♭13, Andalusian tetrachord)
pieges.correction: The piece stays in A minor from first bar to last — the Aeolian ♭13 on the V7 and the Phrygian tetrachord of section B are COLOURS laid over the same tonic, not modulations to another key.

pieges.erreur: Analysing the descent ♭VII7-♭VI∆7-V7-i as a succession of chords with no connection between them
pieges.correction: These four chords harmonise one and the same fixed melodic line (the Phrygian tetrachord A-G-F-E) — each chord is at the service of that line, not a functional progression independent of it.

resume: Motivic development can be applied on the scale of an entire strophe: this Sibelius étude repeats a 36-measure strophe almost identically, but not entirely — 6 measures out of 36 carry minute discrepancies, including the closing clausula, which varies explicitly.

One and the same fixed melodic line (here, a descending Phrygian tetrachord) can be developed by changing only its harmonic clothing: the tetrachord stays, the chords that accompany it (♭VII7-♭VI∆7-V7-i) are new.
The paradox of repetition: repeating identically and transforming a minute detail can produce, to the ear, the impression of one and the same thing.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: A minor from first bar to last — never a real modulation, only colours (Aeolian ♭13, Andalusian tetrachord) laid over the same tonic.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 2/4. Leggiero, ♩=60, moto perpetuo (unbroken arpeggios from first bar to last).
analyseNarrative.forme: A 36-measure strophe in three sections (A m. 1-16, B m. 17-28, A' m. 29-36) played twice in full (m. 37-72 = m. 1-36), with a varied closing clausula.

sections.label: Measures 1-16
sections.titre: A: the textbook i-V alternation — and the Aeolian ♭13 from the outset
sections.chiffrage: i | V7♭13 | ... iv (pedal) ... III∆7 6/4 ... | (chromatic neighbours) | V (closed period)
sections.texte: A textbook period built on the simplest tonic-dominant polarity — but from the second measure onwards the V7 carries a C natural that is anything but diatonic: the minor sixth of the Aeolian mode (♭13), placed there from the outset without any modulation calling for it. The detour passes through a iv over an A pedal, then a III∆7 in 6/4 that brushes against the relative major without ever establishing it, before chromatic neighbours (D♯, F♯) tighten the tension onto V. The period closes, then repeats note for note.

sections.label: Measures 17-28
sections.titre: B: the Andalusian descent and the ascending chain
sections.chiffrage: ♭VII7 – ♭VI∆7 – V7 – i | ♭VII7 → V7 (ascending chain, cresc.) → V (climax, ff)
sections.texte: The heart of the piece, and a descent with nothing Classical left about it: the Phrygian tetrachord A-G-F-E, harmonised in colour sevenths (G7-F∆7-E7-Am) — the same gesture as Purcell's lament (course 38), but in a diatonic, dancing version, with the harmonic clothing of the early twentieth century. Then the reverse: an ascending chain of dominants (G7 → A7 → B7, in crescendo) hoists the line up to a fortissimo climax on V, where the high note is balanced by its chromatic neighbour — the ♭6→5 already encountered elsewhere in this corpus, promoted here to the status of a summit figure.

sections.label: Measures 29-36
sections.titre: A': the Aeolian dominant in full
sections.texte: The darkened reprise opens on the most saturated chord in the whole piece: a V7 carrying its minor ninth and its minor thirteenth SIMULTANEOUSLY — the Aeolian dominant complete, the same aggregate as Beethoven's Grave or Chopin's cadences, here a mere passing colour, pianissimo. A chromatic descent in the bass closes the strophe on the tonic.

sections.label: Measures 37-69
sections.titre: The great reprise: almost identical
sections.texte: The whole 36-measure strophe returns, and the vast majority of it is a note-for-note replica (30 of the 36 measures, checked one by one) — but not absolutely all of it: the reprise opens on a slightly redistributed left-hand voicing (a gesture of relaunch), and three isolated measures each carry a single different melodic note. The repetition is therefore not a simple copy-and-paste: it is a device that allows itself minute discrepancies, invisible unless you hunt them down one at a time — the very paradox of repetition in music, where repeating identically and transforming one tiny detail can produce, to the ear, a rigorously similar impression.

sections.label: Measures 70-72
sections.titre: The closing clausula: poco rit., the minor owned to the end
sections.texte: The only variation announced in advance: the very end. A poco rit. slows the moto perpetuo for the first time in the piece, and the strophe ends on the lowest note of the whole work (A1) — an A minor chord that keeps its minor third right to the end, with no Picardy third: the modal colour of the piece is owned through to the very last sonority.

synthese.titre: The paradox of repetition, on the scale of the whole form
synthese.texte: This étude pushes to the extreme what the course explores at the scale of the motive: here it is an ENTIRE 36-measure strophe that is repeated — and note-by-note checking reveals that the repetition is never quite total (30 measures out of 36 strictly identical, but a slightly redistributed reprise and 3 isolated melodic substitutions). Repeating identically and transforming a minute detail can produce, to the ear, the impression of one and the same thing: musical material can repeat itself without ever being a simple copy-and-paste.

synthese.titre: New vocabulary on an old syntax
synthese.texte: The systematic Aeolian ♭13 and the descent in colour sevenths (G7-F∆7-E7-i) belong to the harmonic vocabulary of the early twentieth century — but the form that carries them (closed period, clear-cut cadences, i-V alternation) retains a wholly Classical clarity. The vocabulary changes; the formal grammar does not budge.

synthese.titre: Corpus link: the Andalusian descent and Purcell's lament
synthese.texte: The Phrygian tetrachord harmonised in sevenths (♭VII7-♭VI∆7-V7-i) of section B takes up, in entirely different clothing, the same principle as the descending chromatic tetrachord of the ground in Dido's Lament (course 38, 1689): a fixed, ancient melodic line, rediscovered as a harmonic grid at very nearly every major period in the history of tonality.

cours17.title: Musical Phrase and Form
cours17.subtitle: Motif, 4-step development, repetition techniques, antecedent-consequent period and major musical forms.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — musical phrase and form hold no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few forms still to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep listening to the examples — the ear learns to recognise forms with practice!

narrative.phraseIntro: The musical phrase is the basic unit of musical discourse. It rests on a motif — the smallest distinctive musical element — which is repeated and transformed in 4 typical steps. Unlike support music (which accompanies an action), discourse music develops its own ideas autonomously.
narrative.beethovenBoxDesc: Just 4 notes — and yet the seed of an entire symphony. This motif is fragmented, transposed, augmented, and liquidated throughout all 4 movements.
narrative.stepsTitle: The 4 steps of a phrase (8 bars)
narrative.step1Desc: Presentation of the main motif — the statement of the musical subject.
narrative.step2Desc: Strict or transformed — anchors the motif in the listener's ear.
narrative.step3Desc: Fragmentation and liquidation — the harmonic rhythm accelerates.
narrative.step4Desc: Conclusive harmonic resolution (V for half-cadence, I for perfect cadence).
narrative.liquidationBox: Liquidation (Schoenberg's term): at the end of a phrase (step 3), the motif progressively loses its distinctive characteristics. First the rhythm is retained, then just the contour, then almost nothing — the phrase dissolves into the cadence. A highly expressive rhetorical device for 'conclusion'.
narrative.techStricteDesc: The motif is repeated identically — same pitches, same rhythm. The most direct technique: the listener recognizes the motif unambiguously. Used only once before varying.
narrative.techTransfoDesc: The motif is transposed to another pitch while retaining its rhythmic contour. The rhythmic identity maintains coherence; the new pitch brings variety.
narrative.techMarcheDesc: The motif repeats at successive scale degrees (tonal sequence) or by strict transposition (real sequence). Schoenberg carefully distinguishes the two types: the tonal sequence stays diatonic, the real sequence may leave the scale.
narrative.techComplementaireDesc: A second motif answers the first and completes the rhythmic or melodic space. Together, the two motifs form the complete phrase — each is incomplete without the other.
narrative.techHarmoniqueDesc: The melodic contour is preserved but the chords underneath change, altering the harmonic colour. The melody is recognizable; the harmony renews the expression.
narrative.warnBox: Key point: repetition must be varied — repeating identically more than twice creates monotony. The art is to maintain recognition of the motif (coherence) while renewing it (variety). Beethoven never repeats the same motif in exactly the same way twice in a row.
narrative.periodeTitle: The period and the large forms
narrative.periodeIntro: The period is a structure of two phrases: the antecedent asks a question (weak cadence on V), the consequent provides the answer (strong cadence on I). The large forms organize these periods into contrasting sections to build a musical discourse on a larger scale.
narrative.antecedentDesc: The half-cadence on V leaves the phrase 'open' — the ear awaits a resolution.
narrative.consequentDesc: The perfect cadence on I resolves the tension — the 'answer' is given, the period is complete.
narrative.periodCompleteBtn: ▶ Listen to the complete period (antecedent + consequent)
narrative.formeAbaDesc: Section A (main), contrasting section B (new key or mode), return of A. The symmetry creates balance and satisfaction: we depart, we return.
narrative.formeAbaExamples: Chopin Nocturnes, opera arias (aria da capo)
narrative.formeAABADesc: Section A (8 bars) repeated twice, contrasting bridge B (8 bars), return of A (8 bars). Standard form of American jazz from the 1930s–60s. The bridge B is often in a neighbouring key.
narrative.formeAABAExamples: Autumn Leaves, I Got Rhythm, Stardust, Over the Rainbow
narrative.formeBluesDesc: Question/answer/resolution in 12 bars: tonic statement (4 bars), subdominant response (2 bars), return (2 bars), turnaround (4 bars). Predictable structure exploited by musicians and improvisers.
narrative.formeBluesExamples: 12-bar blues, jazz blues with II–V substitutions
narrative.formeABACDesc: Variant of the standard form: A returns twice but ends differently (B then C). Each return of A creates a slight surprise in the conclusion.
narrative.formeABACExamples: All The Things You Are, My Romance
narrative.formeSonateDesc: Exposition: theme A (tonic) + theme B (dominant/relative). Development: thematic manipulation in distant keys. Recapitulation: A and B in tonic. The most complex form of classicism.
narrative.formeSonateExamples: 1st movement of sonatas by Beethoven, Mozart, Haydn
narrative.tipBox: Jazz and form: an improviser who knows the form plays 'with' the structure. More tension in bridge B, more marked resolution at the return of A, climax at the right moment of the chorus. Ignoring the form means improvising in a vacuum — technically correct, musically inexpressive. Form is the framework of discourse.
narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: At UCLA in the 1940s, Schoenberg asked his students to analyze Beethoven's 5th Symphony: 'See how these four notes — Sol–Sol–Sol–Mib — generate twenty minutes of symphony. A motif is not an ornament: it is the seed of all musical thought.' His treatise Fundamentals of Musical Composition formalises these principles for his American classes.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: The motif is the smallest unit of musical discourse. Before composing a phrase, ask yourself: is my basic idea distinctive enough to be recognizable? Flexible enough to be transformed? A good idea generates a phrase; an excellent idea generates a symphony.
narrative.beethovenFormulaCaption: Sol – Sol – Sol – Mib  (3 repetitions + minor third drop)

conservatoire.intuition: An eight-bar phrase, a bare arpeggio, a textbook tonic-dominant alternation — and yet Haydn draws a coup de théâtre out of it. The simplest form can carry the most effective surprise, provided you know exactly where to place the accent.

reference.citation: That will make the ladies jump.
reference.auteur: Joseph Haydn, on the stroke at measure 16 (as reported by his biographers)

voix: A Classical phrase divides into motive, development and cadence — the Surprise theme lays this anatomy bare in the most stripped-down state imaginable: eight measures, a single arpeggio, a single polarity (tonic-dominant).
The repeat of a phrase can replay exactly the same material note for note while completely changing its effect — here, simply by changing the dynamic (p, then pp, then, suddenly, ff).

A binary form (theme = two halves A/B, and each variation likewise) organises the phrase on a larger scale: the surprise itself falls exactly at the moment when the repeat of the A section was about to close in on itself.

pieges.erreur: Looking for a strange or chromatic harmony to explain the surprise effect at measure 16
pieges.correction: The chord is a plain V, exactly the one the theme's half cadence was calling for — the effect lies not in the chord but in its dynamic (ff after two p/pp phrases) and in its placement on a weak beat. A phrase can surprise without any harmonic rule being broken.

pieges.erreur: Believing that so simple a theme (an arpeggio, a I-V alternation) is a flaw in the writing
pieges.correction: The bareness of the theme is a strategy, not a weakness: the material has to be minimal so that the four variations have room to dress it up, and so that the surprise stands out against a background of total innocence.

pieges.erreur: Analysing each variation as a harmonically independent piece
pieges.correction: Except for Variation II (the minore, the only real excursion away from the tonic), every variation keeps the SAME harmonic frame as the theme — only the texture (countermelody, hammered octaves, repeated notes, fanfare) changes from one variation to the next.

resume: A Classical phrase articulates into motive + development + cadence — the Surprise theme (Haydn, 1791) presents it in its barest state: naked arpeggio, I-V alternation, half cadences at measures 4 and 8.

Binary form with repeats organises theme AND variations on a larger scale than the phrase alone: each half is repeated, and it is precisely on a repeat (pp) that Haydn places his coup de théâtre (m. 16, ff).

Humour is a harmonic category in its own right: measure 16 breaks no rule (a plain V), it changes only the status — dynamic, orchestration — of that chord. Nothing proves the existence of a norm better than the possibility of laughing at it.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C major from first bar to last — the only excursion away from the tonic is the passage through C minor in Variation II (m. 49-74).
analyseNarrative.metrique: 2/4. Andante (♩=64), with a slight broadening (♩=58) exactly at the start of the coda (m. 135).
analyseNarrative.forme: Theme and four variations with coda, binary form with repeats (theme m. 1-16, Variation I m. 17-48 [in 2 halves A/B], II m. 49-74, III m. 75-98, IV m. 99-134, coda m. 135-148).

sections.label: Measures 1-8
sections.titre: The theme: a calculated bareness
sections.texte: Eight measures of deliberate plainness: the C major arpeggio picked out note by note (C-E, then G-E), the most elementary harmony in the Classical language — tonic-dominant polarity in its pure state, punctuated by a half cadence on G at measure 4 and again at measure 8. A nursery-rhyme theme was needed so that the variations would have everything to dress up, and so that the surprise would stand out against a background of innocence.

sections.label: Measures 9-16
sections.titre: The pp repeat, and the surprise
sections.texte: The same theme returns note for note, but pianissimo — the lullaby as a trap, the listener invited to doze off. Then, at measure 16, the chord: a G major spread across the whole keyboard (G2 to G5), ff, on a weak beat. Harmonically it is perfectly ordinary — the V that the theme's half cadence was calling for in any case. Nothing foreign, nothing chromatic: the surprise is a dynamic and an orchestration, not a harmony.

sections.label: Measures 17-32
sections.titre: B: the return (the binary form of the theme)
sections.texte: After the jolt, the second half of the theme closes its binary form: a brief detour, then the assured return to the tonic, as though nothing had happened.

sections.label: Measures 33-48
sections.titre: Variation I: the theme + a countermelody
sections.texte: The theme remains intact — the same C-E-G arpeggio, the same framework — but a countermelody in sixteenth notes comes to dress it. Variation by addition: the harmony does not change, only the texture grows richer.

sections.label: Measures 49-74
sections.titre: Variation II: the minore
sections.texte: The regulation shadow of the Classical variation cycle: C minor, ff, a C and then an E♭ hammered out across the whole keyboard before detours towards E♭ major (the relative major) — the only real harmonic excursion in the entire movement, between two outer halves that themselves remain firmly anchored on the tonic.

sections.label: Measures 75-98
sections.titre: Variation III: repeated notes
sections.texte: Back to the major: the same C major chord struck four times in a row, then its first inversion four times more — repeated notes and dialogues in the upper parts, the textural opposite of the florid countermelody of Variation I.

sections.label: Measures 99-134
sections.titre: Variation IV: fanfare, and the fermata
sections.texte: The fanfare tutti: the theme in brassy glory, projected in arpeggios that climb to the top of the keyboard, then a second half, dolce, that calms the dynamic. The variation halts on a suspensive fermata at measure 134 — a C diminished chord (first inversion, E♭ in the bass) that holds the breath before the coda.

sections.label: Measures 135-148
sections.titre: Coda: tenderness
sections.texte: The finest harmonic moment of the movement: the theme falls asleep again pianissimo over a dominant pedal, thickens for an instant into a complete G7 at measure 140 — D and F are already sounding, held over from the previous measure, only G and B are struck anew: the one seventh in the piece that is truly savoured, at the softest dynamic of the whole movement — then resolves onto the last two measures of C major. The joke opened the movement; a tenderness closes it.

synthese.titre: The surprise is a dynamic, not a harmony
synthese.texte: The chord at measure 16 is a V in exactly its rightful place, the one the theme's half cadence was calling for in any case — nothing foreign, nothing chromatic. Haydn demonstrates by absurdity that the effect lies not in the chord but in its status: the same V, murmured, lulls you to sleep; hammered out, it makes you jump. The exact comic counterpart of the sforzandos in Beethoven's Grave (his pupil, seven years later): the same rhetorical lever, turned towards laughter.

synthese.titre: The degree zero of K. 545, pushed as far as deliberate innocence
synthese.texte: The Surprise theme (the naked arpeggio, the tonic-dominant alternation) is even more stripped down than that of Mozart's Sonata K. 545 (course 28, three years earlier) — Mozart kept things simple out of elegance, Haydn keeps them simple out of strategy: a nursery-rhyme theme is needed so that the four variations have everything to dress up, and so that the surprise stands out against a background of innocence.

synthese.titre: Humour as a harmonic category
synthese.texte: Between K. 545 (transparent grammar) and the Pathétique (dramatised grammar), the Surprise documents a third path: grammar at play, in the ludic sense. Nothing proves the existence of a norm better than the possibility of laughing at it — measure 16 is the demonstration, in a single chord, that Classical tonality was a shared language, the precondition for everything the rest of the corpus goes on to recount, when that same language becomes dramatised, suspended, dissolved and reinvented.

cours11.title: Chord Extensions
cours11.subtitle: 9ths, 11ths, 13ths — stacking thirds beyond the 7th to enrich harmonic color.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — chord extensions hold no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more chords to practice and you'll have it.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep listening actively — the ear learns with practice!

narrative.extIntro: A basic chord (triad or tetrad) can be enriched by extensions: we continue stacking thirds beyond the 7th. The 9th is the 2nd an octave higher, the 11th is the 4th an octave higher, the 13th is the 6th an octave higher.
narrative.extInfoBox: The chain of thirds: root → 3rd → 5th → 7th → 9th → 11th → 13th. Each step adds a third. A complete 13th chord contains 7 notes — the entire scale at once. In practice, several are omitted to maintain clarity.
narrative.extClickHint: Click an extension to hear it and see its details.
narrative.maitreAnecdote: Bill Evans had studied Ravel, Debussy, and Chopin before joining Miles Davis in 1958. When Kind of Blue was recorded, Evans introduced a radically new voicing style: 9ths in inner voices, 11ths in clusters, 13ths replacing 5ths. His trio (with Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian) redefined chamber jazz. Waltz for Debby (1961) remains the benchmark for piano extensions.
narrative.maitreLesson: A 9th doesn't 'replace' a chord tone — it enriches it. The difference between a chord and a color is often just one note an octave higher.
narrative.appIntro: Extensions apply to all three tonal functions (T, SD, D) without changing their role in the progression. Dm9 remains subdominant, G13 remains dominant, CMaj9 remains tonic — but each chord gains richness and color.
narrative.appTensionsInfoBox: The available tensions rule: an extension is « available » if it does not create a ♭9 interval (semitone + octave) with a chord tone. The ♭9 is the unacceptable dissonance — except when it is itself the desired tension.
narrative.appWarnBox: Key exception: the perfect 11th is avoided on major chords (it creates a ♭9 with the major 3rd), but it is available and very common on minor chords (the ♭3 is a whole tone away from the 11th). That is why Dm11 works, but CMaj11 sounds wrong.
narrative.appTipBox: Practical voicing: in jazz piano, keep 3rd + 7th as the core (shell voicing) and add the desired tension in the soprano or an inner voice. The root is played by the bass — no need to double it at the piano.
narrative.quizFeedbackExcellent: Excellent — chord extensions hold no more secrets!
narrative.quizFeedbackGood: Good — a few more chords to practice and you'll be perfect.
narrative.quizFeedbackKeepGoing: Keep listening to extensions actively — the ear learns!

conservatoire.intuition: An extension is a color stacked above the 7th — the 9th, 11th, and 13th don't change a chord's function, they enrich its timbre without betraying it.

reference.badge: Nettles & Graf · The Chord Scale Theory & Jazz Harmony
reference.citation: Each available tension colors the chord without changing its underlying function, provided the avoid notes of its underlying scale are respected.

voix: The 9th (major), 11th (perfect or augmented), and 13th (major) are the most consonant tensions of seventh chords
An alteration (b9, #9, #11, b13) strongly colors a dominant chord without changing its function
On a minor 7th chord the 9th is almost always available; the natural 11th clashes with the major 3rd of a major chord

pieges.erreur: Adding the natural 11th to a dominant or major chord (it clashes with the 3rd)
pieges.correction: Prefer the raised 11th (#11) on these chords, or omit the extension

resume: 9th = 2nd degree an octave up, 11th = 4th, 13th = 6th
#9 and b9 are typical tensions of the altered dominant chord
"All the Things You Are" (Kern/Hammerstein): an introductory vamp built entirely on altered dominant chords (#9)

analyseNarrative.tonalite: A♭ major (key signature of four flats) — but this introductory vamp never settles into it: it alternates two altered dominants without ever resolving onto A♭.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4, swing (uneven eighths), quarter note = 140.
analyseNarrative.forme: A two-bar vamp (a held chord, then a neighbour-note figure in the bass) repeated before the standard itself begins, at measure 9 of the original file (not included here; it opens on F minor) — this introduction is only a chromatic preparation, not yet the tune.

sections.label: Measure 1
sections.titre: The upbeat
sections.texte: The excerpt opens on a rest, then on a single bass note (A natural), which immediately falls a semitone to A♭ — the 5th of the chord that arrives in the next measure, not its root. So this is not a tonal upbeat: it is a colour approached by chromatic step.

sections.label: Measures 2-3
sections.titre: Db7(#9), the tritone substitution
sections.texte: The bass lays down the root (D♭) then the fifth (A♭); on the offbeat the right hand strikes the three notes that carry the whole colour of the chord: F (the third), B natural (spelled as the minor 7th) and E natural (the augmented 9th) — neither root nor fifth in that hand: the tensions alone carry the harmonic identity. Db7 replaces G7 by tritone substitution (the same F–B tritone), leading towards C7 in the following measure.

sections.label: Measures 4-5
sections.titre: C7(#9), the dominant of the relative minor
sections.texte: The same gesture, a third lower: here again the right hand plays only the third (E), the 7th (B♭) and the augmented 9th (E♭) — with no root and no fifth. This is the secondary dominant of the key's relative minor (F minor), which does not appear until measure 9 of the original file. Measure 5 ornaments this harmony with a descending line in the right hand (A♭-G-C-F-A) before the cycle sets off again.

sections.label: Measures 6-7
sections.titre: Db7(#9) returns, with a richer colour
sections.texte: The same chord comes back — but not identically. The analytical label changes this time (“SubV7/V” rather than “SubV/V”), and the right hand has grown richer: its shape brushes past other colours along the way — a 13th (B♭) and an augmented 11th (G) — absent from the first statement in measures 2-3. A vamp that repeats may therefore allow itself a little more colour with each return: this is the very spirit of the extensions taught in this lesson.

sections.label: Measure 8
sections.titre: A last C7(#9), ending in suspense
sections.texte: The final chord of the excerpt: C7(#9), also voiced more richly than at its first appearance (the right hand adds the fifth, absent in measure 4). The excerpt stops here, at full tension — the standard begins just afterwards, at measure 9 of the original file, on F minor.

synthese.titre: Tensions with neither root nor fifth
synthese.texte: The two chords of this vamp (Db7(#9), C7(#9)) are voiced in exactly the same way: the bass carries the root and the fifth, the right hand plays only the third, the 7th and the altered 9th — a classic rootless jazz-piano voicing in which the tensions do all the work of colour.

synthese.titre: The colour grows richer with every return
synthese.texte: The vamp is not simply copied out again: on its return (measures 6-8) the right hand adds touches of the 13th and the augmented 11th that were absent from the first statement — a repeated vamp is never quite identical to itself.

synthese.titre: A first taste of alteration before the tune
synthese.texte: This introduction never touches the tune's tonic (A♭): it prepares the ear with two altered dominants before the standard proper — far more diatonic — begins at measure 9.

cours22.title: Reharmonization
cours22.subtitle: Transform a progression while preserving the melody — diatonic and tritone substitutions, modal borrowing, parallel harmonization.

quiz.perfect: Excellent — reharmonization holds no more secrets!
quiz.veryGood: Well done! A few more progressions to consolidate.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep listening to the progressions — the ear learns by doing!

narrative.principeIntro: Reharmonising means replacing the chords of a progression while keeping the melody intact. The fundamental constraint: every melody note must remain consonant with the new chord.
narrative.principeInfoBox: Principle: the melody is fixed — it is "the roof". The chords can change — they are "the floor". Choosing a new chord means choosing the light under which the melody will be heard.
narrative.principeClickHint: Click on a technique to see and hear the progressions.
narrative.principeWarnBox: Melodic check: before any reharmonisation, identify the long notes of the melody. A held note that creates a half-step with a chord tone = strong dissonance. Check systematically.
narrative.applicationIntro: Three examples from the jazz repertoire, each illustrating a different technique. Compare the original and reharmonised progressions by listening to them.
narrative.applicationTip: Exercise: take a standard you know (Autumn Leaves, All The Things You Are) and reharmonise 2–3 chords using the techniques from this lesson. Start with diatonic substitution — it is the closest to the original.
narrative.quizFeedbackExcellent: Excellent — reharmonisation holds no more secrets!
narrative.quizFeedbackGood: Good — just a few more progressions to listen to and it will be perfect.
narrative.quizFeedbackKeepGoing: Keep listening to progressions actively — the ear learns!
narrative.maitreAnecdote: In 1958, Bill Evans recorded 'Peace Piece' in a single take. For eight minutes, he explored every harmonic colour possible over a single bass pedal — C. He borrowed chords from the minor mode, slid chromatic Maj7 blocks down, never leaving the root C. This piece is a manifesto of reharmonisation as colour.
narrative.maitreLesson: Reharmonising means seeing the same notes under different lights. The melody is the soloist — the chords are the light you choose to illuminate it.

conservatoire.intuition: A motionless ostinato is not a constraint — it is a fixed ground on which a single curve (the density of notes foreign to the key) can carry, all by itself, the entire form of a piece.

reference.badge: Bill Evans · liner notes, Kind of Blue
reference.citation: There is a Japanese visual art in which the artist is forced to be spontaneous. He must paint on a thin stretched parchment with a special brush... Erasures or changes are impossible.
reference.auteur: Bill Evans, “Improvisation in Jazz,” liner notes to Kind of Blue (1959)

voix: An ostinato built on two colour chords (a major seventh, an unresolved neighbouring chord) can sustain an entire piece without ever producing a single cadence.
When the accompanying harmony stays rigorously fixed, one melodic parameter alone — the density of notes foreign to the key — can carry the whole formal curve of a piece.
A suspended fourth (a “sus” chord) that never resolves to the third is not a dominant kept waiting: it is a second colour, of the same rank as the first.

pieges.erreur: Labelling the G chord as a plain G7 calling for its resolution on C
pieges.correction: It is a G9sus: the fourth (C) is never replaced by the third (B). A G7 calls for a resolution; a G9sus floats alongside, with no directed tension — that nuance of notation changes the whole meaning of what we hear.

pieges.erreur: Looking for a harmonic progression to account for the wave of tension in the piece
pieges.correction: There is none: the ostinato does not change a single note from beginning to end. The whole curve of tension comes exclusively from the right hand (the density of notes foreign to the key), not from any movement of chords.

pieges.erreur: Treating the major seventh of the opening chord as a dissonance that ought to resolve
pieges.correction: In this idiom the major seventh belongs to the constitutive colour of the chord — it is neither prepared nor resolved, it IS the opening sonority.

resume: An ostinato built on two colour chords (C∆7, G9sus) can sustain an entire piece without ever producing a single cadence — function gives way to pure colour.
The G9sus is not a G7: its fourth never resolves to the third, which makes it a second colour rather than a dominant kept waiting.
While the harmony stays fixed, the density of notes foreign to the key in the melody can carry the whole form by itself — a wave that rises and then subsides above a motionless ground.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C major — but never a cadence: a rocking between two colour chords (C∆7, G9sus) that never resolve into one another.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. The left-hand ostinato is rigorously IDENTICAL, note for note, in each of the 8 measures.
analyseNarrative.forme: The pendulum sets itself going alone (mm. 1-2), the right hand enters in pure diatonicism (mm. 3-4), a chromatic wave rises and then subsides (mm. 5-7), and everything closes on absolute white, with no cadence (m. 8).

sections.label: Measures 1-2
sections.titre: The pendulum sets itself going
sections.texte: The left hand alone lays down the two colours that will carry the whole piece: C∆7 (major seventh included, never treated as a dissonance to be resolved), then G9sus — a suspended fourth that is NEVER brought back to its third. This is not a dominant waiting for C: it is a second colour, of the same standing as the first.

sections.label: Measures 3-4
sections.titre: Complete diatonicism
sections.texte: The right hand enters, and for these two measures it does not touch a single note foreign to C major — not the slightest accidental. The ostinato, meanwhile, has not budged by so much as an eighth note.

sections.label: Measures 5-7
sections.titre: The chromatic wave
sections.texte: A first foreign note (m. 5), then the summit: a spray of four altered notes stacked all at once (m. 6), thrown against an ostinato that does not flinch — then the ebb (m. 7), a single foreign note once more. Dissonance here is neither prepared nor resolved: it rises and falls like a tide, while underneath nothing changes.

sections.label: Measure 8
sections.titre: Return to absolute white
sections.texte: The final C is not a resolution in the classical sense — the ostinato carrying it is exactly the same as in measure 1. It is a return of colour, not a cadence.

synthese.titre: The same pendulum, another century
synthese.texte: A major seventh never treated as a dissonance, a neighbouring chord with no functional link, not a single cadence across the whole span: it is the same principle as a rocking between two colour chords already encountered in this corpus, carried over from the French post-Romantic piano to the jazz piano — function gives way to pure colour.

synthese.titre: A single parameter makes the whole form
synthese.texte: While the accompanying harmony remains rigorously motionless, one parameter alone carries the entire form: the density of notes foreign to the key in the right hand, which rises and then falls like a curve. The same principle as a piece that moves along one axis only (timbre, register, density) while the chord itself stays fixed.

synthese.titre: The ostinato become a cell
synthese.texte: A two-chord ostinato conceived for a solitary meditation at the piano can become, a few months later, the harmonic footing of an entirely different number — the same repeated cell, reused exactly as it stands in a collective, improvised context. An ostinato is not merely an accompaniment: it is an object that can travel from one piece to another.

cours23.title: Composing in the style of the masters
cours23.subtitle: Bach, Mozart, Chopin, Debussy, Jazz, Rock — learn to identify and reproduce the harmonic signatures that define each great style.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered the great stylistic signatures.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few nuances to refine between close styles.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep exploring the styles — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Brahms spent years studying Bach and Beethoven before publishing his first symphony at age 43. He said he could hear the footsteps of giants behind him. Yet his style is immediately recognizable: dense harmonies, syncopated rhythms, Nordic melancholy. Studying the masters does not dilute one's style — it forges it.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Knowing the styles of others is the shortest path to finding your own.
narrative.stylesIntro: Every composer or movement has a harmonic signature — a set of techniques, progressions and colors that make it immediately recognizable. Click on a style to hear its typical progression.
narrative.stylesInfoBox: How to recognize a style? Look for these 3 clues: (1) which chords are used (diatonic? borrowed? extensions?); (2) how the chords follow each other (by fifths? by thirds? in parallel?); (3) is there a V7→I resolution or not?
narrative.stylesClickHint: Click on a style to see its characteristics and hear its typical progression.
narrative.stylesWarnBox: Styles are not rigid boxes: a composer can blend several styles in a single piece. Chopin borrows from Bach (counterpoint) and anticipates Debussy (modal borrowings). Recognizing a style means identifying the dominant language, not making an absolute classification.
narrative.exIntro: For each style, choose the progression that matches it. Listen to each option before answering — the ear guides theory.
narrative.exTipBox: Method: listen to all options first (▶ button) before choosing. The ear recognizes the style before the theory — trust your listening, then check with the explanations.
narrative.quizScoreGood: Excellent — the masters' styles hold no more secrets!
narrative.quizScoreOk: Good — a few more comparative listens and you'll have it.
narrative.quizScoreLow: Keep listening to the progressions of each style — the ear learns!

conservatoire.intuition: Imitating an older style never entirely erases the period it comes from — every detour leaves a fingerprint of the moment when it was written, however discreet that fingerprint may be.

reference.citation: Fra Holbergs tid — from Holberg's time.
reference.auteur: Edvard Grieg, subtitle of the Holberg Suite op. 40 (1884)

voix: A neo-archaism reproduces the FRAMEWORK of an older style (here, the Baroque prelude in moto perpetuo over a pedal) while letting the harmonic reflexes of its own real period show through in the details.

A pedal point can hesitate between major and minor without ever settling — a modal ambiguity the Baroque would never have allowed itself, and which here betrays the hand of a nineteenth-century composer.
A deceptive resolution (a ii-V surfacing where the ear expected a direct resolution) can slip into the very heart of a page that otherwise scrupulously observes eighteenth-century syntax.

pieges.erreur: Analysing this prelude as a purely Baroque piece, without looking for traces of the period it was actually written in (1884)
pieges.correction: The framework is Baroque (tonic pedal, moto perpetuo, oscillation between 6/4 and diminished chords over a dominant pedal), but several details betray Romanticism: the structural fz/ff dynamics, the dominant pedal that hesitates between major and minor (mm. 38-39), the deceptive resolution (mm. 40-41), and the fleeting augmented eleventh of the coda (m. 70).

pieges.erreur: Looking for a classical preparation of the deceptive resolution in measures 40-41
