pieges.correction: There is none: the dominant pedal of E (B, nine measures) ought to resolve to E minor, but slides straight into ii7-V7 of G (Am7-D7) — a pure Romantic reflex of thwarted expectation, at the heart of an otherwise very regular page.

pieges.erreur: Treating the augmented eleventh of measure 70 as a mere passing note with no analytical consequence
pieges.correction: It is a genuine, deliberate harmonic colour (an F♯ added to a C major chord) — a sonority no eighteenth-century grammar would have produced, and which for the space of an instant signs the hand of a nineteenth-century composer.

resume: The Holberg Suite (Grieg, 1884) is a deliberate neo-archaism: a Baroque prelude in moto perpetuo over a tonic pedal, written with the harmonic means of late Romanticism — fifteen years before Ravel's Pavane, forty years before Stravinsky's neoclassicism.

The dominant pedal of E (mm. 30-39, nine measures) explicitly alternates major and minor (D♯ against D natural) before sliding into a deceptive resolution (Am7-D7) rather than resolving as expected — two typically Romantic reflexes inside an otherwise Baroque machine.

Every imitation of an older style leaves its own fingerprints: here the structural dynamics, the modal ambiguity of the pedal, the deceptive resolution and the augmented eleventh of the coda (m. 70) betray 1884 beneath the eighteenth-century mask.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: G major — with a firmly established detour through the second theme in D (V) and an episode in the relative minor, E minor, at its centre.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Allegro vivace (quarter note = 154), f — an unbroken moto perpetuo from beginning to end.
analyseNarrative.forme: Baroque prelude form in three panels: exposition (mm. 1-22, two themes and their reprise), development (mm. 23-41, the episode in the relative minor and its dominant pedal), recapitulation and coda (mm. 42-72).

sections.label: Measures 1-8
sections.titre: The Baroque prelude: tonic pedal, then express modulation
sections.texte: The moto perpetuo settles in at once over a sustained tonic pedal (G1, verified as sounding without interruption for four measures) — the very principle of Bach's arpeggio preludes, pushed to its highest degree of purity. Then, with no detour, an express modulation installs the dominant, D.

sections.label: Measures 9-22
sections.titre: The second theme, the retransition, the reprise
sections.texte: A cantabile second theme sings in D, in sequences. Then, in measures 19-20, a D7 with F♯ in the bass carries a C natural that does not belong to the key of D — the seventh that quietly recalls G, drawing the ear back towards the main key before the reprise has even taken place. The opening motif returns, fp.

sections.label: Measures 23-41
sections.titre: The episode in the relative minor: the dominant pedal and its two faces
sections.chiffrage: B7 → e … A♯°7/C → B (pedal) → Am7 – D7
sections.texte: A ff secondary dominant (B7) installs the relative minor, E. A sequence of seventh chords over a descending bass leads to the only genuinely Romantic bite in the piece (fz): a complete diminished seventh chord, built on A♯, with C in the bass. Then comes the structural centrepiece — nine measures of pedal on B, the dominant of E, with oscillations alternating the tonic in 6/4 and a diminished chord, exactly as in a Bach prelude. But Grieg slips HIS own ambiguity into it: the pedal hesitates explicitly between B major (D♯, m. 38) and B minor (D natural, m. 39) — confirmed note for note. Then, instead of resolving towards E as expected, the music slides into Am7-D7: the ii-V of G coming in through the window, a pure Romantic reflex of deceptive resolution inside an otherwise thoroughly Baroque machine.

sections.label: Measures 42-55
sections.titre: Recapitulation: the plagal expansion
sections.texte: The return of the main key (fz) is enriched by a colour of which Grieg's Baroque is fond: plagal expansion. A G7 with F in the bass (V4/2 of IV) opens the door straight onto IV, before a broad ff cadence descends a chain of seventh chords back to the tonic.

sections.label: Measures 56-72
sections.titre: Tranquillo and coda: #11 and the final window of return
sections.texte: The tranquillo sings the closing theme over a new tonic pedal. The coda stacks one last cycle of secondary dominants, with a fleeting colour in measure 70: an F♯ over a C major chord — the augmented eleventh, a note belonging to no eighteenth-century grammar, which for the space of an instant betrays the hand of a nineteenth-century composer. The V7-I cadence closes the piece.

synthese.titre: Neo-archaism: a Bach prelude written in 1884
synthese.texte: The whole framework (opening tonic pedal, alternation of 6/4 and diminished chords over a dominant pedal, unbroken moto perpetuo) faithfully reproduces the design of the Baroque arpeggio prelude. But every detour leaves a nineteenth-century fingerprint: the structural fz and ff dynamics, the pedal hesitating between major and minor, the deceptive resolution instead of the expected one, the fleeting augmented eleventh of the coda. The past one imitates is never entirely neutral — it is always told through the reflexes of the one doing the imitating.

synthese.titre: A dated chain of backward glances
synthese.texte: 1884: Grieg writes an eighteenth-century prelude with the harmonic means of late Romanticism — fifteen years before Ravel's neo-Renaissance Pavane, forty years before Stravinsky's neoclassicism. The “return to the past” as a compositional gesture is therefore not an isolated phenomenon of the early twentieth century: it runs through several generations, and each one leaves its own mark on it.

synthese.titre: The same device as the Pavane, fifteen years before it
synthese.texte: The sequence of diatonic seventh chords over a descending bass (mm. 27-28) is exactly the device Ravel would use in his Pavane pour une infante défunte (1899) — a bass descending by step beneath a chain of seventh chords, one of the most recognizable harmonic signatures of the “old style” revisited through modern language.

cours24.title: Augmented Sixth Chords
cours24.subtitle: It+6, Fr+6, Ger+6 — three Romantic altered chords, their contrary-motion resolution, and their use in 19th-century music.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered all three augmented sixths and their resolutions.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few details to refine on resolutions and usage.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep studying augmented sixth chords — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Liszt used the German augmented sixth as his harmonic signature — a chord that concentrates all romantic tension in 3 or 4 notes.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: One well-placed altered chord is worth ten ordinary ones.
narrative.pTypes: The augmented sixth chord is an altered pre-dominant chord characterized by the augmented sixth interval between bVI (in the bass) and #IV. Three variants exist — Italian, French and German — each with its own construction and color.
narrative.infoBoxContext: Context in C major: In all the examples below, we are in C major. bVI = Ab, I = C, #IV = F#. These three notes form the common core of all augmented sixth chords.
narrative.clickHint: Click a chord to expand it and listen.
narrative.infoBoxRegle: Universal rule of augmented sixths: Regardless of type (It+6, Fr+6, Al+6), the augmented sixth interval (bVI–#IV) always resolves by contrary motion to the dominant fifth. In C major: Ab moves down to G, F# moves up to G. This convergence is mandatory.
narrative.pApplication: Augmented sixth chords do not appear randomly — they follow a precise harmonic scheme and reveal their full power in late Baroque, Classical and Romantic music.
narrative.infoBoxSchema:
Classic scheme: IVm → It+6/Fr+6/Al+6 → V → I
The augmented sixth is a pre-dominant chord: it always appears before V (or I6/4–V). The minor subdominant (IVm) prepares it gently.
narrative.infoBoxJazz: Al+6 and the tritone substitution: The German sixth Ab–C–Eb–F# is enharmonically identical to Ab7 (Ab–C–Eb–G♭). In jazz in C major, Ab7 = bII7 (written as 'Db7'). Jazz musicians exploit this ambiguity for tritone substitution: replacing G7 (V7) with Db7 (bII7) works for exactly the same reason that Al+6 creates tension toward V.
narrative.warnBox: Common pitfall: Do not confuse Al+6 with V7/IV (same chord, opposite functions). Al+6 resolves to V (Ab and F# converge to G by contrary motion). V7/IV (Ab7) resolves to IV = Db major (normal dominant resolution). The same combination of notes can lead in two completely different directions depending on context.
narrative.sixteItDesc: The simplest of the three — only 3 voices. The augmented sixth in its purest form.
narrative.sixtefrDesc: Contains the dominant ninth (D). More colorful than the Italian, it already hints at the sound of V9.
narrative.sixteAlDesc: The richest and most commonly used. Enharmonically identical to a dominant seventh chord (Ab7), but its resolution is different.
narrative.sixteAlResolution: Resolves to V with doubled fifth (to avoid parallel fifths)
narrative.epoqueBaroque: Bach and Handel use the augmented sixth at important cadences. The chord is functional, without expressive excess — purely structural.
narrative.epoqueClassique: Mozart and Beethoven codify the formula Al+6 → I6/4 → V → I as the par excellence final cadence. The augmented sixth acquires its rhetorical role.
narrative.epoqueRomantique: Schubert, Schumann, Brahms and Liszt use it expressionistically: modulations via enharmony, unexpected progressions, dramatic delays.
narrative.epoqueJazz: Jazz rediscovers the equivalence Al+6 ↔ bII7 as tritone substitution. Db7 in C = enharmonic Ab7 = functional Al+6 — same tension, different language.
narrative.commentSchubert: Schubert uses Al+6 to create a moment of intense melancholy before the resolution. The harmonic richness of the chord amplifies the dark color of the lied.
narrative.commentBeethoven: Beethoven uses the Italian sixth (3 voices, absolute purity) for a targeted dramatic effect. The chord's restraint reinforces the moment's intensity.
narrative.commentBrahms: Brahms exploits Fr+6 for its particular color: D (2nd degree = dominant 9th) prefigures the sound of V9 and enriches the final cadence.
narrative.bassePremierRenversement: Always in first inversion — bass on bVI:
narrative.bassePremierRenversementDesc: Ab (bVI) is invariably in the bass → it descends by semitone to G (dominant fifth)

conservatoire.intuition: A chord that compresses the whole tonal tension into a single point — like a spring ready to release towards the dominant.

reference.badge: Aldwell & Schachter · Harmony and Voice Leading
reference.citation: The augmented sixth chord is the most intensely dissonant pre-dominant chord in tonal music; its two characteristic tones resolve outward by half step to the dominant fifth.

voix: The augmented sixth (A♭–F♯) always resolves to the dominant fifth (G–G) by obligatory contrary motion
The bass is invariably on bVI (A♭ in C major) — first inversion is constitutive of the chord
The German sixth (bVI–I–bIII–#IV) is enharmonically identical to a V7/IV — its resolution differs radically

pieges.erreur: Forgetting the contrary motion: making A♭ and F♯ rise together
pieges.correction: A♭ descends to G, F♯ rises to G — the outer voices must converge on the dominant fifth

pieges.erreur: Resolving the German sixth like a V7/IV (towards IV) rather than towards V
pieges.correction: Ger+6 resolves towards V by contrary motion; V7/IV resolves towards IV — same notes, opposite resolutions

pieges.erreur: Placing the augmented sixth outside the pre-dominant context (not before V or I6/4–V)
pieges.correction: The augmented sixth is idiomatic only in the pre-dominant zone, always immediately before the dominant

resume: 3 types: It+6 (bVI–I–#IV), Fr+6 (bVI–I–II–#IV), Ger+6 (bVI–I–bIII–#IV)
Universal resolution: augmented sixth → dominant fifth, by contrary motion
Ger+6 = enharmonic equivalent of V7/IV — same notes, wholly different contexts and resolutions

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C minor (key signature of three flats). Two passing excursions: A♭ major (the relative) in measure 2, then G major (the dominant) tonicized in measures 3-4 by a chain of secondary dominants.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Largo, very slow (quarter note = 40 — absent from the source file, added).
analyseNarrative.forme: 13 measures = A (measures 1-4) + B (measures 5-8) + B taken up unchanged (measures 9-12) + final chord (measure 13). A funeral chorale in homorhythmic chords, four to a measure — one chord per beat, 49 harmonies in all. The dynamics (added, absent from the source file) organize a steady ebbing: ff (measures 1-4), p (measures 5-8), pp for the repeat (measures 9-12) — a procession moving away into the distance.

sections.label: Measure 1
sections.titre: The parent cadence
sections.texte: The complete cadential formula in a single breath. The iv carries its seventh (E♭ over F-A♭-C: Fm7), inherited from the preceding tonic. Over the V7, the E♭ struck together with the chord on beat 3 is a ♭13 appoggiatura that resolves to D only at the end of the beat — this E♭→D sigh over the dominant will return at every cadence of the prelude.

sections.label: Measure 2
sections.titre: The same block, transposed to the relative
sections.chiffrage: A♭ major (I) – D♭ major (IV) – E♭7 (V7) – A♭ major (I)
sections.texte: The entire formula of measure 1 is played again just as it stands, transposed as a block into A♭ major (I-IV-V7-I, with the same C→B♭ appoggiatura over the E♭7) — a brutal real sequence, with no transition.

sections.label: Measures 3-4
sections.titre: The return by chain of dominants
sections.chiffrage: G7 (V7) – C7 (V7/iv) – Fm (iv) – C major (IV/V) | D7 (V7/V) – G (V) – D7 (V7/V) – G (V)
sections.fonctions: D – D – SD – SD (towards V) | D – D – D – D (half cadence)
sections.texte: G7 does not resolve to C minor: it slides towards C7 (V7/iv), then F minor, then a C MAJOR (E♮, the fourth chord of the measure) that works as IV of G. The phrase tips over towards the dominant and settles there: D7-G-D7-G, tonicization of V and half cadence. The balance sheet of period A: C minor → A♭ → circle of fifths → dominant, in four measures.

sections.label: Measures 5-6
sections.titre: The chromatic lament and the French sixth
sections.chiffrage: Cm (i) – A♭ major/C (VI6) – B°7 (vii°7) – Gm/B♭ (v6) | Am7 (passing chord) – Fr+6 (D7♭5/A♭) – G (V) – G7/F (V4/2)
sections.fonctions: T – T – D – D (passing minor) | ? – D – D – D
sections.texte: Beneath a melody climbing into the treble, the bass begins a complete chromatic descent across two measures: C-C-B-B♭-A-A♭-G-F, harmonized chord by chord — including an incomplete vii°7 (B-D-A♭, the diminished seventh without its root, the imprint of a G7♭9). Alongside it the alto traces A♭-F♯-G, a chromatic double neighbour around the fifth. Then the summit: A♭-C-D-F♯, the French augmented sixth — legible also, in jazz notation, as a D7(♭5) over an A♭ bass — which crushes its double dissonance onto V, prolonged as V4/2.

sections.label: Measures 7-8
sections.titre: The widened cadence, and the Neapolitan
sections.chiffrage: Cm/E♭ (i6) – Fm (iv) – G/B (V6) – Cm (i) | A♭ major (VI) – D♭ major (♭II) – G7 (V7) – Cm (i)
sections.fonctions: T – SD – D – T | T – SD (Neapolitan) – D – T
sections.texte: The 4/2 of measure 6 resolves onto i6, then the widened cadence iv-V6-i. Measure 8 replays the chords of measure 2, reinterpreted: the A♭ is no longer a local tonic but VI, and the D♭ major, which was IV of A♭, becomes ♭II — the Neapolitan sixth in root position, linked directly to V7 (with the same ♭13 appoggiatura as in measure 1). The same two chords thus change meaning between measure 2 and measure 8: diatonic in a neighbouring key there, chromatic in the main key here.

sections.label: Measures 9-13
sections.titre: The echoed reprise, and the bare ending
sections.chiffrage: (complete reprise of 5-8, sonority by sonority) | Cm (i, final)
sections.texte: Measures 9-12 take up 5-8 note for note — in the original, only the dynamic marking (pp) turns the repetition into an echo. Measure 13 closes the prelude on a bare tonic chord, with no Picardy third: the minor mode owned right to the end.

synthese.titre: Three Romantic colours brought together
synthese.texte: The chromatic lament bass (the Baroque legacy of the descending tetrachord), the Neapolitan sixth and the French augmented sixth all three appear within these 13 measures — the very tool kit of Romantic chromaticism.

synthese.titre: The same chord, twice, two meanings
synthese.texte: A♭ major and D♭ major return in measure 8 with the same notes as in measure 2 — but diatonic and passing there (in a neighbouring key), chromatic and heavy with meaning here (VI and ♭II of the tonic).

synthese.titre: A cadential tic that becomes grammar
synthese.texte: The ♭6→5 appoggiatura over the dominant (E♭→D in measure 1) returns at every cadence of the prelude — one and the same expressive gesture, repeated until it becomes a habit of writing rather than an accident.

cours25.title: Chromaticism and Advanced Chromatic Harmony
cours25.subtitle: Chromatic lines, the Tristan chord, enharmonic modulation — exploring the limits of tonality with Wagner and Liszt.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered chromaticism and tonal ambiguity.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few nuances to refine on enharmony and resolutions.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep exploring chromaticism — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: The Prelude to Tristan und Isolde opens with a chord that theorists still debate today. Wagner pushed chromaticism so far that tonality itself becomes uncertain — opening the path to Schoenberg and 20th-century music.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Chromaticism is not decoration — it is a deeper harmonic logic.
narrative.subtitle: Chromatic lines, Tristan chord, enharmonic modulation — tonality pushed to its limits.
narrative.pLignes: Chromaticism is organized into directional lines — movements by semitones that create their own logic, distinct but complementary to diatonic harmony. Each chromatic line carries a precise expressive meaning.
narrative.pClickHint: Click a line to explore it and listen.
narrative.infoBoxRegle:
Universal rule of chromatic resolution:
♯ rises (C# → D) · ♭ descends (Db → C)
Never resolve a chromatic note in the direction opposite to its accidental — this is the most common mistake in harmonization.
narrative.descAscendant: Leads upward. Expresses aspiration, dramatic rise, desire.
narrative.descDescendant: Darkens downward. Expresses resignation, lamentation, mourning — the chromaticism of the Baroque lamento.
narrative.pAmbiguite: Chromaticism pushed to the extreme creates chords whose tonal function becomes deliberately ambiguous. Wagner, Liszt and their contemporaries explored this borderland where tonality itself wavers.
narrative.tristanIntro: This chord opens the Prelude of Tristan und Isolde (1865). For 160 years, theorists have debated its analysis:
narrative.tristanAnalyse2exp: G#7 (= Ab7) in inversion, 2nd inversion with added 9th
narrative.tristanAnalyse3exp: Altered VII9 of A minor — G# is drawn toward A
narrative.tristanConclusion: Conclusion: The ambiguity IS the message. Wagner refuses any clear resolution — the key of A minor is suggested but never confirmed, creating permanent tension throughout the prelude (16 minutes).
narrative.dim7Intro: The diminished 7th is symmetrical — built from equal minor thirds. This makes it enharmonically ambiguous: the same chord can be reinterpreted in 4 different ways, resolving to 4 distinct keys.
narrative.dim7Conclusion: Enharmonic modulation: Changing the interpretation of a chord without changing its notes. The same sound, a new tonal direction — a fundamental technique of Schubert, Liszt and Wagner for imperceptible modulations.
narrative.warnBox:
Common pitfalls:
· Gratuitous chromaticism without direction — every altered note must have a logical resolution
· Enharmonic confusion: G# (rises → A) ≠ Ab (descends → G)
· Losing the tonal center by accumulating chromaticisms without diatonic anchoring
narrative.lamentoDesc: Chromatic descent of a fourth, from tonic to dominant. The most expressive bass line of the Baroque — it evokes mourning, lamentation, the inevitable. Purcell, Handel, Pachelbel all use it for their most intense moments.
narrative.lamentoExemple: C – B – Bb – A – Ab – G (in C minor)
narrative.sensibilisationDesc: Chromatic ascent by semitones — each note is sensitized toward the next. Creates growing, inevitable tension. Common in Romanticism to express aspiration, desire, dramatic rise.
narrative.sensibilisationExemple: C – C# – D – D# – E – F (in C major)
narrative.broderieDesc: Auxiliary note a semitone from the main note — tighter than a diatonic neighbor. The effect is of intensified expression, a shiver around a central note. Bach and Chopin use it with great refinement.

conservatoire.intuition: Chromaticism is tonality looking at itself in a distorting mirror — the same logic, but pushed to its limits.

reference.citation: Dissonance is not the opposite of consonance — it is a more distant consonance, one the ear has yet to learn to hear.

voix: Ascending chromaticism (leading-tone inflection) strengthens the pull towards the target note by rising semitone
Descending chromaticism (darkening) creates an expressive tension that calls for resolution by falling semitone
Every chromatic note must resolve in the direction of its alteration: ♯ rises, ♭ falls — never the reverse

pieges.erreur: Gratuitous chromaticism with no harmonic direction — a pile-up of altered notes with no logic of resolution
pieges.correction: Every chromatic note creates a pull towards its resolution; chromaticism is a logic, not an ornament

pieges.erreur: Enharmonic confusion: treating G♯ and A♭ as equivalent without distinguishing their direction of resolution
pieges.correction: G♯ rises to A (ascending chromaticism), A♭ falls to G (descending chromaticism) — the enharmonic spelling changes everything

pieges.erreur: Losing the tonal centre by piling up chromaticisms with no diatonic anchor
pieges.correction: Keep at least one diatonic reference chord before stringing chromaticisms together or modulating enharmonically

resume: Chromatic lines: lament bass (descending), leading-tone inflection (ascending), chromatic neighbour tone
The Tristan chord: F–B–D♯–G♯ — a deliberate functional ambiguity, debated to this day
Enharmonic modulation: the dim7 gives access to 4 different keys depending on the reading chosen

analyseNarrative.tonalite: A minor — never confirmed by a tonic chord in this excerpt: the whole piece flees resolution.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 6/8. Lento (dotted quarter = 52.5).
analyseNarrative.forme: Three statements of the same summoning motif (upbeat + chord + resolution), each one degree more tense than the last.

sections.label: Upbeat – m. 3
sections.titre: The Tristan chord: two readings of a single sound
sections.texte: The motif opens with a three-note upbeat (A-F-E) that rises and then falls back, like a question. At m. 2 the four voices freeze on F-B-D♯-G♯: the most commented-upon chord in the history of harmony. Read vertically, it is a simple dominant seventh with diminished fifth on F (Fø7), a self-sufficient sonority calling for no particular resolution. But G♯ is an appoggiatura: it rises to A, and the chord that then appears — F-A-B-D♯ — is a French augmented sixth in due form, one that pulls mechanically towards the fifth of the dominant. The two readings do not contradict each other: they coexist, and it is this very ambiguity that produces the whole effect of the passage. The resolution arrives at m. 3 on E7 (V7 of A minor), by way of a second appoggiatura in the low register (A♯→B).

sections.label: Measures 4–7
sections.titre: The same chord, a minor third higher
sections.texte: After a silence that prolongs the upbeat, the motif returns note for note, transposed up a minor third. The chord at m. 6 is the same sonority as the one at m. 2, merely displaced: its resolution by appoggiatura produces A♭-C-D-F♯, a French augmented sixth strictly identical — note for note — to the one in the Chopin Prelude studied earlier. Two composers, a century apart, radically different harmonic idioms, and yet exactly the same stack of four notes at the same point in the phrase. This time the resolution slides towards G7, the dominant no longer of A minor but of C major: the second phrase opens up a new tonal region without ever settling in it.

sections.label: Measures 8–13
sections.titre: A tension that is never answered
sections.texte: The third statement is the longest: the upbeat stretches out into a chromatic descent (D-B-B♭-A) that delays the arrival of the chord. When it does appear at m. 10, its seventh (C) has moved into the bass, and the two upper voices diverge instead of converging — one rising (D-D♯-E), the other falling (F-E) — before a fleeting augmented triad, C-E-G♯, crosses the very last instant of the bar. The resolution, at m. 11, falls on B7 (V7 of E), with its own appoggiatura (E♯→F♯) and a doubly held fermata. The chord returns an octave higher at m. 12, like an echo, before dropping one last time onto B7 at m. 13 — but this time with no resolution at all: the dominant is left hanging, and the excerpt stops on the tension itself.

synthese.titre: One chord, two grammars
synthese.texte: The Tristan chord can be read either as a self-sufficient vertical sonority (a dominant seventh with diminished fifth) or as an appoggiatura over a French augmented sixth. Neither reading cancels the other: the argument over which one is “the true one” has been running for more than a century, and it is precisely this refusal to decide that has made the chord so famous.

synthese.titre: The same sonority, two composers
synthese.texte: Once resolved by appoggiatura, the transposed version of the chord (m. 6) yields A♭-C-D-F♯, exactly the French augmented sixth of the Chopin Prelude studied in the previous lesson. The same stack of notes, the same function, in two harmonic languages that nonetheless seem worlds apart.

synthese.titre: A tension never answered
synthese.texte: The excerpt ends on a dominant (B7) that does not resolve: the expected tonic never arrives in these thirteen bars. This deferral of resolution — Wagner's “endless melody” — is already at work from the very opening of the Prelude.

cours30.title: Impressionist Harmony and Advanced Modality
cours30.subtitle: Planing, whole-tone scale, octatonic, pentatonic and Messiaen modes — harmonic color as an autonomous musical language.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered impressionist harmony techniques.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few nuances to refine on special scales and planing.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep exploring impressionism — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Ravel said he was not trying to express emotions but sound colours. His Boléro — a single C major chord for 15 minutes — proves that colour can replace function. Debussy called him 'the clockmaker of sound'.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: When the chord becomes colour, tension is no longer functional — it is sensory.
narrative.pImpressionnisme: Impressionist harmony breaks with the tension-resolution logic of the tonal system. Debussy and Ravel replace harmonic function with sound colour — each chord is a shade, not a role.
narrative.infoBoxPlaning: Planing: moving an entire chord in parallel motion. Parallel fifths and octaves are intentional — they create the effect of a sliding sound block. Do not analyse with T/SD/D functions.
narrative.gamme0description: No leading tone — tonal floating is total. Debussy is its master. All chords are augmented.
narrative.gamme1description: Alternating tone/semitone. Contains 3 diminished 7th chords. Stravinsky and Messiaen loved it.
narrative.gamme2description: 5 notes without any semitone, hence no leading tension. Used in jazz, folk and oriental impressionism.
narrative.gamme3description: Chord of 3 equal semitones. Symmetric — can resolve to 3 different keys. Characteristic of impressionist harmony.
narrative.pPlaning: Three successive Maj7 chords chromatically transposed a tone upward — no resolution, pure sliding colour.
narrative.warnBoxImpressionnisme: Common mistake: Analysing Debussy's harmony with T/SD/D functions. Impressionist chords have no functional role — looking for a dominant in 'Voiles' is looking in the wrong place. Analyse by colour and register.
narrative.pModalite: Messiaen theorised modes of limited transposition — scales whose internal symmetry reduces the number of distinct possible transpositions. Each mode has a unique and recognisable colour.
narrative.infoBoxTranspositions: Limited transpositions: A mode of limited transposition is a scale whose internal symmetry causes certain transpositions to reproduce the same collection of notes. Mode 1: 2 transpositions. Mode 2: 3 transpositions. The lower the number, the stronger the symmetry.
narrative.mode2exemple: Messiaen, 'Quartet for the End of Time'
narrative.h3ModalInterchange: Modal interchange (borrowed chords in C major)
narrative.pModalInterchange: Modal borrowing consists of temporarily using a chord from a parallel mode (same tonic, different mode) without actually modulating. C remains the tonal centre.
narrative.mi0effet: Sudden dark colour — the borrowed IVm is the most expressive
narrative.mi2effet: Romantic colour — very expressive borrowed chord
narrative.warnBoxModalInterchange: Modal interchange ≠ modulation: Modal borrowing is temporary — the tonic does not change. In C major, borrowing Ab (bVI) creates a colour, but C remains the centre. A modulation implies a change of tonal centre confirmed by a cadence.
narrative.h2Quiz: Quiz — Impressionist harmony and advanced modality

conservatoire.intuition: When Debussy plays a parallel ninth chord, he is not thinking “tension-resolution” — he is thinking “sky blue shading into violet”.

reference.badge: Messiaen · The Technique of My Musical Language
reference.citation: The modes of limited transposition are the key to my language. Their internal symmetry creates a unique and inimitable colour.

voix: Planing is not a mistake: it is a movement of chords in parallel in which colour replaces function. Analyse it with your eyes (not with T/SD/D functions).
The whole-tone scale (6 equidistant notes) contains no directional note — the drifting is intended, not an ambiguity waiting to be resolved.
Messiaen's modes have limited transpositions: mode 1 (the whole-tone scale) can only be transposed twice before it comes back to itself.

pieges.erreur: Analysing Debussy with T/SD/D functions
pieges.correction: Impressionist harmony works through colour and register. Looking for a dominant in Debussy's “Voiles” is looking for the wrong thing.

pieges.erreur: Believing that planing is a voice-leading error
pieges.correction: Planing is a deliberate technique — the parallel fifths and octaves are wanted, in order to create the effect of a block of sound sliding without resolution.

pieges.erreur: Confusing the whole-tone scale with the pentatonic scale
pieges.correction: Whole-tone scale: 6 equidistant notes (all whole tones), augmented chords. Pentatonic: 5 notes with no semitone (C–D–E–G–A). Very different colours.

pieges.erreur: Looking for a functional resolution in Impressionism
pieges.correction: The V–I resolution is deliberately avoided. Impressionist tension is sensory (colour, register, dynamic) and not functional.

resume: Planing: displacement of a whole chord without resolution — diatonic (the same type on every degree) or chromatic (the exact same chord transposed)
Special scales: whole-tone (6 equidistant notes, augmented chords) · octatonic (tone/semitone, dim7) · pentatonic (5 notes with no semitone)
Messiaen's modes: internal symmetry + limited transpositions → a unique and recognisable colour (mode 1 = whole-tone scale, mode 2 = octatonic)

analyseNarrative.tonalite: None — the whole-tone collection {C, D, E, F♯, G♯, B♭}, with neither tonic nor any constructible function.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 2/4. Modéré (44 to the quarter note at the outset, highly variable thereafter).
analyseNarrative.forme: A single arch shaped by density and register (not by harmonic tension): exposition — accumulation — pentatonic climax — subsiding — an extinguished coda.

sections.label: Measures 1-4
sections.titre: The theme: the veil as object
sections.chiffrage: Whole tones — parallel major thirds, no bass
sections.texte: Parallel major thirds descend with no bass at all (G♯/E → F♯/D → E/C → D/B♭): the theme slides through the whole-tone collection as over a surface without relief, without the slightest landmark of hierarchised pitch.

sections.label: Measures 5-14
sections.titre: The pedal settles in
sections.texte: A B♭ pedal settles into the bass — and will remain there for fifty-seven measures, all the way to m. 61. Motifs in thirds and descending figures repeat pianissimo above it.

sections.label: Measures 15-22
sections.titre: The augmented organum
sections.chiffrage: Whole tones — parallel augmented triads (A♭-C-E, B♭-D-F♯)
sections.texte: Beneath the theme, the accompanying ostinato reveals the only “harmony” the collection permits: parallel augmented triads — the augmented triad being the only one the whole-tone scale can produce. Debussy makes it his organum, a direct echo of the parallel triads of La Cathédrale engloutie.

sections.label: Measures 23-32
sections.titre: The F♯ stratum and the chromatic ornament
sections.chiffrage: Whole tones — low stratum on F♯; isolated chromatic figure (m. 31)
sections.texte: A low stratum settles on F♯, the collection's other pole. Measure 31 introduces the one real exception in the whole piece: a small chromatic figure (the turn C-D-D♭-C, the slide F♯-G-A♭) that sounds the only pitches foreign to the collection — ornamental chromaticism, not harmony, the exception that proves the rule.

sections.label: Measures 33-41
sections.titre: Amplification
sections.texte: The collection does not change; what changes is density and register — Serrez, dim. molto, Cédez. The intensification is achieved through parameters that classical harmony treated as mere auxiliaries.

sections.label: Measures 42-47
sections.titre: The climax: a change of alphabet
sections.chiffrage: Black-key pentatonic {D♭, E♭, G♭, A♭, B♭}
sections.texte: The only moment in the whole piece where something really changes — and it is neither a chord nor a key, it is the entire collection. Glissandi and pentatonic flurries, mf then f (the only f in the piece), Emporté: the sole “modulation” in Voiles is this tipping over from one alphabet into another.

sections.label: Measures 48-61
sections.titre: Return and subsidence
sections.chiffrage: Whole tones — the B♭ pedal resumed
sections.texte: Theme and ostinato return superimposed in strata, pianissimo, over the same B♭ pedal as at the beginning.

sections.label: Measures 62-64
sections.titre: Coda: the piece goes out
sections.chiffrage: F♯ pedal — bare third C-E (×2), no bass
sections.texte: The pedal abandons B♭ for F♯ over the last three measures, carried by soft sweeps through the collection. Then the third C-E appears alone twice, with no bass — the piece does not conclude, it goes out like a light.

synthese.titre: A collection that makes function impossible
synthese.texte: The whole-tone scale contains neither a perfect fifth, nor a leading note, nor a major or minor triad: no dominant and no cadence is so much as constructible within it. Where La Cathédrale engloutie avoided function while still keeping one, buried, Voiles makes it impossible by construction — one no longer renounces the cadence, one chooses a material in which it does not exist.

synthese.titre: Form as a curve of density
synthese.texte: With no harmonic tension available, it is the number of pitches per measure, the register and the dynamic that draw the form — a gradual accumulation up to the pentatonic climax, then a subsiding into extinction. The B♭ pedal, the only hierarchy that survives, is a “centre” only because it is held.

synthese.titre: The augmented sixth, reduced to a subset
synthese.texte: The most highly charged chord of Romantic chromaticism — the French augmented sixth, the one at Chopin's dramatic summit — is, note for note, no more than a subset of the whole-tone collection in which Debussy lets his veils float for sixty-four measures. The same material, maximum tension turned into weightlessness.

cours31.title: Polytonality and Quartal Harmony
cours31.subtitle: Superimposed tonalities (Stravinsky, Pétrouchka), quartal chords, the So What chord — musical languages beyond classical tonality.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered polytonality and quartal harmony.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few points to consolidate on quartal voicings.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep exploring polytonality — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: The premiere of 'The Rite of Spring' in 1913 provoked a riot in the hall. Stravinsky superimposed tonalities so distant that the audience thought it was a mistake. The Petrushka chord — C major against F# major, a tritone — is the signature of this chosen brutality.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Polytonal tension is not a mistake — it is a language. The distance between tonalities controls the intensity of the clash.
narrative.pPolytonalite: Polytonality superimposes two (or more) distinct tonalities at the same time. Unlike atonality, each layer remains tonal — it is their combination that creates tension or ambiguity.
narrative.infoBoxBitonalite: Bitonality vs polytonality: Bitonality is the most common form — exactly two superimposed tonalities. The distance between the tonics determines the intensity of the clash: third (gentle) → fifth (blurry) → tritone (brutal). Stravinsky favoured the tritone for its maximum tension.
narrative.ex0description: The famous 'Petrushka chord' superimposes C major (C–E–G) and F# major (F#–A#–C#). Interval between the tonics: a tritone — the maximum tension.
narrative.ex0couleur: Brutal tension, tonal clash, tragedy of the character
narrative.ex1description: Two tonalities a fifth apart: much less tension than a tritone. Natural harmonics make C and G close — the polytonality is subtle.
narrative.ex2description: G major chord over F# bass — the F# creates tension with the root G. Common in progressive rock and jazz fusion.
narrative.warnBoxPolytonalite: Polytonality ≠ atonality: In polytonal music, tonal centres are still audible — simply several at once. Analysis must identify each layer separately. Confusing the two systems is the most frequent mistake.
narrative.infoBoxAnalysePolytonale: Polytonal analysis: First identify each layer independently, then note the distance between the tonics (third, fifth, tritone...). The effect depends directly on this distance: tonics a third apart = gentle polytonality (Milhaud); tonics a tritone apart = maximum clash (Stravinsky).
narrative.pQuartale: Quartal harmony replaces the stacking of thirds (C–E–G) with the stacking of fourths (C–F–Bb). Without a third, the chord is neither major nor minor — it creates the modern ambiguity characteristic of modal jazz and 20th-century music.
narrative.infoBoxQuartale: Why fourths change everything: A chord in thirds (triad) has a defined quality (major/minor) and a strong tonal function. A chord in fourths has neither clear quality nor function — it floats. It is precisely this neutrality that Miles Davis and McCoy Tyner exploited in modal jazz.
narrative.aq0description: Three stacked perfect fourths: C–F–Bb. No third → neither major nor minor.
narrative.aq0effet: Pure ambiguity — the chord does not 'pull' toward a resolution
narrative.aq1description: Perfect fourth + augmented fourth (tritone): C–F–B. The final tritone creates a slight harshness.
narrative.aq1structure: C + perfect fourth → F + tritone → B
narrative.aq1effet: More tense than the pure fourth — characteristic harshness
narrative.aq2description: 4-note voicing in fourths: D–G–C–F. Signature of the modal jazz piano (Coltrane quartet).
narrative.aq2effet: Immediately recognisable 'modal jazz' sound — total harmonic openness
narrative.aq3description: Miles Davis's signature chord from 'So What': 4 fourths + major third at the top. D–G–C–F–A.
narrative.aq3effet: Emblematic modal jazz chord — spacious, neither major nor minor
narrative.h3SoWhat: Building the So What chord on any note
narrative.pSoWhat: The So What chord always follows the same formula: Note + fourth + fourth + fourth + major third. On D: D–G–C–F–A. This formula transposes exactly everywhere.
narrative.warnBoxQuartale: Common mistake: Analysing quartal chords with T/SD/D functions. Quartal harmony works by colour and ambiguity, not by functional progression. In 'So What', the two chords (D and Eb) are not a II–III — they are two juxtaposed colours.

conservatoire.intuition: Two keys at once is like two conversations in different languages — the brain hears both and builds a meaning that cannot be pulled apart into either one.

reference.badge: Messiaen · The Technique of My Musical Language
reference.citation: Polytonality is the superposition of two distinct tonal centres. The result belongs to neither one nor the other — it creates a new harmonic space.

voix: Polytonality is not atonality — each layer stays tonal, and it is their combination that creates the tension. You can always still hear the two keys separately.
Quartal harmony has no third → neither major nor minor → controlled ambiguity. It is this absence of quality that creates the 'open', 'modern' sound.
Miles Davis's 'So What chord' (D–G–C–F–A) is the quartal chord par excellence of modal jazz — learn to build it on every note.

pieges.erreur: Confusing polytonality with atonality
pieges.correction: Polytonality superimposes distinct keys — each layer stays tonal. Atonality avoids any tonal reference. They are two different systems.

pieges.erreur: Believing that quartal chords have no logic
pieges.correction: Quartal harmony has a precise logic: stacked fourths (perfect or augmented). The 'So What voicing' follows strict rules of registration.

pieges.erreur: Looking for T/SD/D functions in polytonal music
pieges.correction: Polytonality works by superimposing planes, not by functional progression. The analysis must identify the two (or more) tonal centres, not the functions.

resume: Polytonality: simultaneous superposition of different keys — gentle (neighbouring keys) or brutal (tritone, as in Stravinsky's Petrushka)
Quartal chords: built by stacking fourths (C–F–B♭ or C–F–B). Neither major nor minor → modern ambiguity.
So What chord: D–G–C–F–A (4 fourths + a major third on top) — the emblematic modal-jazz voicing

analyseNarrative.tonalite: No single key — active polarity between C major and F# major, two triads a tritone apart.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. No tempo indication (demonstration sheet).
analyseNarrative.forme: A demonstration in seven stages: the two protagonists on their own, their collision, their melodised form, then two scholarly readings (synthetic scale, octatonic collection), and the closing formula.

sections.label: Bars 1-2
sections.titre: The two protagonists
sections.texte: C major first, the most consonant triad of the tonal system. Then F# major, its exact antipode at the tritone — not a single note in common between the two, the white keys against the black keys.

sections.label: Bar 3
sections.titre: The collision: the Petrushka chord
sections.texte: The two triads sound simultaneously, each perfectly intact, one to a hand. The dissonance is no longer inside the chord — each half remains a plain major triad — but between the systems: the conflict has moved from the level of the interval to the level of tonality itself.

sections.label: Bar 4
sections.titre: The melodised form
sections.texte: The alternating form, that of the two clarinets in the second tableau: the F# appears in first inversion (A# in the bass). The two worlds answer each other instead of striking one another.

sections.label: Bar 5
sections.titre: First scholarly reading: the tritone scale
sections.texte: Taken together, the six pitches of the two triads form a synthetic hexatonic scale alternating major third and semitone — the 'tritone scale'. A scale-object in its own right, not merely the sum of two chords.

sections.label: Bar 6
sections.titre: Second scholarly reading: the octatonic collection
sections.texte: Both triads sit natively within the complete octatonic collection — Taruskin's reading, for whom the Petrushka chord is not a collision between two foreign systems but two diatonic crystallisations of one and the same symmetrical collection.

sections.label: Bar 7
sections.titre: Active polarity
sections.chiffrage: C major + F#/A#, held under a fermata
sections.texte: The chord closes under a fermata, labelled with the formula that sums up the debate: active polarity. Not a passive blend of twelve pitches, but two tonal forces held in tension, neither of them giving way.

synthese.titre: The third way of 1911
synthese.texte: After Wagner, who suspended resolution indefinitely, and Debussy, who made it by turns avoided and then unconstructible, Stravinsky invents a third way out: function is neither suspended nor dissolved, it is preserved but doubled. The conflict itself becomes the material.

synthese.titre: Two readings, one single object
synthese.texte: The Petrushka chord can be heard as a collision of two foreign keys, or as two crystallisations of a single octatonic collection — both readings are true at once, and it is precisely this double status that gives the object its whole theoretical interest.

synthese.titre: Stravinsky lexicalised
synthese.texte: The tritone scale and pairs of triads a tritone apart have become a standard tool of modern improvisation — the 'triad pairs' and the sub-V substitutions of the jazz vocabulary. Stravinsky is taken up sixty years later exactly as Debussy was by Evans: a theoretical object turned into lexicon.

cours32.title: Advanced Jazz Extensions and Modern Reharmonization
cours32.subtitle: b9, #9, #11, b13 — available tensions by chord degree, Coltrane's Giant Steps and advanced substitutions for creative reharmonization.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered altered extensions and Coltrane changes.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few tensions to refine — b9 vs #9, and the Giant Steps cycle.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep studying Coltrane — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Coltrane composed 'Giant Steps' in 1960 — a chord progression rotating around 3 tonal centers a major third apart (B, G, Eb). The tempo was so fast that even the best pianists couldn't accompany him in rehearsals. McCoy Tyner had to learn a whole new harmonic language to keep up.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: When the progression moves too fast to think chord by chord, you need to find the geometric system underneath.
narrative.pExtensions: Altered extensions add notes beyond the seventh. On a dominant chord (V7), these extensions create specific colors — from dark tension (b9) to funky sound (#9) and the Lydian (#11). Each extension has its own source scale.
narrative.infoBoxGuideTones: Guide-tone rule: The third and seventh of a dominant chord (B and F in G7) are the essential notes — they define the chord quality and guide the resolution. Extensions are added on top without obscuring these guide-tones.
narrative.pTensionsTable: Not all extensions are stylistically appropriate on every degree. The table below lists 'available' tensions (that sound good) and those to avoid.
narrative.warnBoxExtensions: Common mistake: Stacking b9 and #9 simultaneously — they create contradictory colors (dark vs funky). Choose ONE extension color per chord based on the desired effect. On G7: b9 (Ravel, flamenco) OR #9 (Hendrix, funk) — not both.
narrative.pColtrane: John Coltrane developed a reharmonization technique based on the cycle of major thirds. Rather than staying in one key, he replaces a chord with three tonal centers a major third apart — forming a perfect triangle on the circle of fifths.
narrative.infoBoxTriangle: Coltrane's triangle: B, G, and Eb are each exactly a major third apart. These three tonics divide the octave into three equal parts. Cycling through all three in 16 bars at fast tempo creates the 'Giant Steps' effect — too fast for the ear to follow, but geometrically perfect.
narrative.pSubstitutions: Reharmonization replaces the original chords with others that maintain the same function or color, but with a different harmonic flavor.
narrative.warnBoxSubstitution: Tritone substitution — the rule: It only works on V7, not on all chords. G7 → Db7 works because they share the same guide-tones (B/C# · F/Eb). Attempting a tritone substitution on IMaj7 or IIm7 produces a non-stylistic dissonance — the characteristic note changes role.
narrative.cycleBtn: ▶ Listen to the cycle BMaj7 → GMaj7 → EbMaj7
narrative.sequenceLabel: Full Giant Steps sequence: B – G – Eb (3 tonics a major third apart)

conservatoire.intuition: Coltrane did not break the rules — he uncovered a deeper level of rules than the one everybody else could see.

reference.citation: Coltrane's substitutions are not harmonic mistakes — they are ultra-fast modulations to keys related by major thirds.

voix: Every chord degree has its own specific set of 'available' tensions: V7 accepts b9/#9/#11/b13; IMaj7 accepts 9/#11/13; IIm7 accepts 9/11. Outside those tensions, the note creates a dissonance foreign to the style.
The b9 (flat ninth) sounds dark and Spanish; the #9 (sharp ninth) sounds 'Hendrix' and funky. Same underlying chord, radically different colors.
Giant Steps revolves around 3 keys a major third apart: B, G, E♭ — a perfect triangle on the circle of fifths, traversed in 16 measures.

repertoire.titre: Giant Steps (piano arrangement in 7/4, Jacob Koller)

pieges.erreur: Using every extension at once
pieges.correction: Extensions can be stacked, but they contradict one another: b9 and #9 together create an unmusical cluster. Choose one color: dark (b9), funky (#9) or lydian (#11).

pieges.erreur: Alterations with no voice-leading direction
pieges.correction: Every alteration implies a resolution: the b9 resolves to the third of I, the #11 to the fifth of I. An alteration that never resolves has no functional meaning.

pieges.erreur: Confusing b9 and #9 (very different colors)
pieges.correction: G7b9 = G–B–D–F–A♭ → dark, expressive, flamenco. G7#9 = G–B–D–F–A♯ → funky, electric, 'Purple Haze'. Same root, completely opposite effect.

resume: Altered extensions: b9 (dark) · #9 (funky/Hendrix) · #11 (lydian dominant) · b5/b13 (altered) — each with its own specific color
Available tensions by degree: IMaj7 (9,#11,13) · IIm7 (9,11) · V7 (b9,#9,#11,b13) · Im7 (9,11,b13) · IIm7b5 (b9,11,b13)
Giant Steps: a cycle of major thirds B–G–E♭ — a perfect triangle sweeping through 3 keys in 16 measures at a fast tempo

analyseNarrative.tonalite: Three equidistant centers — B, G, E♭ — dividing the octave into equal major thirds (an augmented triad), with no hierarchy among them.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 7/4. Very brisk (quarter note = 242).
analyseNarrative.forme: Intro (mm. 1-8) — head (mm. 9-16) — head again in widened voicings (mm. 17-24) — reharmonized variation (mm. 25-32) — written solo, 6 choruses of 8 measures (mm. 33-80) — head out (mm. 81-88) — rubato coda (mm. 89-98).

sections.label: The 7/4 trick
sections.titre: Two measures for the price of one
sections.texte: Koller's arrangement compresses each pair of 4/4 measures of the original changes into a single measure of 7/4: one beat is spirited away from every pair. The most breathless set of changes in jazz — one tonal center per strong beat, or very nearly — is thereby accelerated further still: the ear never gets the eight beats it expects in order to digest a pair of cadences.

sections.label: Measures 9-16
sections.titre: The head: the complete changes
sections.fonctions: T (×8, every measure opens on a local tonic)
sections.texte: Taken one at a time, every cadence is perfectly functional — nothing but textbook V7→I and ii–V–I progressions, Mozart's syntax intact. What changes is the speed at which the center moves: B, G, E♭, B, E♭, G, B, E♭ — never time enough to settle.

sections.label: The Coltrane changes
sections.titre: Three tonics, one augmented triad
sections.texte: The circuit of the three tonal centers divides the octave into three strictly equal parts: B, G and E♭ form an augmented triad — the very same chord as the one yielded by the whole-tone scale of Voiles. That symmetry abolishes hierarchy: three equidistant tonics, none of them dominant, a cycle turning with no center of gravity, exactly as the whole-tone collection turned with no leading tone.

sections.label: Measures 33-88
sections.titre: Solo and head out
sections.chiffrage: 6 choruses of 8 measures over the same cycle, then the theme returns
sections.texte: Six written-out choruses run through the same harmonic cycle, before the head comes back unaltered to close the form.

sections.label: Measures 89-98
sections.titre: The coda: a door that was never there
sections.chiffrage: Sweep over E lydian (E-F♯-G♯-A♯-B-C♯-D♯), ending on a bare E
sections.texte: After ninety-five measures of perfect rotation between B, G and E♭, the coda leaves through a tonic that does not belong to the cycle: a rubato sweep across nearly seven octaves unfurls the E lydian scale, and the piece dies away on a bare E, with no functional relation whatsoever to B-G-E♭. The A♯ of that E lydian is the same color — the #11 — traced from Evans to Debussy throughout the rest of this corpus.

synthese.titre: The final reversal
synthese.texte: Mozart set an asymmetrical cycle (the fifths) turning around a gravitational center. Coltrane sets the very same cadential syntax — V7 to I, textbook ii-V-I — turning on a symmetrical orbit, with no gravity at all. Function survived everything: Beethoven, Wagner, Debussy. It ends here, engine intact, mounted on a chassis that no longer is.

synthese.titre: Two divisions of the octave, one and the same problem
synthese.texte: Stravinsky superimposed two keys a tritone apart (dividing the octave by 2); Coltrane strings together three keys a major third apart (dividing it by 3). Two answers to the same exhaustion of the hierarchy of fifths — one by vertical conflict, the other by horizontal rotation.

synthese.titre: A color that loops back on itself
synthese.texte: The A♯ of the closing E lydian is none other than the augmented eleventh — the same color that, elsewhere in this journey, links Bill Evans's language to Debussy's. The most 'outside' gesture in the piece unwittingly closes one of the loops of the corpus as a whole.

cours27.title: Deep Functional Analysis
cours27.subtitle: Tonal hierarchies, harmonic prolongation and Schenkerian reduction — learning to see the deep structure of a work behind its surface chords.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered deep functional analysis and Schenkerian reduction.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few nuances to refine on the Ursatz and prolongations.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep studying structural analysis — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Schenker was convinced that all great tonal music rests on an identical deep structure — the Ursatz. Behind the apparent complexity of Bach or Beethoven, he always saw the same fundamental arch.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Understanding a work means seeing through the surface notes down to its skeletal structure.
narrative.pHierarchies1: Tonal harmony does not treat all chords equally. Each chord belongs to a functional region — tonic (T), subdominant (SD) or dominant (D) — which determines its role in the directional logic of music.
narrative.pHierarchies2: The essential distinction: surface harmony refers to all chords visible in the score; structural harmony retains only the pillars that carry the deep tonal logic.
narrative.regionToniqueDesc: Chords of rest and stability. Share at least two notes with the tonic chord. Role: anchoring and prolongation of the tonal center.
narrative.regionSousDomDesc: Intermediate preparation chords. Create directional movement between T and D without the maximum tension of the dominant.
narrative.regionDomDesc: Maximum tension chords. Contain the tritone (leading tone + 4th) which demands resolution to I. V7 is the dominant chord par excellence.
narrative.infoBoxDirection: Directional rule: The canonical functional progression is T → SD → D → T. Every well-formed tonal progression follows this direction. The reverse movement (D → SD or SD → T directly after SD) creates functional backwards movements to avoid.
narrative.h3CouchesAnalyse: Layered analysis — surface vs deep structure
narrative.pCouchesAnalyse: The same harmonic progression can be read at three levels of depth. The more one reduces, the more the fundamental tonal structure appears.
narrative.coucheSurfaceDesc: All chords as they appear in the score — passing chords, neighbor notes, ornaments included.
narrative.coucheIntermDesc: Chords grouped by function. Ornaments and passing chords are eliminated. Only the functional pillars remain.
narrative.coucheProfondDesc: The Ursatz: fundamental structure. A single prolongation T→D→T reveals the tonal arch of the work.
narrative.pExempleSonore: Listen to this excerpt from Chorale BWV 227 in C major. The surface melody ornaments a simple deep structure: prolonged I → V → I.
narrative.warnBoxPiege: Common pitfall: Analyzing each chord in isolation, without seeing the functional region to which it belongs. Harmonic logic is directional — T→SD→D→T — not a succession of independent chords.
narrative.pUrsatz: Heinrich Schenker (1868–1935) developed a layered analysis method that reveals the deep tonal structure of every great work. At the foundation of all tonal music, he sees one same structure: the Ursatz, composed of the Urlinie (soprano) and the Bassbrechung (bass).
narrative.urlinieTexte: The Urlinie is the fundamental melodic descent of the soprano. It begins from a Kopfton (covering note: 3̂, 5̂ or 8̂) and descends diatonically to 1̂ (tonic). Three possible forms:
narrative.urlinieLi1: 3̂–2̂–1̂ (third descent) — the most common in short forms
narrative.urlinieLi2: 5̂–4̂–3̂–2̂–1̂ (fifth descent) — very common in Bach and Mozart
narrative.h3Bassbrechung: The Bassbrechung — I–V–I arch in the bass
narrative.bassbrechungTexte: The Bassbrechung is the fundamental bass arch: I–V–I. It describes the fifth movement (C→G→C) that structures tonality at any scale — from a 4-measure phrase to an entire symphony. The Bassbrechung is the universal harmonic law of tonal music.
narrative.h3MethodeReduction: Reduction method in 4 steps — Mozart K.331
narrative.step1Detail: Analyze each chord in the score and name it. Omit nothing at this step — this is the complete Vordergrund.
narrative.step1Exemple: Mozart K.331 mm.1–4: I – V6 – I – IV6 – I6/4 – V – I
narrative.step2Detail: Identify which chords belong to T (I, III, VI), SD (II, IV) or D (V, VII). Locate prolongations.
narrative.step2Exemple: T(prolonged) – SD – T(cad. 6/4) – D – T: intermediate structure
narrative.step3Detail: Locate the opening chord (I), the medial cadence (V or half-cadence), the final cadence (V–I). These are the pillars of the Bassbrechung.
narrative.step3Exemple: Mozart K.331: I (m.1) → V (m.8) → I (m.16) — Bassbrechung over 16 measures
narrative.step4Detail: Extract the fundamental soprano descent (Kopfton → 1̂) and the bass arch (I–V–I). Superimpose them: that is the Ursatz.
narrative.step4Exemple: Urlinie 3̂–2̂–1̂ (E–D–C) over Bassbrechung I–V–I = complete Ursatz
narrative.infoBoxUrsatz: The Ursatz in summary: Superimpose the Urlinie (soprano descending from 3̂/5̂/8̂ to 1̂) and the Bassbrechung (bass I–V–I). This two-voice counterpoint is the universal fundamental structure of all tonal music — every work is an elaborate prolongation of it.
narrative.warnBoxReduction: Caution: Schenkerian reduction does not simplify arbitrarily — it reveals the structural hierarchy. Never skip steps: start with the complete surface, then reduce layer by layer down to the Ursatz.

conservatoire.intuition: A forty-minute symphony is often I–V–I on a vast scale, with ornaments.

reference.citation: All tonal music rests on one and the same fundamental structure: a descent in the soprano and an arpeggiation of the fifth in the bass. The rest is nothing but ornamentation.

voix: Distinguish surface harmony (every chord) from structural harmony (the tonal pillars): a prolongation can make a single chord 'last' for several bars.
The Urlinie always descends to 1̂ (the tonic) — identify the starting note (3̂, 5̂ or 8̂) and trace the fundamental melodic descent.
Do not analyse each chord in isolation: look for the functional group (T, SD, D), then for the prolongation that realizes it.

repertoire.compositeur: J. Crüger / harmonization in the tradition of J. S. Bach (BWV 227)

pieges.erreur: Analysing every chord without seeing the overall structure
pieges.correction: Begin by identifying the pillars: the opening (I), the medial cadence, the final cadence (V–I). Everything else is prolongation.

pieges.erreur: Confusing surface harmony with structural harmony
pieges.correction: A neighbouring or passing chord (between two chords belonging to the same pillar) is not a structural pillar — it prolongs the main chord.

pieges.erreur: Reducing too quickly, without intermediate stages
pieges.correction: Reduce in 3 stages: 1) write down every chord, 2) group them by function (T/SD/D), 3) identify the principal prolongation.

resume: Layered analysis: surface (every chord) → middleground (functions grouped together) → background (a single T→D→T prolongation)
Urlinie: a soprano descent from 3̂, 5̂ or 8̂ down to 1̂ — the fundamental line of the melodic argument
Bassbrechung: the bass arch I–V–I — the tonal structure on the scale of the entire work

analyseNarrative.tonalite: B minor.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Tempo quarter = 64.
analyseNarrative.forme: Bar form AAB: Stollen (3 phrases, mm. 1–6) repeated note for note (mm. 7–12), then Abgesang (mm. 13–19).

sections.label: Phrase 1 (mm. 1–2)
sections.titre: A bass descent that parcels out the tonic
sections.chiffrage: i – v6 – iv6 – vii°4/2 – VI – iiø6/5 – V7 – i
sections.texte: The bass descends by step (B-A-G) beneath a held soprano note, each step carrying its own chord — i, v6, iv6 — before a passing chord slips in on the upbeat: a diminished seventh on the leading tone in third inversion (vii°4/2, the seventh in the bass), which resolves onto VI. The cadence that follows presents the first half-diminished chord of the piece (iiø6/5) before the V7 and the tonic.

sections.label: Phrase 2 (mm. 3–4)
sections.titre: A tonicization in a flash, a climb back to the dominant
sections.chiffrage: i – V/A – I6/A – III – i – i6 – V
sections.texte: A brief detour tonicizes A major (its own dominant, E, appears for the space of a single chord) before sliding onto III (D). The bass then climbs back by step (B-C♯-D-E) towards the half cadence on F♯ major, which closes the phrase on the dominant.

sections.label: Phrase 3 (mm. 5–6) — and its repeat (mm. 7–12)
sections.titre: The 4–3 suspension and the tonic held under a fermata
sections.chiffrage: VI – i6/4 – V (4–3 suspension) – V7 – i (fermata)
sections.texte: The finest cadence of the Stollen: over the dominant, an inner voice holds B against the F♯ in the bass (a 4–3 suspension) and gives way only on the very last beat of the bar — the chord becomes a complete V7 only at the instant of resolution itself. The tonic that follows is held under a fermata. The whole six bars (mm. 1–6) then return note for note (mm. 7–12): the same bass, the same chords, the same resolution of the suspension — a Stollen written out in full, not merely indicated by a repeat sign.

sections.label: Abgesang, phrases 4–5 (mm. 13–14)
sections.titre: The only stretch of major in the whole chorale
sections.chiffrage: i – III – V6/5/III – III – ii6/5 – V7/III – III
sections.fonctions: T – (modulation to the relative) – SD – D – T
sections.texte: The Abgesang opens with a genuine modulation to the relative major (D), properly installed by its own secondary dominant (A7) and then confirmed by a full cadence (ii6/5 – V7 – I) in D major — the only moment in the whole piece that frankly leaves the minor mode.

sections.label: Phrase 6 (mm. 15–17)
sections.titre: The dramatic summit
sections.chiffrage: III – vii°/A – I6/A – III – i – v – iiø4/3 of F♯ – V7/v – F♯: I = B minor: V
sections.fonctions: T – T (passing) – T (minor) – D (arrival on the majorized dominant)
sections.texte: A return to B minor by way of its own dominant (F♯ minor), then a second half-diminished chord (iiø4/3 of F♯, this time the subdominant of the dominant) which prepares a C♯7 (V7/v) resolving onto F♯ major — a complete ii–V–i towards the dominant, but with the final chord turned major. This bar carries an editorial slip: the E♯ expected in the C♯7 is notated as F natural in an inner voice, an enharmonic spelling that would make the reading absurd for a singer reading that third in the choir rather than playing it at the keyboard. The following bar opens out into rests after its first chord — the breathing of the German text, preserved by the hymn.

sections.label: Final phrase (mm. 18–19)
sections.titre: The cadential formula in full
sections.chiffrage: iv6 – cadential i6/4 – iiø6/5 – V7 – I
sections.texte: The final cadence deploys the complete formula — subdominant, cadential tonic, half-diminished chord, dominant, tonic — and the last chord carries the only D♯ in the whole piece: a Picardy third, sung by the lowest inner voice above the bass.

synthese.titre: A single prolongation for the whole Stollen
synthese.texte: Beneath the many surface chords (v6, iv6, vii°4/2, VI, iiø6/5…), the Stollen in fact carries out one single structural gesture: a tonic that arpeggiates towards its dominant (the half cadence of m. 4) before returning to it (the fermata of m. 6). Everything else — every chord figured phrase by phrase — prolongs one or other pole of this i–V–i framework, without ever calling it into question.

synthese.titre: From the summit to the tonic: a single melodic line
synthese.texte: The soprano opens on the fifth (F♯) and closes the piece on the tonic (B): the same descending trajectory that organizes the surface melody — each phrase rising and then falling back — is found again, on a far larger scale, in the form of the whole chorale.

synthese.titre: The diminished chord: nothing but an interval filled in
synthese.texte: The diminished seventh of m. 1 and the half-diminished chords of mm. 2, 16 and 18 look, on the surface, like dramatic events. Reduced to their structural function, they are no more than harmonized chromatic passing notes — the bass could have descended without them. Ornament makes the colour; it does not make the structure.

cours28.title: Musical Forms in Depth
cours28.subtitle: Binary, ternary, rondo, sonata form — anatomy of the great musical architectures, with guided analysis of Mozart, Bach and Beethoven.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered all the major musical forms.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few points to consolidate on sonata form.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep studying musical forms — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Beethoven stretched sonata form to its limits — the Ninth Symphony lasts 70 minutes where Mozart would take 25. He understood that form is not a container but a dramatic force in itself.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Form is not where you put the music — it is what the music becomes.
narrative.pFormes: Musical form is the organization of discourse in time. It determines how musical ideas succeed, contrast and resolve. Each major period developed its own formal architectures.
narrative.infoBoxPrincipe: Fundamental principle: Every great form creates a tonal tension that awaits resolution. In sonata form, it is T2 at the dominant that demands a return to the tonic. Form is not a container — it is a harmonic force that unfolds through time.
narrative.formeBinaireDesc: Binary form alternates two repeated sections. Section A creates tonal instability (often moving to the dominant); section B resolves to the tonic. It is the structure of Baroque dances.
narrative.formeBinaireEx2: Allemandes and courantes from the Well-Tempered Clavier
narrative.formeTernaireTonalite: A → tonic · B → contrasting key · A' → tonic
narrative.formeTernaireDesc: Ternary form presents a theme (A), a contrasting section (B), then the return of the theme (A'). It structures the minuet, scherzo, nocturne and many Romantic pieces.
narrative.formeRondoTonalite: A always at the tonic · B, C → contrasting keys
narrative.formeRondoDesc: The rondo alternates a refrain (A) always at the tonic with contrasting episodes (B, C…). It is the typical form of Classical finales — its cyclical character suits the conclusion.
narrative.formeRondoEx1: Finale of the Pathétique Sonata op. 13 (Beethoven)
narrative.formeSonateTonalite: T1 tonic · T2 dominant → modulations → T1 + T2 at the TONIC
narrative.formeSonateDesc: Sonata form is the great instrumental form of Classicism. It creates a tonal tension (T2 at the dominant) that only the recapitulation can resolve (T2 at the tonic). It is a complete musical dramaturgy.
narrative.sonateExpTonalite: T1 at the tonic · T2 at the dominant (major) or relative major (minor)
narrative.sonateExpDetail: The exposition presents the two main themes in two distinct keys. T1 establishes the home key; a transition modulates to T2 in the dominant key (in major). This tonal tension is the driving force of the whole sonata.
narrative.sonateDevTonalite: Free modulations — FORBIDDEN to stay in the tonic
narrative.sonateDevDetail: The development fragments, combines and modulates from the material of the exposition. It must pass through several keys — that is its dramatic role. It concludes on V (dominant), preparing the return.
narrative.sonateReexTonalite: T1 at the tonic · T2 at the TONIC (fundamental resolution)
narrative.sonateReexDetail: The recapitulation restates the exposition but with T2 at the TONIC instead of the dominant. This is the harmonic resolution of the entire form. The transition is modified to stay in the tonic.
narrative.pAnalyse: Comparing works in different forms allows us to perceive how each architecture organizes harmonic and temporal space differently. These three works illustrate three distinct formal logics.
narrative.oeuvre1Desc: This prelude is a continuous harmonic progression in arpeggios — no distinct themes, no formal binary or ternary structure. Bach unfolds a succession of arpeggiated chords from I to I, with remarkable harmonic enrichments (II7, V7). It is a pre-Classical form close to the toccata.
narrative.oeuvre2Desc: K. 331 is unique among Mozart's sonatas: its first movement is a theme and variations — not a sonata form. The theme in A major is followed by six variations that transform its rhythm, melody and harmony. The famous Rondo alla Turca is the finale of this sonata.
narrative.oeuvre3Desc: The Pathétique is distinguished by a slow introduction (Grave) in C minor that precedes the Allegro di molto e con brio. Beethoven brings this Grave back in the middle of the development and at the end of the recapitulation — an original formal expansion that goes beyond the classic sonata scheme.
narrative.infoBoxRetenir: Key takeaway: Bach (harmonic arpeggiation) → no distinct themes, contrapuntal logic. Mozart K. 331 (theme and variations) → a single transformed theme. Beethoven op. 13 (enriched sonata form) → two themes, harmonic tension, and return of the opening Grave in the development.

conservatoire.intuition: Form is harmony unfolding in time.

reference.citation: Musical form is not a mould into which one pours the music — it is the logical consequence of thematic and harmonic development.

voix: In sonata form, the second theme is always in the TONIC in the recapitulation — even if it was in the dominant in the exposition. It is the harmonic resolution of the entire form.
The development MUST modulate: staying in the main key throughout the development is a serious formal fault.
Distinguish phrase form (antecedent–consequent) from large-scale form (exposition–development–recapitulation) — two distinct hierarchical levels.

repertoire.titre: Sonata in C major K. 545, first movement — complete exposition

pieges.erreur: Confusing phrase form with large-scale form
pieges.correction: Phrase form (a 4-bar antecedent + a 4-bar consequent) is a micro level. Large-scale form (sonata, rondo) is a macro level lasting several minutes.

pieges.erreur: Putting the second theme in the dominant in the recapitulation (in the major mode)
pieges.correction: In the recapitulation the second theme ALWAYS returns in the tonic. That is the fundamental harmonic resolution of sonata form — without it there is no resolution.

pieges.erreur: A development without modulations
pieges.correction: The development must travel through several keys — that is its dramatic role. A development that stays in the main key misses its purpose.

pieges.erreur: A recapitulation identical to the exposition
pieges.correction: The recapitulation always differs from the exposition on one crucial point: the second theme is in the tonic, not in the dominant. Often the transition is shortened as well.

resume: Sonata form: Exposition (T1 in the tonic + T2 in the dominant) → Development (modulations) → Recapitulation (T1 and T2 both in the TONIC)
Simple forms: binary (AB, tonally unstable→stable) · ternary (ABA) · rondo (ABACA, cyclical return)
Analysis: identify the sections by their key, not only by their themes

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C major, modulating to G major (the dominant) for the second theme.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Tempo quarter = 140.
analyseNarrative.forme: Sonata-form exposition: first theme (1–4), scales (5–8), modulating transition (9–13), second theme (14–17), descending-fifths sequence (18–21), cadence and codetta (22–28).

sections.label: Measures 1-4
sections.titre: First theme: harmony as breathing
sections.texte: Four bars, four function-and-tonic pairs: each bar steps away from the tonic by way of a gentle inversion (the seventh of the V4/3 within the Alberti bass, the neighbouring six-four of the IV) before falling straight back onto it. The tonic is never left for more than half a beat — the simplest harmony imaginable, yet laid out with no economy whatsoever.

sections.label: Measures 5-8
sections.titre: The scales: a harmony slower than the virtuosity
sections.texte: The runs that terrify students carry, harmonically, no more than one chord per bar (two in m. 7): the left hand marks out half notes while the right hand unwinds its scales. Virtuosity is always laid over a harmonic rhythm slower than itself.

sections.label: Measures 9-13
sections.titre: The transition: a modulation in three gestures
sections.chiffrage: ii (C♯, melodic minor) – G: V6 (sequence F-G-A-F♯) – G: I (= C: V) – link C♯→C♮
sections.texte: First ii (D minor), whose rising melodic-minor scale sounds the C♯ — the first accidental in the piece. Then a sequence: the bass F-G-A-F♯ converts that C♯ into a genuine local leading tone (D/F♯ becomes V6 of G). The arrival on G (mm. 11–12), asserted in arpeggios, is the medial caesura — that same G is still heard as V of C at the very moment it settles in as I. Measure 13, a single unaccompanied line, closes the transition: the left hand alone oscillates C♯-D and then C♮-D, the same pair of notes separating two functions of the same chromatic degree.

sections.label: Measures 14-17
sections.titre: Second theme: a periodic rocking
sections.texte: In G major the second theme curls up over a simple I6–V7 rocking, the left-hand figuration decorating a D pedal while the C♮ installs the seventh above it. Appoggiaturas G→F♯ punctuate the ending of each period.

sections.label: Measures 18-21
sections.titre: The sequence: the complete circle of fifths
sections.chiffrage: I – IV – vii°6 – iii – vi6 – ii – V6/5 – I
sections.fonctions: T – SD – D – T – T – SD – D – T
sections.texte: The analytical summit of the exposition: eight functions, two per bar, not one exception — a diatonic circle of fifths traversed in its entirety (G-C-F♯°-Bm-Em-Am-D7-G), with the melody descending above it in an exact sequence.

sections.label: Measures 22-28
sections.titre: Cadence and codetta
sections.chiffrage: ii6 (×2) – I6/4 (cadential) – V7 (trill) – I – I (low 8ve) – I
sections.texte: The cadential formula is stretched out with relish: two full bars of ii6 (A minor over C, in tremolo), then the cadential six-four, the V7 adorned with the regulation trill on A, the resolution, and a codetta in octave echoes. The exposition closes on G — the dominant of the main key: the contract of sonata form is signed, and it falls to the development to untie it.

synthese.titre: The textbook written by the piece that illustrates it
synthese.texte: Every section of the exposition occupies its exact place in the plan of sonata form — first theme, modulating bridge, second theme in the dominant, pre-cadential sequence, cadence — without the slightest deviation. This is the very piece from which generations of treatises drew their model plan.

synthese.titre: A single modulation, three distinct gestures
synthese.texte: Getting from C to G takes only a handful of bars, but each of its three stages (local tonicization, chromatic sequence, arrival at the medial caesura) has its own logic — classical modulation is not a leap, it is a demonstration in several steps.

synthese.titre: The circle of fifths, a universal circuit
synthese.texte: The sequence of mm. 18–21 runs through the whole diatonic circle of fifths — the same circuit that, dressed differently (minor mode, jazz-style sevenths), structures progressions written far later. Here it is a sequence inside the form; elsewhere, that same circuit can become the entire form.

cours29.title: Comparative Repertoire Analysis
cours29.subtitle: Baroque, Classical, Romantic, Impressionist — 5 historical periods and their harmonic signatures, illustrated by one melody harmonized 5 different ways.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You can precisely identify styles and historical harmonic periods.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few stylistic nuances to refine.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep comparing styles — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Debussy refused to be called 'impressionist'. He preferred 'French musician'. But when asked about his harmonic rules, he replied: 'My pleasure is my rule.' Paradoxically, his apparent freedom rests on a perfect knowledge of everything he was transgressing.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: To break free from the rules, you must first master them perfectly.
narrative.pEvolution: From the Baroque to Impressionism, harmonic language passed through 5 major stylistic periods. Each redefines the relationship to dissonance, resolution and tonal functions. Click a period to explore it.
narrative.infoBoxCritere: Identification criterion: what is the relationship to the dominant? Bach: mandatory — Mozart: assertive and economical — Schubert: enriched — Wagner: suspended — Debussy: absent.
