narrative.pComparaison: The melody C–E–G–C is harmonized here in 5 different styles. Same melody, radically distinct harmonic worlds. Compare the treatment of the dominant, dissonances and colors for each period.
narrative.harmonisationBaroqueDesc: Strict counterpoint, assertive V7–I cadence. The melody is supported by an independent counterpoint.
narrative.harmonisationClassiqueDesc: I–IV–V–I economical and clear. The Alberti bass accompanies discreetly.
narrative.harmonisationRomantiqueDesc: I–bVI–V–I with chromaticism. The borrowing from the minor creates an unexpected dark color.
narrative.harmonisationPostRomDesc: I–III–bVII–I with tonal ambiguity. The tonic arrives but after an unexpected detour.
narrative.harmonisationImpressDesc: Parallel 9th chords. No functional resolution — color takes precedence over tension.
narrative.infoBoxObserver: To observe: compare the bass on the 2nd chord of each harmonization. Bach descends toward the dominant G. Debussy rises in parallel motion. The difference lies there — in the logic of bass movement.

conservatoire.intuition: The history of harmony is the history of dissonance turning into consonance.

reference.citation: Every dissonance is a consonance that has not yet been resolved. The ear grows accustomed to anything — what shocks today will be commonplace tomorrow.

voix: Identify the historical period of a work from three clues: the density of the chromaticism, the presence or absence of a V–I resolution, and the treatment of dissonance.
Analyse Debussy with his own tools (colour, parallelism, modes) and not with T/SD/D functions — his chords are patches of colour, not functions.
Historical context is no excuse for analytical mistakes: Debussy knew perfectly well the rules he was breaking.

repertoire.titre: La Cathédrale engloutie (Préludes, Book I, No. 10)

pieges.erreur: Believing that Debussy has no harmonic rules
pieges.correction: Debussy had a complete mastery of counterpoint and of classical harmony. His freedom is a conscious, calculated transgression, not ignorance.

pieges.erreur: Confusing style with period
pieges.correction: Bach and Handel are contemporaries, yet very different. Analysing a composer by his period alone is not enough — individual signatures come first.

pieges.erreur: Analysing Debussy with T/SD/D functions
pieges.correction: Debussy refuses those functions. His chords progress by colour, register and melodic contour — not by tension and resolution. Looking for “dominants” in Debussy is looking for the wrong thing.

pieges.erreur: Ignoring historical context in an analysis
pieges.correction: A parallel fifth in Bach is a mistake. In Debussy it is a deliberate effect (planing). Context decides whether it is an error or a technique.

resume: 5 periods: Baroque (counterpoint + clear functions) → Classical (symmetrical forms + affirmed cadences) → Romantic (chromaticism + modulations) → Post-Romantic (extended tonality) → Impressionist (colour without functions)
The same melody, 5 harmonisations: the melody C–E–G–C reveals stylistic differences better than any treatise
Criterion for identification: what is the relationship to the dominant? (Bach: obligatory → Debussy: non-existent)

analyseNarrative.tonalite: No fixed functional key — pentatonicism and modes (Mixolydian), with a single real tonicisation (G♯, m. 47-67).
analyseNarrative.metrique: 6/4. Tempo 60 to the dotted quarter note, highly variable (up to 120 at the climax, falling back to 40 at the close).
analyseNarrative.forme: A narrative arch following the legend of Ys: the cathedral rising from the water, full peal of bells, the engulfing, an underwater echo, the return to silence.

sections.label: Measures 1-15
sections.titre: The bells
sections.chiffrage: Open fifths + pentatonicism — planing G→F→E — bells on C
sections.texte: The opening chord says it all: open fifths stacked across six octaves (G1 to D7), and inside them a complete pentatonic aggregate {G-A-B-D-E} — no third, no leading note, not one pitch that would decide between the modes. The bass then descends G-F-E beneath the same bells: planing pure and simple, the chords sliding in parallel without any one of them “functioning”. A modal theme floats above in bare octaves, monody without harmony. The bells return on C (m. 14): the same sonority, transposed, still without a third.

sections.label: Measures 16-27
sections.titre: The rising
sections.texte: Parallel chords settle over a B pedal — the cathedral “emerging from the mist”. Then, with no transition, the same material is transposed to E♭: a tritone leap between the two planes, the most anti-tonal relationship there is, used here as a simple change of lighting. Fourth-chords {G-C-D} and a long descent in the bass prepare the summit to come.

sections.label: Measures 28-41
sections.titre: The chorale: the climax without a dominant
sections.chiffrage: C Mixolydian — G, F, D minor, A minor, E minor, B♭ (♭VII), G minor (v) — C
sections.texte: The cathedral sounds at full voice: an organ chorale in C Mixolydian over an immovable C pedal, parallel diatonic triads treated as a giant organum, with the mode's signature colour — the B♭, the lowered seventh (♭VII) — and the minor v as mixture. Fourteen measures of triumph without the slightest functional dominant: the greatest climax in the piano literature, built exclusively out of plagal and parallel motion.

sections.label: Measures 42-46
sections.titre: The engulfing
sections.texte: Over the same fourth-chords the bass sinks by chromatic steps (B♭, then A♭), while high bells ring C-D at the top of the keyboard — the cathedral goes under from the bass upwards while the treble keeps on chiming.

sections.label: Measures 47-67
sections.titre: The middle section: a relic of grammar at the bottom of the sea
sections.chiffrage: G♯ pedal — D♯ø7 (colour) — F♯7 (colour) — D♯7 → G♯(7)
sections.fonctions: ? — ? — D — T (the only true cadence in the piece)
sections.texte: An almost unbroken G♯ pedal carries a lamenting reprise of the theme. Colour first: a half-diminished chord (D♯ø7) rocks over the pedal — neither leading note nor augmented sixth, here pure timbre. Then F♯7, colour once again. And suddenly, buried in the darkest section of the piece, a genuine V7-I progression (D♯7 to G♯, with F## and B♯ duly spelled out): the only functional cadence in the whole of La Cathédrale engloutie.

sections.label: Measures 68-83
sections.titre: Transition and echo
sections.chiffrage: Dyads a tritone apart (F♯/G♯ – C/D) — echo of the chorale (C-G-D pedal, ♭VII, v)
sections.texte: A transition reduced to two dyads a tritone apart, like a pulse of mist. Then the whole chorale returns, but pianissimo, over a composite pedal (C-G-D) — the same harmonic grid as at the climax, and yet another world entirely: here the function of a chord is its dynamic and its register, not its figuring.

sections.label: Measures 84-89
sections.titre: The conclusion: the third granted at last
sections.texte: The pentatonic bells close the arch, identical to the opening. But the very last chord is a complete C major, spread across four octaves, pianissimo: the third (E), carefully avoided in every bell of the piece, is granted only in the very last word.

synthese.titre: Parallelism as a system, not as a provocation
synthese.texte: Every usual parameter of functional harmony finds a substitute here: mode replaces key, the pedal replaces function, register and dynamic replace the cadence. This is not an absence of rules — it is an entirely different system, applied with the same rigour as a fugue.

synthese.titre: The half-diminished chord, reduced to pure timbre
synthese.texte: The half-diminished chord in m. 55 prepares nothing, suspends nothing, substitutes for nothing: it is a colour over a pedal, with not the slightest obligation to resolve. The very aggregate that elsewhere carries the whole weight of a cadence or of an enharmonic ambiguity becomes here a simple sound object.

synthese.titre: One cadence, one only, buried
synthese.texte: In eighty-nine measures, a single genuine V7-I progression — and it occurs in the darkest and most intimate section of the piece, almost hidden. The cadence, the engine of tonal music for three centuries, is no more here than a fleeting quotation in the middle of a wholly different language.

cours26.title: DEM Harmonization: Given Bass and Given Soprano
cours26.subtitle: The two fundamental exercises of the DEM exam — step-by-step method, guided exercises with detailed corrections.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered DEM harmonization techniques.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few points to consolidate on bass or soprano.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep practicing harmonization — restart when you are ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: César Franck was renowned for his ability to harmonize any bass at sight impeccably. His students (Duparc, d'Indy, Chausson) testified that he instantly saw all the harmonic possibilities of a given bass line.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: A well-harmonized bass already tells the whole story — the upper voices just need to follow.
narrative.pBasse: The given bass is one of the two major harmonization exercises in the DEM exam. Each bass note reveals the chord position — you must choose which one is most relevant according to functional logic.
narrative.methodeBasse1Detail: Analyze the key signature and confirm via the final cadence. Distinguish major and minor (presence of the leading tone?).
narrative.methodeBasse2Detail: Root → root position. Third → 1st inversion. Fifth → 2nd inversion (rare, cadential). Foreign note → do not place a chord.
narrative.methodeBasse3Detail: Each bass note may correspond to several chords compatible with the key — list the options.
narrative.methodeBasse4Detail: Follow T → SD → D → T. Avoid backward movements (IV–V–IV). Prepare the final cadence with V or I6/4–V.
narrative.methodeBasse5Detail: Avoid parallel fifths and octaves. Double the root in root position, the third in 1st inversion. Favor contrary motion.
narrative.infoBoxCadence: Critical rule — the cadential 6/4: The 6/4 is never placed on a weak beat. It appears only on the strong beat (2nd or 4th beat), followed obligatorily by V then I. Any other use of 2nd inversion is extremely rare.
narrative.exB1Desc: Harmonize this bass in C major. First identify the position of each note (root, third or fifth).
narrative.exB1Notes: C – G – A – F – G – C
narrative.exB1Analyse: I – V6 – VI – IV – V – I (perfect final cadence)
narrative.exB1Indice: G in the bass = third of E (V6) or root of V. Here, G after C suggests V6 because A follows — VI is more logical after V6 than after V.
narrative.exB2Desc: Harmonize this bass in G major. Watch for the leading tone (F#) and inversions.
narrative.exB2Notes: G – D – E – C – D – G
narrative.exB2Analyse: I – V – VI – IV – V – I (classic symmetrical structure)
narrative.exB2Indice: D is the root of V or the fifth of I. Here, after G (I), D → E suggests a V–VI movement (deceptive cadence) before the conclusion IV–V–I.
narrative.exB3Desc: Bass in harmonic D minor. The leading tone C# must appear before the final D. Watch for bVI (Bb).
narrative.exB3Notes: D – A – Bb – G – C# – D
narrative.exB3Analyse: Im – V – bVI – IVm – V(harm.) – Im (perfect cadence in harmonic minor)
narrative.exB3Indice: C# in the bass = VII#6 (1st inversion of VII# = leading tone of harmonic minor). This V6 rises to Im by semitone — maximum tension before resolution.
narrative.pSoprano: Harmonizing a given soprano first requires identifying real notes from foreign notes — then constructing a coherent bass and inner voices beneath the melody.
narrative.methodeSoprano1Detail: The melody reveals the key — locate characteristic accidentals (leading tone, 6th in minor) and the final note.
narrative.methodeSoprano2Detail: What chord position can it occupy? Root, third, fifth, or seventh of the chord?
narrative.methodeSoprano3Detail: Short or ornamental notes: passing (between two chord tones), neighbor (around a note), suspension (resolved dissonance), anticipation.
narrative.methodeSoprano4Detail: For each real soprano note, list the chords that can contain it (maximum 2–3 options).
narrative.methodeSoprano5Titre: Build the bass and inner voices
narrative.methodeSoprano5Detail: Choose chord positions according to the desired harmonic rhythm. Prefer root position at cadences. Vary inversions in the body of the phrase.
narrative.notePassageDef: Stepwise between two chord tones, unaccented. Ascending or descending.
narrative.broderieDef: Around a chord tone — goes up and comes back down (or the reverse). Diatonic or chromatic.
narrative.retardDef: Strikes on the strong beat in place of the chord tone — resolves downward.
narrative.anticipationDef: Anticipates the next note before the harmonic resolution — short and unaccented.
narrative.warnBoxSoprano: Golden rule: Never harmonize a foreign note. First identify all passing notes, neighbors and suspensions — then harmonize only the real notes. A chord on a neighbor note creates a fatal error in the exam.
narrative.exS1Desc: Harmonize this soprano in C major. All notes are real (no foreign notes).
narrative.exS1Analyse: I6 – V6 – I – V – I (or I6 – II6 – I – V – I depending on the chosen harmonic rhythm)
narrative.exS1Indice: E in the soprano can be the third of I (root position C–E–G) or the root of III (rarely). Starting with I6 (third in soprano) is elegant.
narrative.exS2Desc: This soprano contains a foreign note. Identify it before harmonizing.
narrative.exS2Notes: G – F# – G – E – D – C
narrative.exS2Analyse: I – (passing note) – I – I6 or VI – V – I · F# = chromatic passing note between G and E
narrative.exS2Indice: F# is too short and non-harmonic to receive a chord — it is a chromatic passing note between G and E. Do not harmonize F#: maintain the G chord (I) on the first two notes.

conservatoire.intuition: A given bass is the skeleton — the harmonization is the flesh and blood the musician gives it.

reference.citation: The art of harmonizing a bass is nothing other than the art of thinking musically: every bass note already carries, in germ, the voices that rise above it.

voix: Work out the function of each bass note before choosing the chord: is it a root (root position), a third (first inversion) or a fifth (second inversion)?
The cadential six-four appears only on a strong beat, obligatorily followed by V and then I — never on a weak beat
Identify the non-chord tones in the soprano (passing tone, neighbour tone, suspension) before harmonizing, so as not to build false chords on notes that are not chord tones

repertoire.titre: Wachet auf, ruft uns die Stimme (chorale prelude BWV 645)

pieges.erreur: Changing chord on every fast note of the soprano
pieges.correction: Short notes are often passing or neighbour tones — harmonize according to the rhythmic structure, not according to every individual note

pieges.erreur: Placing a six-four on a weak beat, or without its obligatory resolution through V
pieges.correction: The cadential six-four occurs exclusively on a strong beat (2nd or 4th beat), always followed by a V resolving to I

pieges.erreur: Ignoring the non-chord tones and building incorrect chords on neighbour or passing notes
pieges.correction: First identify passing tones, neighbour tones, suspensions and anticipations — then harmonize the chord tones only

resume: Given bass: identify root/third/fifth, propose 2–3 possible chords, choose according to T→SD→D→T
Given soprano: long notes = chord tones to be harmonized, short notes = potentially non-chord tones
Cadential six-four: on a strong beat only, with an obligatory and immediate V–I resolution

analyseNarrative.tonalite: E♭ major, with two passing excursions (C minor, G minor) in the Abgesang.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Tempo quarter = 68 (Lento).
analyseNarrative.forme: Ornamented chorale in bar form (AAB): ritornello (R1) — Stollen (two phrases repeated identically + a third) — return of the ritornello (R2) — Abgesang (four closing phrases + climax) — concluding ritornello. This piano transcription writes the Stollen out only once (54 bars), where the version for organ and voice writes it twice in succession.

sections.label: Upbeat – m. 13
sections.titre: The ritornello: pedal point, then tonicization of the dominant
sections.fonctions: T – SD/T – D (secondary dominant) – D – pivot
sections.texte: Twelve bars before the chorale even enters: a ritornello built over a tonic pedal (E♭ held in the bass) crossed by an alternation of I and IV, then a short sequence that tips towards the dominant — the A♮ of mm. 9–10 tonicizes B♭ by way of its own dominant seventh chord (F7). Measure 13 closes the section on a double meaning: B♭ is first heard as a local tonic (I of B♭) before being immediately reinterpreted as V of E♭ — the exact hinge by which the ritornello reaches the chorale.

sections.label: Measures 14–20
sections.titre: The chorale enters, on the submediant
sections.texte: The chorale enters at m. 14, on the third beat — but not on the tonic. The first chord to carry the beginning of the melody (the rising E♭-G, the very incipit of “Wachet auf”) is a C minor chord with a seventh: vi7, a false harmonic entry that delays the arrival of the real tonic by a whole phrase. The B♭ that follows, repeated four times in a row (m. 15) before settling onto C-B♭ in long values (m. 16), traces the chorale's characteristic phrase-ending. A second entry (m. 17, again on vi) prepares a cadence on the dominant, reached at m. 20 after a tonicization by F7.

sections.label: Measures 21–24
sections.titre: Third phrase: back to the tonic
sections.texte: The third phrase of the Stollen closes the first half of the chorale on E♭, before one last harmonic gesture (IV–V) prepares the return of the ritornello.

sections.label: Measures 25–30
sections.titre: R2: the ritornello, note for note
sections.fonctions: T – D (secondary dominant) – D – T – D
sections.texte: The second half of the opening ritornello returns unchanged — the same progression, the same tonicization of B♭ by F7, the same closing pivot chord — only the pianistic registration differs from one occurrence to the other. The file itself annotates this reprise as covering exactly mm. 8 to 13 of the opening, pivot included: a repetition written out in full, not a mere repeat sign.

sections.label: Measures 31–43
sections.titre: The Abgesang: two modal excursions
sections.chiffrage: B♭ – E♭ – G/B: V6/Cm – Cm – A♭ – G7 – Cm (cad.) – D/F♯: V6/Gm – Gm (cad.)
sections.fonctions: D – T – D then T (C minor) – T – D – T (G minor)
sections.texte: The closing phrases of the chorale venture, for the first time, outside E♭ major. A B♮ (m. 34) tips the harmony towards C minor — the relative of E♭ — with a full cadence at m. 37. Then an F♯ (m. 40) opens a second excursion, this time towards G minor, cadencing at m. 43 before the text itself announces the return: “E♭: return”. Two successive tonicizations, each negotiated by its own dominant, before the chorale at last recovers its original tonic.

sections.label: Measures 44–54
sections.titre: Climax and close
sections.chiffrage: Gm → E♭ – A♭ – B♭ – E♭ (climax) – A♭: V7/IV – B♭7 – E♭
sections.fonctions: T – SD – D – T – SD – D – T
sections.texte: The return to E♭ (m. 44) prepares the last phrases of the chorale, carried up to a climax in octaves (mm. 47–49) that culminates on a high note no organ and no voice could ever reach — the signature of the pianist-transcriber, not of the original chorale. The cantus firmus ends at m. 50 on a repeated E♭, before a brief concluding ritornello closes the piece: a coloristic D♭ (m. 51, a V7/IV brushed past without ever lingering on it) lends the final cadence a plagal flavour before it closes, perfectly conventionally, on the tonic chord.

synthese.titre: An entry that does not enter on the tonic
synthese.texte: The chorale begins on vi7, not on I: the real tonic arrives only at the end of the first phrase. A lesson that transfers directly to the given bass / given soprano exercise — the first note of a melody does not necessarily demand a tonic chord beneath it.

synthese.titre: A ritornello written out again in full, note for note
synthese.texte: The return of the ritornello (mm. 25–30) leaves nothing to chance: every chord, every tonicization of the first occurrence (mm. 8–13) comes back identical. A well-built progression can repeat itself without needing to vary.

synthese.titre: Two tonicizations, a single way back
synthese.texte: C minor, then G minor: the only two incursions outside E♭ major in the whole chorale, each introduced by its own dominant and closed by its own cadence, before a return spelled out in so many words by the figuring itself.

cours33.title: Classical Writing: Fugue and Chorale
cours33.subtitle: Four-voice Bach-style chorale and fugue structure — the summit of strict counterpoint and polyphonic writing.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered Bach chorale and fugue structure.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! Review the chorale rules and fugue anatomy.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — try again when you're ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Bach composed his fugues mentally before writing them down. The Art of Fugue, his musical testament, stops in the middle of a bar — the day of his death. His name (B-A-C-H in German notation: Bb-A-C-B) is the last thematic motif he wrote in the unfinished fugue.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: The fugue is not a form — it is a way of thinking in multiple voices simultaneously.
narrative.pChoral: The four-voice chorale (SATB) is the fundamental exercise of classical writing. Bach harmonized ~400 Lutheran chorale melodies — these harmonizations are the absolute model of the genre. Each voice is an independent melodic line; their combination produces the harmony.
narrative.infoBoxSATB: The 4 SATB voices: Soprano (high female voice, given chorale melody) · Alto (low female voice) · Tenor (high male voice, sounds an octave lower than written) · Bass (low male voice, harmonic foundation). The goal: 4 independent lines that sound good together at every moment.
narrative.step1Desc: Find the main key, identify phrase endings (textual punctuation = musical cadence)
narrative.step2Desc: The bass establishes the harmony. Prefer root positions, fifths in the bass for strong cadences
narrative.step3Desc: Fill the inner voices while avoiding errors. Contrary motion preferred over parallel voices
narrative.step4Desc: Parallel fifths/octaves? Leading tone resolved? 7th descending? Correct doublings?
narrative.warnBoxChoral: Most common mistake: Moving the leading tone up to the dominant instead of the tonic. B in C major (leading tone) moving to D instead of C — this is a serious stylistic error. The leading tone MUST rise by a semitone to the tonic, without exception in Bach style.
narrative.h3ExemplesAccords: Examples of SATB chords in C major
narrative.pFugue: The fugue is a form of counterpoint where multiple voices enter successively with the same theme (subject), then develop it by weaving independent lines. It is not a 'form' in the sense of the sonata — it is a contrapuntal process.
narrative.infoBoxAnatomie: Anatomy of a fugue: Exposition (successive subject/answer entries) → Development (episodes, entries in other keys) → Stretto (overlapping entries) → Coda (tonic pedal, final cadence). The structure follows the logic of counterpoint, not a predefined form.
narrative.infoBoxArtFugue: The Art of Fugue BWV 1080: 14 fugues (Contrapuncti) and 4 canons, all built on the same subject in C minor. Contrapunctus XIV stops in the middle of a bar — Bach died before completing it. The last note Bach wrote: a B (the B-A-C-H motif ends on B in French notation).
narrative.warnBoxFugue: Common mistake: Analyzing the fugue as a succession of chords. The fugue is a fabric of independent melodic lines — harmony results from their meeting, it is not planned chord by chord. Analyze each voice separately before analyzing their intersection.

conservatoire.intuition: A fugue is not a constraint — it is a conversation in several voices where everyone speaks and listens at the same time. Bach thought in fugue the way we think in sentences.

reference.badge: Bach · The Art of Fugue BWV 1080
reference.citation: Fugue is the art of bringing the voices into a subject one after another, then leading them together without any one of them crushing the others — it is the absolute democracy of counterpoint.

voix: In the four-part chorale, the bass is the foundation — it establishes the harmony. Alto and tenor are not 'filler voices': they carry the voice leading. Bad voice leading kills a chorale.
The leading tone (7th degree) MUST rise to the tonic. The dominant seventh MUST fall. In Bach's style these rules are inviolable — breaking them creates a serious stylistic error.
When analyzing a fugue, begin by identifying the subject, the answer and the countersubject before analyzing anything else. Those three elements are the raw material of the entire fugue.

repertoire.titre: Prelude and Fugue No. 2 in C minor, BWV 847 (complete)

pieges.erreur: Making the leading tone rise to the dominant (G instead of the tonic)
pieges.correction: The leading tone (B in C major, not B flat — the natural 7th degree) must ALWAYS resolve to the tonic by an ascending semitone. It is the strictest rule of the baroque chorale.

pieges.erreur: Confusing subject and answer in a fugue
pieges.correction: The subject is on the tonic; the answer is on the dominant (transposed a fifth higher or a fourth lower). The answer may be tonal (slightly modified) or real (an exact transposition).

pieges.erreur: Analyzing a fugue as a succession of classical chords
pieges.correction: A fugue is a contrapuntal fabric — each voice is an independent melodic line. The harmony results from the intersection of those lines, not from a planned chord progression.

resume: Bach chorale: 4 voices (SATB), strict voice-leading rules, leading tone resolved to I, dominant seventh falling
Fugue: subject (tonic) → answer (dominant) → countersubject → stretto — a contrapuntal fabric, not a chord progression
The Art of Fugue BWV 1080: Bach's musical testament, 14 fugues on a single subject, left unfinished at his death

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C minor, with a clearing into the relative major (E♭ major) in the fugue, and a Picardy third right at the end.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Allegro moderato (118), Presto (145) at m. 28, Adagio (20) at m. 34, Allegro at m. 35; the fugue Andante.
analyseNarrative.forme: A figuration prelude in 38 measures (tonic pedal, sequence of subdominants, harmonic sequence, dominant pedal, cadenza, recitative, coda) followed by a three-voice fugue of 31 measures (exposition, sequential episodes, 6 entries of the subject).

sections.label: Measures 1-4
sections.titre: The prelude: tonic pedal
sections.texte: The opening breath: a single sixteenth-note figure in which every chord can be read plainly, one harmony per measure. The tonic held in the bass carries a vii°7 over the pedal (already a V♭9 color) before closing back onto the tonic.

sections.label: Measures 5-12
sections.titre: The cascading sequence of subdominants
sections.chiffrage: VI6/4 | V4/2 of v – v6 | V4/2 of iv – iv6 | V4/2 of III – III6 | VI6/5
sections.texte: The piece's great find: every degree is preceded by its own dominant in 4/2, the bass descending two notes at a time (C-B♭, B♭-A♭, A♭-G) — the circle of fifths disguised as a chromatic slide of inversions.

sections.label: Measures 13-27
sections.titre: Sequence, then dominant pedal
sections.chiffrage: sequence (mm. 13-20) — i6/4 ↔ vii°7 over a G pedal (mm. 21-27) — V7♭9
sections.texte: A harmonic sequence leads toward the dominant, before the prelude tips over into its second nature: seven measures of dominant pedal, an i6/4 / vii°7 oscillation beneath a melody rising chromatically (E♭-F♯-G-A♭ — the gesture of Beethoven's Grave, a century early), thickening into V7♭9.

sections.label: Measures 28-38
sections.titre: Cadenza, recitative and coda
sections.chiffrage: Presto (rocket cadenza) — Adagio (V7/iv, recitative) — Allegro (vii°7, Neapolitan ♭9) — cadence
sections.texte: The Presto unleashes the rocket cadenza over the sustained dominant. The single-measure Adagio arpeggiates a C7 — the dominant of the subdominant, brandished like a question, a recitative gesture. The closing Allegro answers over a tonic pedal, with the Neapolitan D♭ as one last shadow before the resolution.

sections.label: Measures 39-45
sections.titre: The fugue: the exposition
sections.chiffrage: Subject (alto) — Tonal answer (soprano, on G) + 1st countersubject — Subject (bass)
sections.fonctions: ? (counterpoint — roman-numeral analysis has no purchase here)
sections.texte: Subject in the alto, in C minor, with its characteristic leap of a fourth. Tonal answer in the soprano on G: the head replies with a descending fifth where the subject had a fourth — the textbook adjustment — against the first countersubject, a descending scale in the alto. Subject in the bass: the exposition is complete.

sections.label: Measures 47-69
sections.titre: Episodes, entries and Picardy third
sections.chiffrage: sequential episodes — entry in the relative major (E♭) — return to C — final entry over a pedal — Picardy third
sections.texte: Sequential episodes built on the head of the subject lead to a single clearing, the entry in E♭ major (the relative major). The return to C prepares the last entries — bass, then soprano over a tonic pedal — before the final resolution on a Picardy third (the E natural of the very last measure). No learned artifice: neither stretto nor inversion — this fugue is famous precisely for its legibility.

synthese.titre: Bach's two faces
synthese.texte: The prelude, where harmony comes first and figuration second, and the fugue, where the lines engender everything: the same composer, two opposite ways of writing, brought together in a single diptych.

synthese.titre: An inventory in thirty-eight measures
synthese.texte: Pedal, sequence, prolonged dominant, cadenza, recitative, coda: the prelude alone parades almost every device tonal harmony can mobilize, each one clearly isolated as in a textbook.

synthese.titre: A lesson without artifice
synthese.texte: The fugue resorts neither to stretto nor to inversion — the learned tools of counterpoint are deliberately absent. It is precisely this plainness that has made it the default analysis fugue of every conservatory.

cours34.title: Composing for the Screen: Film Harmony
cours34.subtitle: Harmonic emotion map, leitmotif and transformation — Morricone, Williams, Zimmer and the art of guiding the viewer's emotion.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered film harmony and the leitmotif.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! Review the emotion map and transformation techniques.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — try again when you're ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Morricone composed his music BEFORE filming with Sergio Leone. Actors sometimes played on set listening to the music in their earpiece — the melody dictated the rhythm of their performance. For 'Il Buono, il Brutto, il Cattivo', he invented an orchestration with human whistling, coyote voice and jaw harp. Recognizable in 2 seconds anywhere in the world.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Film music does not tell what we see — it says what we feel watching what we see.
narrative.pEmotions: Every emotion in cinema has its harmonic color. Great composers (Williams, Morricone, Zimmer, Herrmann) use a precise harmonic vocabulary to guide the viewer's emotion — often without them realizing it. This map is their toolbox.
narrative.infoBoxPrincipe: Fundamental principle: Emotion in film music comes from harmonic color (which scale, which chord), timbre (which instrument) and dynamics (which volume) — not harmonic complexity. A simple chord well orchestrated is more powerful than a complex harmony poorly played.
narrative.outil2: Open fifth + fanfare brass at the octave
narrative.orchDesc0: Brass in the low register (tuba, trombone) evoke threat. High strings in the high register = tension.
narrative.orchDesc1: Plucked strings create a lightness and softness that the bow cannot. Ideal for comedy or carefree moments.
narrative.orchDesc2: A motif that repeats unchanged creates a sense of imminence and inevitability — tension rising without resolution.
narrative.orchDesc3: Silence after loud music is the most powerful tool. The sudden absence of sound creates an emotional shock stronger than the music itself.
narrative.warnBoxEmotions: Common mistake: Using the same harmonic register for all emotions. If sadness sounds like heroism, the viewer does not know how to react. The harmonic emotion map is a precision tool — each color has a distinct narrative function.
narrative.pLeitmotif: A leitmotif is a musical motif (melody, harmony, rhythm) associated with a character, object or idea in a work. It can be transformed harmonically to reflect the narrative evolution of the character — without changing the notes.
narrative.infoBoxOrigine: Origin: Richard Wagner invented the leitmotif in his operas of the tetralogy Der Ring des Nibelungen (1876). Each character, magic object or feeling has its motif. John Williams applied this technique to cinema with equivalent mastery in Star Wars.
narrative.lm0Description: Darth Vader's theme — hammered brass in minor, warlike dotted rhythm. The minor third and diminished fifth at the end evoke oppression and threat.
narrative.lm0Transformation: The same theme played by harp or soft strings = Vader's hidden vulnerability — double effect without changing a single note.
narrative.lm1Description: Heroic theme in D major, initial ascending fifth = aspiration and grandeur. The Lydian mode appears in the fantasy passages (Tatooine sunset).
narrative.lm1Transformation: In minor mode or slow tempo = melancholy, loss, nostalgia — the same melody says the opposite.
narrative.lm2Nom: Il Buono, il Brutto, il Cattivo
narrative.lm2Film: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966)
narrative.lm2Description: Aeolian mode with human whistling, voice imitating a coyote, electric jaw harp, chimes. The harmonic color is simple; the absolutely unique orchestration creates the sonic identity of the spaghetti western.
narrative.lm3Description: Only 4 chords — C–G–Am–F — repeated 18 times over 4 minutes. The progressive orchestration (piano → strings → full ensemble) creates all the tension and emotion. Lesson: harmonic complexity is not the engine of emotion.
narrative.transDesc0: The same melody in minor mode signals threat, corruption or the character's loss. The viewer recognizes the theme and feels the change instantly.
narrative.transDesc1: Hammered brass → harp or soft strings. Same melody, opposite emotion. Vader's Imperial March on harp = his human vulnerability.
narrative.transDesc2: The theme in 2–3 note fragments creates anxiety. The ear seeks to complete the melody — the composer refuses to finish it.
narrative.transDesc3: Doubled note values (slower = epic grandeur) or halved (faster = urgency and danger). Contrapuntal technique applied to cinema.
narrative.infoBoxMorricone: Morricone and Leone: Morricone composed BEFORE filming. Leone showed the music to actors on set — they played while listening. The music dictated the rhythm and emotion of the performance, the reverse of the classical method. This unique collaboration explains the perfect fusion of image and sound in their films.
narrative.warnBoxLeitmotif: Advanced technique: A leitmotif in major that becomes minor is more powerful than a new sad theme. Why? The viewer already has an emotional connection to the original theme — its transformation amplifies the impact. Creating a leitmotif is investing in an emotional resource the composer can exploit throughout the film.

conservatoire.intuition: Film music does not narrate what we see — it says what we feel in front of what we see. That is the difference between commentary and revelation.

reference.citation: Music is the invisible language of film. Sergio gave me the images and I composed without looking at them — I composed the emotions he wanted the audience to feel.

voix: The unresolved tritone is the most effective tension device in cinema. A single augmented fourth left hanging, never resolved, puts the viewer on the alert. The human brain waits for the resolution — and the composer can take possession of that wait.

A leitmotif transformed harmonically is more powerful than a new theme. When Williams's Imperial March tips into minor-major, or is played by a single harp, it is more heartbreaking than any melody invented from scratch.

John Williams, Hans Zimmer and Ennio Morricone share a secret: their harmonies are often plain (I–V–VI–IV), but their orchestration is exceptional. The emotional power comes from timbre, not from harmonic complexity.

repertoire.titre: Il Buono, il Brutto, il Cattivo (main theme, complete)

pieges.erreur: Thinking that film music has to be harmonically complex in order to work
pieges.correction: The I–V–VI–IV progression (used in Zimmer's “Time” and in Williams's “Can't Help Falling in Love”) creates more emotion than complex harmony does, because it frees the ear to concentrate on timbre, dynamics and melody.

pieges.erreur: Using the same harmonic register for every emotion
pieges.correction: Each emotion has its own harmonic map: tritone (tension), descending minor (sadness), major with an open fifth (heroism), Phrygian (mystery). Choosing the wrong harmonic colour destroys the emotional effect.

pieges.erreur: Confusing underscoring with source music
pieges.correction: Underscoring is music the characters do not hear (background scoring). Source music is music inside the diegesis (a radio, a band on screen). The harmony may be identical; the narrative function is the opposite.

resume: Map of the emotions: unresolved tritone (tension) · descending minor (sadness) · major with open fifth (heroism) · Phrygian/diminished (mystery) · add9 (love)
Leitmotif: a theme attached to a character or an idea, transformed harmonically as the story unfolds
The emotional power of cinema comes from orchestration, not from harmonic complexity — I–V–VI–IV can be epic if the scoring is right

analyseNarrative.tonalite: D Aeolian tinged with Dorian (the B♮ of the IV chord) — no classical functional key whatsoever.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 2/2. Fast tempo (in 2), ♩ = 200.
analyseNarrative.forme: A form built on repeat signs: verse (1-49) — To Coda (50) — the event (51-58) — verse repeated (59-89) — D.S. al Coda (90) — the event a second time (91-94) — coda in decrescendo (95-111).

sections.label: Measures 1-16
sections.titre: The call and the complete modal set
sections.fonctions: ? (no function can be built here — modal, not tonal)
sections.texte: A D-F-G-A drone establishes the colour before the call proper — the fourth A-D, the famous “coyote howl” — comes in, harmonised by an open fifth (D-A, no third): the same inaugural gesture as La Cathédrale engloutie, the bare interval before any harmony at all. The verse then unfolds the complete vocabulary of the mode: i (D minor), IV (G major, with its Dorian B natural — the folk colour par excellence), ♭VII (C major, the chord classical tonality forbade), v (A minor, a dominant with no leading tone).

sections.label: Measures 27-49
sections.titre: The bridge
sections.texte: The bridge moves over to the relative side — v, ♭III, ♭VII — with strings and voices hovering above, still without the slightest leading tone.

sections.label: Measures 51-58 (repeated at 91-94)
sections.titre: The event: the one and only dominant
sections.chiffrage: ♭V (A♭) → V7 (A7, carrying the only C♯ in the piece)
sections.texte: Then comes the event: a chord a tritone away from the tonic (A♭ major, ♭V) rises out of nowhere and slides onto A7 — the only genuine functional dominant in the whole piece, containing the only C♯ in the entire transcription, kept in reserve for the moment of dramatic reversal before the immediate return to a world without leading tones. The repeat structure (To Coda at m. 50, D.S. al Coda at m. 90) makes this same gesture sound twice.

sections.label: Measures 95-111
sections.titre: The coda
sections.chiffrage: the call receding (dim.) — open fifth (106-109) — complete resolution (110)
sections.texte: The coda brings the call back, receding in a decrescendo through passages in bare fifths — until the very last held chord finally reintroduces the minor third: the piece closes on a complete D minor chord, not on the desert of an open fifth.

synthese.titre: Bach's economy, inverted
synthese.texte: In the Bach chorale, the modal was the coloured exception within a functional world (a single passing minor v). Here the dominant is the special effect of a modal world — one single bar of true function out of a hundred and eleven. A century of harmonic history summed up in a complete reversal of the proportions.

synthese.titre: Timbre as a formal parameter
synthese.texte: Across seven parts the call travels from ocarina to voice, to electric guitar, to trumpet — and it is this rotation of timbre, not the harmony, that articulates the form. The lesson Debussy had theorised (register and dynamics taking over from the cadence), carried into a worldwide vernacular by way of the western.

synthese.titre: A language that became a mother tongue
synthese.texte: The ♭VII Aeolian of this theme has been, ever since 1966, the basic harmonic vocabulary of rock, of pop and of screen music — the same modal economy, broadcast to hundreds of millions of listeners.

cours35.title: Advanced Jazz: Reharmonization and Improvisation
cours35.subtitle: Advanced substitutions, chord scales and professional voicings — Miles Davis, Bill Evans and the art of creative reharmonization.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered advanced reharmonization and jazz voicings.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! Review the substitutions and chord scales.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — try again when you're ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Kind of Blue (1959) was recorded in two sessions without rehearsal — the musicians discovered the modal charts in the studio. Miles gave them a scale and a color, not chords. The result: the best-selling jazz album in history. Miles Davis said: 'Don't play what's there — play what's not there.'
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Harmonic sophistication in jazz does not come from complexity — it comes from knowing exactly what to put in and what to leave out.
narrative.pReharmonisation: Reharmonising means replacing the chords of an existing chart with other chords under the same melody. The absolute constraint: every melodic note must remain compatible with the new chord (root, 3rd, 5th, 7th or available extension — never an avoid note).
narrative.infoBoxGuideTones: Guide-tones: The third and seventh of the chord are the notes that define its harmonic color. These are the essential notes never to clash with the melody during a reharmonisation. If the melody is a semitone above or below a guide-tone, the chord is poorly chosen.
narrative.sub0Principe: I ↔ III ↔ VI — chords sharing 2 notes in the same key
narrative.sub0Exemple: CMaj7 can be replaced by Am7 (same key, 2 common notes: E, G)
narrative.sub1Principe: V7 replaced by the dominant chord a tritone lower — shared guide-tones
narrative.sub1Exemple: G7 → Db7: B (3rd of G7) = C# (7th of Db7), F (7th of G7) = Eb (3rd of Db7)
narrative.sub2Principe: Borrow chords from the parallel mode — bVI, bVII, bIII from the aeolian scale
narrative.sub2Exemple: In C major: Fm (parallel minor), Ab Maj, Bb Maj — dark and unexpected color
narrative.sub3Principe: Replacement by a chord a third away — major or minor, different mode
narrative.sub3Exemple: CMaj7 → EMaj (major third) or AbMaj (major sixth) — cinematic color
narrative.h3ChordScales: Chord scales — which scale over which chord?
narrative.cs3Gamme: Altered = 7th mode of Ab melodic minor
narrative.warnBoxReharmo: Classic mistake: Using the tritone substitution on all chords. It only works on dominant V7 chords — because that is the only time the guide-tones (3rd and 7th) are shared with the substitute. Applying it to a IMaj7 or IIm7 produces a non-stylistic dissonance.
narrative.pVoicings: A voicing is the arrangement of a chord's notes in register. For the same chord, there are dozens of possible voicings — each with its color, context of use and sonic effect. Mastering voicings distinguishes the harmonist from the ordinary pianist.
narrative.infoBoxVoicings: Fundamental principle: There is no 'correct' voicing in absolute terms — there are voicings suited to each context. The shell voicing to accompany a voice, the drop 2 for a richer texture, the Evans voicing for the jazz trio, the quartal for modal color.
narrative.v0Description: Root + 3rd + 7th without fifth. The skeleton of the chord — stripped down, leaves space for melody and bass.
narrative.v0Construction: CMaj7: C–E–B (fifth G omitted). G7: G–B–F. Dm7: D–F–C.
narrative.v0Style: Voice accompaniment, double bass plays the root
narrative.v1Description: Closed chord whose 2nd voice (from the top) drops an octave — opening the register.
narrative.v1Construction: CMaj7 closed: C–E–G–B → Drop 2: C–G–B–E (G drops an octave)
narrative.v1Style: Jazz guitarists, pianists — wider and more natural register
narrative.v2Description: Root omitted (played by the double bassist). 3rd–7th–9th in a light, airy voicing.
narrative.v2Construction: CMaj9 Evans: E–B–D (3rd–7th–9th). The root C is implied.
narrative.v3Description: Chord built in stacked fourths. Miles Davis and Bill Evans for 'So What'.
narrative.v3Construction: D–G–C–F–A: four successive fourths + third at the top
narrative.v3Style: Modal jazz, open sound without defined major/minor color
narrative.v4Description: Left hand plays 3rd–7th (+ optional extensions), right hand plays melody/solo.
narrative.v4Construction: G7 left hand: B–F–A (3–7–13) or B–F–Ab (3–7–b13 altered)
narrative.v4Style: Pianists accompanying a soloist or singer
narrative.warnBoxVoicings: Common mistake: Confusing chord scale and mode. A chord scale is always tied to a specific chord in a precise harmonic context. CMaj7 in C major uses ionian by default — but if you want the lydian color (#11), you choose lydian. The context (tonal or modal) determines the chord scale, not the chart alone.

conservatoire.intuition: Miles Davis used to say: “Don't play what's there — play what isn't there.” Reharmonisation is exactly that: hearing the possibilities the melody does not impose.

reference.citation: Reharmonisation is not cheating — it is a conversation between the original composer and the jazz musician. You respect the melody, and you invite the harmony to dance differently.
reference.auteur: Mark Levine, The Jazz Theory Book, 1995

voix: Guide tones (the third and the seventh of the chord) are the notes that define the harmonic colour. When you reharmonise, make sure the melody does not rub against the guide tones of the new chord — that is the principal constraint.
The shell voicing (root + 3rd + 7th, no fifth) sounds more modern and leaves more room for the melody and the bass line. Removing the fifth does not impoverish the chord — it clarifies it.

Miles Davis's Kind of Blue was recorded with no rehearsal — the musicians discovered the charts in the studio. This is not total improvisation: it is a precise modal structure with total freedom inside it. The difference is essential.

repertoire.titre: Blue in Green (Kind of Blue, complete)

pieges.erreur: Reharmonising without respecting the notes of the melody
pieges.correction: The melody is untouchable in a reharmonisation. Every chord chosen must allow the melodic note to be the root, the third, the fifth, the seventh or an available extension — never an avoid note.

pieges.erreur: Using tritone substitution indiscriminately on every chord
pieges.correction: Tritone substitution only works on dominant chords (V7). Applying it to IMaj7 or IIm7 produces a dissonance that is outside the style, because the guide tones are no longer shared.

pieges.erreur: Confusing chord scale and mode
pieges.correction: A chord scale is a scale played over one specific chord in one specific tonal context. CMaj7 in C major → Ionian scale (or Lydian). Modal CMaj7 → any appropriate major scale may be used. The harmonic context determines the chord scale.

resume: Reharmonisation: diatonic substitution (I↔VI↔III) · tritone substitution (V7→bII7) · modal interchange · chromatic mediant
Guide tones: third + seventh of the chord — never let the melody rub against them when reharmonising
Professional voicings: shell (1-3-7) · drop 2 · Bill Evans (7-9 without the root) · So What quartal

analyseNarrative.tonalite: An off-centre D minor / an implicit B♭ major — the ambiguity is not a failure of hearing, it is the subject of the piece. The material is genuinely functional (real dominants, everywhere) but set in orbit without ever settling durably on a centre.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 3/4 rubato, key signature of one flat. Nominal tempo 172 (indicative only — the piece is played rubato). “Sempre dopo” pedalling from the second bar onwards: legato re-pedalling after every new harmony, the Evans/Debussy signature.
analyseNarrative.forme: A ten-bar functional cycle (neither the twelve of the blues nor the multiples of eight of the song), spread over some twenty bars of 3/4 per chorus: B♭maj9 – A7 – Dm9 – E7 – Am9 – Dm9 – B♭maj7 – A7 – Dm – (Cm9–F13). The closing turnaround is a ii–V of B♭, not of D: the cycle never leads back to its tonic, it leads back to its own harmonic point of departure — which is not the tonic. During the solo sections the cycle contracts (harmonies with halved durations, an annotation present in the file at m. 77): the same tonal drift, replayed faster.

sections.label: Measures 0-9 (the intro and the first turn of the cycle)
sections.titre: A centre that announces itself without imposing itself
sections.fonctions: T (i, rubato) → ? (♭VI/I ambiguous) → D (real V) → T (i, real resolution)
sections.texte: The rubato intro sets D minor (Dm13) as the centre — but the cycle that follows opens on B♭ major 9, a chord whose identity is double from the very first bar: the lowered sixth degree of D minor, or the implicit tonic of a B♭ major that keeps surfacing without ever declaring itself. The A7 that follows is, by contrast, a real dominant of D minor, and the Dm9 that receives it is a real resolution — the piece is not atonal, it is functional in fragments.

sections.label: Measures 9-32 (the ten-bar circle)
sections.titre: A ii–V that never leads back to the tonic
sections.fonctions: D (V7 deflected) → T (v, minor resolution) → ? (♭VI) → D (V) → T (i) → ? (off-centre turnaround)
sections.texte: E7 is a real dominant — but it resolves onto A minor, never onto A major: a minor dominant, a fifth degree that refuses the very hierarchy it announces. The cycle closes its first turn on Dm13, then tips into the Cm9–F13 turnaround: a perfectly regular ii–V, but of B♭, not of D. This is the gesture that makes the form circular in the literal sense — the cycle never returns to its supposed centre, it returns to its own point of departure, which is not that centre. D minor does exist, asserted three times within the cycle, but it never occupies the beginning of a section: the key is there, but off-centre.

sections.label: Measures 38-39 (the deflected dominants, at their densest)
sections.titre: Alteration as density, not as a tension to be resolved
sections.texte: At m. 38 the B♭1 in the bass, beneath a chromatic movement, reveals a tritone-substitute chord (subV) sliding onto A7 — the transcriber's “B7” is a one-semitone slip, the most dangerous kind for the ear as well as on the page. The following bar saturates that A7: a flat ninth (B♭) and a sharp ninth (C natural) coexist with the third (C♯) and a natural thirteenth (F♯, the bright colour — no flat thirteenth here, not a single F natural in the whole bar). The pedal held over from the previous bar makes this ascending linear gesture sound all at once: Evans treats alteration as a colour that accumulates, not as a tension that calls for its resolution.

sections.label: Measures 77 and 219 (the same faulty enharmonic spelling, twice)
sections.titre: A spelling no instrumentalist can read
sections.chiffrage: B♭ major (the file's “A# major”, at both occurrences)
sections.texte: Twice in the transcription the same B♭ major chord (F–B♭–D) is spelled “A# major” — an exact enharmonic equivalent, but unreadable for a player, who would see an F♯♯ or a C♯♯ where the hand simply plays an F natural. The correction changes no actual pitch; it merely makes the score playable.

sections.label: Measures 308-310 (the ending: colour as the last word)
sections.titre: Neither major nor minor — the last word is a timbre
sections.chiffrage: D–E–A (sus2) → D + A + C♯ (written D♭): ∆7 without a third
sections.texte: The piece dies away on a suspended colour (D-E-A, a ninth without a third) before closing on a major-seventh chord wholly deprived of its third: D, A (the fifth), C♯ (the major seventh, notated D♭ by an accident of writing — the leading tone of D, at the very instant it ceases to function as one). Neither major nor minor: the ∆7 as pure terminal colour, exactly the sonority Satie set down in 1888 as an inaugural provocation (the Gmaj7/Dmaj7 rocking of the Gymnopédie), and which seventy years later has become the natural last word of a ballad.

synthese.titre: 1959, the year of two answers
synthese.texte: In the same year, on the same record, two opposite solutions to the same problem (does tonal function still have a future?): Giant Steps pushes the dominant to its limit through hyperactive symmetry (three keys a major third apart, the cycle closed); Blue in Green suspends the same materials (ii-V, subV, alterations) in an off-centre circle that never closes on its tonic. The same vocabulary, two destinies.

synthese.titre: The Evans/Debussy inheritance
synthese.texte: The “sempre dopo” pedalling, the maj7 without a third as terminal colour, the modal ambiguity of the tonal centre: Bill Evans inherits Debussy's vocabulary directly, and reinjects it into a thirty-two-bar form reworked as a ten-bar cycle. The bridge between this project and its own past (Voiles, La Cathédrale engloutie) closes here.

synthese.titre: The sub-V, always the same gesture
synthese.texte: The tritone substitute heard at m. 38 (B♭7 for A7) is the same mechanism as elsewhere in this corpus — a dominant replaced by the one that shares its leading tones a tritone away. Here it is a passing texture inside an improvisation; elsewhere, a taught rule of reharmonisation. The same tool, two uses.

cours36.title: Debussy and Ravel Harmony: Impressionism in Depth
cours36.subtitle: Whole-tone scale, planing, polychords, neoclassical modality — the two opposing logics of French impressionism.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered the impressionist techniques of Debussy and Ravel.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! Review planing, the long pedal point and polychords.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — try again when you're ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Satie invented 'furniture music' (1920) — music meant to blend with ambient noise, like a sonic piece of furniture. At its premiere, the audience politely sat and listened. An outraged Satie stormed through the hall shouting: 'Talk! Move! Don't listen!' He prefigured Brian Eno and ambient music by 50 years.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Music can exist without tension or resolution — harmonic colour is an end in itself.
narrative.debussyP: Debussy dissolved the classical tonal system not by rejecting it, but by circumventing it. He replaced harmonic functions (T/SD/D) with sound colours — a chord no longer has a role, it has a texture. Tension-resolution gives way to atmosphere.
narrative.debussyInfoBox: Fundamental principle: In Debussy, harmonic progression follows the melody and the sonic image — not functional logic. Analysing Debussy using T/SD/D functions is like applying chess rules to dice. The analytical framework is inappropriate.
narrative.debussyH3Analyser: How to analyse an impressionist piece
narrative.debussyWarnBox: Classic mistake: Looking for V→I cadences in Debussy. Debussy systematically avoids them — it is the very principle of his aesthetic. The Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun (110 bars) contains no classical dominant-tonic cadence. The harmony 'floats' without ever resolving.
narrative.tech_d0_principe: 6 whole tones with no semitone — C–D–E–F#–G#–A#
narrative.tech_d0_effet: Total floating: without a leading tone, no note pulls toward the next. All chords are augmented.
narrative.tech_d1_principe: 8 notes alternating tone and semitone — C–D–Eb–F–F#–Ab–A–B
narrative.tech_d1_effet: Ambiguous, symmetrical colour — tonality is impossible to establish (the scale repeats at a minor third).
narrative.tech_d2_principe: All voices move in the same rhythm with the same chord type transposed
narrative.tech_d2_effet: The chord moves as a sound block — parallel fifths are intentional, creating the characteristic sliding effect.
narrative.tech_d3_principe: Stationary bass (held note) while the harmony changes freely above
narrative.tech_d3_effet: Temporal suspension — harmonic time stops in the bass. Medieval technique (organum) reinvented.
narrative.tech_d4_principe: Root + fifth chord with no third — neither major nor minor
narrative.tech_d4_effet: Archaic, timeless purity, evoking plainchant and bells (La Cathédrale Engloutie).
narrative.step1_desc: Whole-tone (6 whole tones), octatonic (tone-semitone), pentatonic, or church mode?
narrative.step2_desc: Planing? Pedal point? Open fifths? Parallel homorhythm?
narrative.step3_desc: Chord quality, extensions present, register. No harmonic function.
narrative.step4_desc: Colour changes often come from register and volume, not chord progressions.
narrative.ravelP: Ravel shares with Debussy the impressionist surface — coloured chords, extensions, modes — but his logic is the opposite. Ravel described himself as a 'watchmaker': every chord is calculated, every voicing measured. The Pavane, the Bolero, the Valses nobles are architectural constructions disguised as reveries.
narrative.ravelInfoBox: Essential difference: Debussy creates intuitively through images and sonic colours. Ravel calculates with near-mathematical rigour. Same impressionist surface, opposite compositional logics. Debussy himself clearly distinguished between them and refused to be associated with Ravel.
narrative.tech_r0_principe: Two complete chords stacked — C Maj + D Maj = hybrid cluster
narrative.tech_r0_effet: Dense, unprecedented harmonic colour — both chords remain recognisable but create something new.
narrative.tech_r1_effet: Luminous softness — less 'jazzy' than Maj7, more 'naive' and tender. Signature of Ravel's style.
narrative.tech_r2_effet: Openness and clarity — the chord seems to aspire upward. Very different from Maj9 (which also adds the 7th).
narrative.tech_r3_principe: Ancient modes (Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian) in a modern language
narrative.tech_r3_effet: Modal colour without archaism — the Dorian mode on G gives a particular light absent from harmonic minor.
narrative.tech_r4_principe: A single chord (C7) for 15 minutes — tension comes from progressive orchestration
narrative.tech_r4_effet: Demonstration that harmonic progression is not the only driver of tension — timbre and dynamics suffice.
narrative.satieP: Satie precedes Debussy and Ravel and prefigures minimalism by 50 years. His Gymnopédies (1888) use major 7th chords in slow oscillation — two colours alternating without ever progressing dramatically. His Vexations (1893, discovered after his death) anticipate Steve Reich: a 52-second piece to be played 840 times in a row.
narrative.ravelWarnBox: Common mistake: Believing Debussy and Ravel are the same composer with the same style. Their surfaces are similar (impressionism, colours) but their methods are opposite. Ravel can write in strict classical forms (Piano Sonatine, String Quartet) with an impressionist language. Debussy avoids classical forms. This difference is fundamental.

conservatoire.intuition: Debussy and Ravel share the same surface — non-functional chords, sonorous colors, impressionism. But Debussy dreams and Ravel calculates. Beneath the same veil, two opposite intelligences.

reference.citation: I want a music that seems to come out of the shadows and sometimes returns to them — a music whose harmonic content is not subject to rigid, artificial rules.
reference.auteur: Claude Debussy, letter to his publisher Durand, 1907

voix: In Debussy, the harmonic progression follows the melody — not the other way round. A chord is chosen for its sonorous color, not for its T/SD/D function. Analyzing Debussy with classical functions is like reading a poem as an instruction manual.

Ravel is the architect of impressionism: his chords look non-functional, but their succession is rigorously calculated. Boléro is a single chord (C7), and yet its progressive orchestration creates a tension that no chord progression could ever have produced.

Debussy's long pedal points — an immobile bass while the harmony shifts above it — create an effect of temporal suspension. It is a medieval technique (organum) reinvented in the service of modern color.

pieges.erreur: Applying T/SD/D functional analysis to Debussy's harmony
pieges.correction: Debussy's music does not follow classical tension-resolution logic. The chords are colors, not functions. A correct analysis identifies the source scales (whole-tone, octatonic, pentatonic) and the planing effect, not harmonic functions.

pieges.erreur: Confusing Ravel and Debussy stylistically
pieges.correction: Debussy: intuitive harmony, fluid structure, no rigid classical form. Ravel: harmony calculated with precision, classical forms reinterpreted (sonatina, minuet), watchmaker's orchestration. The same impressionist surface, opposite compositional logics.

pieges.erreur: Believing that Ravel's polychords are arbitrary
pieges.correction: In Ravel, superimposing two chords (C major + D major) is calculated: the common tones create links, the divergent tones create the color. This is not chance — it is harmonic algebra.

resume: Debussy: planing (parallel chords), whole-tone/octatonic/pentatonic scales, long pedal points, non-functional harmony by color
Ravel: polychords, added notes (6th, 9th), neoclassical modality, harmonic ostinato (Boléro), precise and calculated orchestration
Satie: furniture music, static harmony, hypnotic repetition — prefiguring minimalism and ambient music 50 years ahead of its time

analyseNarrative.tonalite: G major, a fully functional key — unlike Debussy or Satie, Ravel never renounces tonal grammar. He merely changes its vocabulary: every degree carries its 7th or its 9th as standard equipment.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4 (notated with a cut-C sign), ♩=80. « Assez doux, mais d'une sonorité large » (fairly soft, but with a broad sonority) — Ravel's own indications are the only ones on stage in this edition.
analyseNarrative.forme: A French rondeau, legible in the score's own indications: refrain (mm. 1-12) and its « Très lointain » (very distant) echo (m. 13 ff.); couplet 1 « un peu plus lent » (a little slower) (m. 26, orbiting B minor/D); refrain 2 « Reprenez le mouvement » (resume the tempo) (m. 28, reharmonized); couplet 2 « subitement très doux et très lié » (suddenly very soft and very smooth) (m. 39, the dark side, mixtures with flats, a doubled « Très grave » passage at mm. 48 and 58); final refrain « marquez le chant » (bring out the melody) (m. 61) and its cadence « En élargissant beaucoup » (broadening greatly) (m. 70). Three refrains, two couplets, perfect symmetry.

sections.label: Measures 1-4 (the refrain: a chain of sevenths)
sections.titre: Modern color over ancient grammar
sections.fonctions: T – SD – T – T – SD – SD – D – T
sections.texte: The refrain is a small manifesto: every degree of the scale carries its seventh or its ninth as standard equipment, the tonic itself included, arriving as early as m. 4 crowned with its own major seventh (the F♯). Yet the successions remain perfectly functional — a textbook ii-V-I closes the phrase in mm. 3-4. This is the neo-archaism of the pavane: a Renaissance dance revisited by gaslight, the color of the dawning twentieth century laid over a syntax that does not budge.

sections.label: Measures 5-12 (the cadence on the mediant)
sections.titre: A false door, and the melancholy that follows from it
sections.chiffrage: viiø7 – iii (cédez) – V13 – V/iii (first chromaticism) – iii
sections.texte: The first chromatic note of the whole piece — a single G♯ in m. 11 — manufactures a secondary dominant (E7, V of iii) that sets the phrase down not on the tonic but on B minor. Closing a theme in G major on its mediant degree is the archaic-modal cadence par excellence: a false door that gives the piece its processional melancholy. The « Très lointain » (very distant) echo that follows hovers over a B pedal before G reclaims its rights.

sections.label: Measures 13-38 (couplet 1 and refrain 2)
sections.titre: The same material, displaced then reharmonized
sections.texte: Couplet 1, « un peu plus lent » (a little slower), sets the discourse in orbit around B minor and D, with passing G♯ and C♯ — a harmonic region neighboring the refrain, never wholly foreign to it. The refrain then returns (« Reprenez le mouvement » — resume the tempo) reharmonized, yet supported by the same functions in the same places: the material does not change, only its clothing is renewed.

sections.label: Measures 39-59 (couplet 2: the dark side)
sections.titre: The flats come in, and the lament repeats itself
sections.fonctions: ? (modal color, no classical function at this level)
sections.texte: « Subitement très doux et très lié » (suddenly very soft and very smooth): couplet 2 brings in the degrees that distinguish G minor from G major — B♭ first, then F natural and E♭ — a mixture that darkens without ever entirely leaving the tonic's orbit. At its heart, a doubled passage marked « Très grave » (very grave) at mm. 48 and 58: a lament folding back on itself, the only literal repetition of gestures in the entire piece.

sections.label: Measures 60-72 (final refrain and closing cadence)
sections.titre: Marquez le chant
sections.texte: The third and last refrain returns « marquez le chant » (bring out the melody) — the most explicit indication in the whole score about melodic intent. The piece ends « en élargissant beaucoup » (broadening greatly), the only truly conclusive cadence in the entire form: the two previous refrains had turned aside toward the mediant, this one at last closes on the tonic.

synthese.titre: Neo-archaism: modern color, ancient grammar
synthese.texte: In 1899, between Satie's Gymnopédie (1888) and Debussy's Cathédrale engloutie (1910), Ravel systematizes what Satie had decreed — the seventh is no longer a tension, it is the chord's default timbre — without ever giving up functional syntax. Satie abolishes function; Debussy will dissolve it into pure color; Ravel keeps both hands on the table.

synthese.titre: The direct ancestor of jazz
synthese.texte: The I∆9 of m. 4 is, note for note, Bill Evans's default tonic chord (course 35) — and Evans listed Ravel among his declared influences. Sixty years separate this pavane from modal jazz, and a single sonority links them directly.

synthese.titre: The diplomat between two worlds
synthese.texte: Satie, Ravel, Debussy: the second narrative of this corpus (harmony after function) needs all three in order to be told. Ravel occupies the diplomat's position — neither abolition nor dissolution, but a new color patiently grafted onto a grammar that, for its part, holds firm.

cours37.title: Advanced Analysis: Schenker and Motivic Analysis
cours37.subtitle: Ursatz, Urlinie, 4 reduction levels and motivic analysis — seeing the deep structure of a work beyond its surface.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered Schenkerian analysis and motivic analysis.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! Review the 4 reduction levels and motivic transformations.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — try again when you're ready.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Schoenberg is famous for twelve-tone music, but he was also a major analyst and theorist. He developed the concept of Grundgestalt (basic shape) — a 2-to-6-note motif from which an entire work unfolds. His manual 'Fundamentals of Musical Composition' is still used in conservatories. Paradox: the father of atonality was obsessed with the motivic coherence that only tonal music can establish clearly.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: Analysis does not explain why music is beautiful — it reveals the framework beneath the surface. It is a tool, not a value.
narrative.schenkerP: Heinrich Schenker (1868–1935) developed a theory according to which all tonal music is an elaboration of a simple fundamental structure — the Ursatz. His approach reveals the layers of meaning hidden beneath the surface of music.
narrative.schenkerInfoBox: The Ursatz: The Urlinie (descending melodic line from the 5th, 3rd, or 8th degree to the tonic) supported by the Bassbrechung (bass arpeggiation I–V–I). All tonal music is a prolongation and elaboration of this Ursatz. In C major: G–F–E–D–C (soprano) / C–G–C (bass).
narrative.n0desc: The complete musical surface: all chords, ornaments, melodies, passing notes, neighbour notes, arpeggios. This is the music as performed.
narrative.n1desc: Reduction eliminating surface ornaments. Only the main harmonic functions and prolongations remain.
narrative.n2desc: Reduction showing only tonal regions and major harmonic prolongations.
narrative.n3desc: The fundamental structure (Ursatz): Urlinie + Bassbrechung. The harmonic framework of the entire work in a few notes.
narrative.o0desc: Connects two structural notes by stepwise motion: C–D–E, the D disappears at the reduction level
narrative.o1desc: Leaves a structural note, moves one step away, returns: C–D–C, the D is a neighbour note
narrative.o2desc: Unprepared foreign note on a strong beat, resolved by descending stepwise motion
narrative.o3desc: Resolution of a note is delayed — the non-structural note holds on the strong beat and resolves afterwards
narrative.schenkerWarn: Classic mistake: Confusing Schenkerian reduction with simplification. Reduction does not remove notes "at random" — it identifies structural notes according to precise criteria (metric position, duration, harmonic role). Ornamental notes are not less important: they are the expressive surface. Reduction reveals structure; it does not judge value.
narrative.motiviqueP: Motivic analysis identifies the melodic cells of 2 to 6 notes that form the raw material of a work, then tracks their transformations. This level of analysis reveals the organic unity of a composition — how everything derives from very little.
narrative.beethInfoBox: Beethoven — 5th Symphony: The opening motif (G–G–G–Eb) is not just the beginning of the first movement. This rhythmic (3 eighth notes + quarter note) and melodic (descending minor third) motif organises all 4 movements — in the 2nd movement theme, in the 3rd movement fanfares, in the 4th movement finale transition. This is the very definition of organic unity.
narrative.beethDesc: Two simultaneous dimensions: rhythm (short–short–short–long) and melody (descending minor third). Both are inseparable in analysis. In the 2nd movement the rhythm is transformed, but the melodic third persists.
narrative.t0desc: The motif transposed to another degree — intervals are preserved
narrative.t0ex: Beethoven 5th: motif repeated from bar 2 a tone lower
narrative.t1desc: Intervals reversed — what went up now goes down and vice versa
narrative.t1ex: Bach: inversions of the subject in fugues
narrative.t2desc: The motif in doubled values — slower, more solemn
narrative.t2ex: In a higher register to mark the augmentation
narrative.t3desc: Only the first 2–3 notes of the motif — creates unease and urgency
narrative.t3ex: Beethoven 5th: development fragments the 4 notes into 2 + 2
narrative.s1desc: 2 to 6 notes appearing at the start and repeating. A distinctive interval or rhythm is the key.
narrative.s2desc: Mark every appearance of the motif in the score — transpositions and transformations included.
narrative.s3desc: Inversion, augmentation, diminution, fragmentation, sequence. How does the motif develop?
narrative.s4desc: Does the motif create exposition, development, climax? What narrative role does it play?
narrative.brahmsInfoBox: Brahms and motivic unity: In his quartets and symphonies, Brahms often derives the entire work from a single interval (a second or a third). This generating interval appears in the melody, the bass, the transitions, the counter-melodies — always recognisable, always transformed. Brahms's motivic analysis reveals a thematic density comparable to Bach's.
narrative.motiviqueWarn: Common mistake: Analysing each surface chord without seeking the deep structure. Saying "C–G–F–C" says nothing about structural significance. Motivic analysis complements harmonic analysis: on one side the vertical structure (chords), on the other the horizontal structure (motif and its destiny). Together they reveal compositional logic.

cours38.title: Non-Chord Tones
cours38.subtitle: Passing tone, neighbor tone, appoggiatura, suspension, escape tone, anticipation and pedal point — the melodic ornamentation of harmony.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You identify and use every non-chord tone.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few subtleties left to consolidate (suspension, escape tone, appoggiatura).
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — review the definitions and listen to the examples again before retrying.

narrative.maitreCardAnecdote: Théodore Dubois, director of the Paris Conservatoire and author of a Treatise on Harmony that trained generations of musicians, classified non-chord tones with a watchmaker's precision. For him, telling an appoggiatura from a suspension, or a neighbor tone from a passing tone, was no game of labels: it was understanding how a single note, foreign to the chord, could by itself color, tense or soften an entire phrase. His students first learned to spot them in Bach before daring to write any themselves.
narrative.maitreCardLesson: A non-chord tone is never a mistake: the chord decides, and the ear is the judge.
narrative.defP1: A non-chord tone is a note that does not belong to the chord heard at that precise moment. It ornaments the melodic line, creating motion and expression without altering the actual harmony.
narrative.defInfoBox: The principle: at every instant, some notes are chord tones (they make up the chord), others are non-chord tones (they ornament it). Telling one from the other is the key to all harmonic analysis.
narrative.defP2: Non-chord tones are classified by three criteria: the beat on which they fall (strong or weak), the way one approaches them (by step or by leap) and the way one leaves them (resolution). These three criteria are enough to name every non-chord tone.
narrative.defTipBox: Remember: most non-chord tones are unprepared and fall on a weak beat. Two major exceptions: the appoggiatura (strong beat) and the suspension (strong beat AND prepared).
narrative.typesP1: Here are the most common non-chord tones, apart from the suspension (covered in its own section). Each is defined by its place on the beat and by the way it is approached and resolved.
narrative.typesClickHint: Click a non-chord tone to hear it and read its definition.
narrative.typePassageDesc: It links two different chord tones by step, on a weak beat. It may be diatonic or chromatic. Example: C → D → E, where the D (non-chord tone) links C and E (chord tones).
narrative.typeBroderieDesc: It leaves a chord tone by step, then returns to it, on a weak beat. The upper neighbor rises a step; the lower neighbor falls. Example: E → F → E (upper neighbor of E).
narrative.typeAppogiatureDesc: A non-chord tone placed on the strong beat, approached by leap or by step, then resolved by step (most often downward) onto a chord tone. It is unprepared — that is what sets it apart from the suspension. Example: F (on the strong beat) → E.
narrative.typeEchappeeDesc: It leaves a chord tone by step, then "escapes" by a leap in the opposite direction onto a tone of the next chord. Example: C → D (by step) → B (downward leap in the opposite direction).
narrative.typePassageAccDesc: This is a passing tone that, exceptionally, falls on the strong beat. Connected by stepwise motion on both sides, it resembles the appoggiatura but keeps its nature as a passing tone.
narrative.typeAnticipationDesc: It sounds in advance a note that will belong to the next chord: it arrives too early, over the chord still in progress, creating a brief dissonance before the harmony changes.
narrative.typesWarnBox: Do not confuse: the neighbor tone returns to its starting note, whereas the passing tone links two different notes. The appoggiatura arrives by leap on the strong beat; the escape tone leaves by leap.
narrative.retardP1: The suspension is the only non-chord tone that requires preparation. A consonant chord tone is held over (tied or repeated) as the harmony changes: it then becomes dissonant on the strong beat, before resolving downward by step.
narrative.retardInfoBox: What sets the suspension apart from the appoggiatura: both strike on the strong beat and resolve downward by step. But the suspension is prepared (heard first as a consonance), whereas the appoggiatura is approached freely.
narrative.retardStepsH3: The three stages of the suspension
narrative.retardStepsHint: Click each stage to see its details.
narrative.retardStepPrepDesc: The note is first heard as a consonance, in the same voice, within the preceding chord. It is this preparation that "legitimizes" the dissonance to come.
narrative.retardStepPercDesc: The harmony changes, but the note is held over: it becomes dissonant and strikes on the strong beat. This is the peak of tension of the suspension.
narrative.retardStepResDesc: The dissonant note descends by step onto a chord tone. The resolution is almost always downward.
narrative.retardAudioLabel: Listen to a 4-3 suspension on the C chord
narrative.retardAudioDesc: On the C chord (C–E–G), the suspended F strikes in place of the E (a dissonance of a fourth), then steps down onto the E: this is the 4-3 suspension.
narrative.retard43Desc: The fourth (dissonant) steps down onto the third of the chord. The most frequent suspension pattern.
narrative.retard76Desc: The seventh (dissonant) steps down onto the sixth (consonant).
narrative.retard98Desc: The ninth (dissonant) steps down onto the octave (the root).
narrative.retard23Desc: Suspension in the bass: the suspended bass forms a second with an upper voice, then steps down to give a consonant third (or tenth).
narrative.pedaleP1: The pedal point is a sustained note — most often the tonic or the dominant, in the bass — held while the harmony moves above it. It may become momentarily dissonant with the passing chords, without ever moving.
narrative.pedaleInfoBox: Tonic pedal: often at the end of a piece, it anchors the conclusion. Dominant pedal: often before a recapitulation, it creates a long tension and a strong expectation of resolution.
narrative.pedaleP2: Unlike other non-chord tones, the pedal point does not ornament a single note but holds beneath an entire progression. It is a non-chord tone by its duration and by the passing dissonances it generates.
