narrative.pedaleAudioDesc: The low C is held while the upper voices move from E–G to F–A and then return to E–G: the harmony changes, the pedal remains.
narrative.emploiP1: At the DEM, non-chord tones come into play in two fundamental exercises: spotting non-chord tones to analyze a work, and using them to realize a given melody or a given bass with naturalness and style.
narrative.emploiTipBox: Spotting method: for each note, ask whether it belongs to the chord. If not, look at the beat (strong / weak), the approach (by step / by leap) and the resolution. These three clues name it.
narrative.emploiStepsH3: Spotting a non-chord tone in four questions
narrative.emploiStep1: Does it belong to the chord? If yes, it is a chord tone — not a non-chord tone.
narrative.emploiStep2: On which beat does it fall? Strong beat → appoggiatura or suspension. Weak beat → passing tone, neighbor tone, escape tone, anticipation.
narrative.emploiStep3: How is it approached? By step (passing tone, neighbor tone, suspension, stepwise appoggiatura) or by leap (appoggiatura, anticipation).
narrative.emploiStep4: Is it prepared? If yes, and on a strong beat with a downward resolution: it is a suspension.
narrative.emploiWarnBox: In realization: do not add non-chord tones at random. Each ornament must obey its rule of resolution, and the suspension must always be prepared. A poorly resolved appoggiatura or an unprepared suspension is penalized.
narrative.emploiP2: The reference repertoire remains the J.S. Bach chorale: within a few bars you find passing tones, neighbor tones, 4-3 and 7-6 suspensions, and pedal points — always led with rigor. It is the model to imitate for the DEM.
narrative.emploiGallonBox: A school of voice leading: alongside Théodore Dubois's Treatise, the teaching of Noël Gallon, professor of harmony at the Paris Conservatoire, is a benchmark for the use of non-chord tones. His work on harmonic sequences and voice leading reminds us that an ornament has value only through the melodic line it draws: every non-chord tone must serve the melody, never overload it.

conservatoire.intuition: A bass that never changes by so much as a single note across eleven statements — and yet nothing ever repeats: the whole invention lives in the non-chord tones the sung voice lays over that unvarying descent.

reference.badge: Purcell · preface to the Sonnata's of III Parts
reference.citation: Musick is yet but in its Nonage, a forward Child, which gives hope of what he may be hereafter in England, when the Masters of it shall find more Encouragement.

voix: The suspension (7-6, then 4-3) is the non-chord tone par excellence of the ground: one voice holds on to a note of the previous chord while the bass has already moved on, creating the dissonance before the expected resolution.
A ground bass can carry different harmonies at every return — the non-chord tone is born of the gap between what the bass imposes and what the sung voice chooses to hold a moment longer.

The phase shift between the length of the vocal phrases and that of the ground (five measures) is itself a non-chord tone on the scale of the whole form: the lament and the bass almost never cadence together.

repertoire.titre: Dido's Lament — “When I am laid in earth” (Dido and Aeneas)

pieges.erreur: Mistaking the chromatic tetrachord in the bass (G-F♯-F-E-E♭-D) for a series of non-chord tones
pieges.correction: That descending line IS the structural cantus firmus (the ground itself, repeated without a single variant) — these are not passing tones but the harmonic foundation. The real non-chord tones (the suspensions) are in the sung voice above that bass.

pieges.erreur: Resolving a suspension upwards
pieges.correction: Like every classical suspension, each suspension over the ground resolves by downward motion — the sung voice falls one step onto the actual chord tone.

pieges.erreur: Expecting the same harmonic reading at every return of the ground
pieges.correction: Purcell reharmonises the same bass differently at each statement (the “clothing” changes) — only the bass line is invariant; the actual chord above it varies from one statement to the next.

resume: The suspension: consonant preparation → dissonant strike → downward resolution — Dido's Lament (Purcell, 1689) illustrates it in 7-6/4-3 chains across eleven statements of the same ground.

The ground (ostinato bass, here a descending chromatic tetrachord G-D, the passus duriusculus) stays invariant while its harmonic clothing changes at every return — the non-chord tone is born of that gap.
1689, public domain: the oldest piece in the Harmonia corpus, and the common source of the lament bass (Chopin), the prepared seventh (Bach) and the deferred resolution (Wagner).

analyseNarrative.tonalite: Recitative in C minor, modulating step by step towards D (the dominant of G minor), which becomes the threshold of the aria. The aria itself — the ground — is in G MINOR, the real key of the whole second half of the piece.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4. Largo (♩=50) for the recitative, Adagio con moto (♩=80) from m. 10 onwards — the change of tempo falls exactly on the beginning of the ground.
analyseNarrative.forme: Accompanied recitative “Thy hand, Belinda” (mm. 1-9), then an aria over a ground (mm. 10-65): eleven statements of a five-measure ostinato bass (the passus duriusculus, a descending chromatic tetrachord G-D), each reharmonised differently, plus a closing ritornello (mm. 60-65).

sections.label: Measures 1-9
sections.titre: Recitative: “Thy hand, Belinda”
sections.texte: The recitative opens in C minor (C-E♭-G), then brightens for an instant into a “passing” C major (m. 2, C-E-G) before darkening towards F minor (m. 3, F-A♭-C): a bass that descends by steps and mutations, exactly the image of the text (“darkness shades me”). The frictions of F♯ accumulate until, in m. 8, they crystallise into a genuine D7 chord (F♯-A-C) — the dominant of G minor, the key not yet named but already prepared. Measure 9 answers in pure D major, laid bare: the threshold on which the recitative sets down the aria.

sections.label: Measures 10-14
sections.titre: The ground, stated alone
sections.texte: As the cello does in the original, the bass states alone, with no harmony whatsoever above it, the chromatic tetrachord that will carry everything that follows: G-F♯-F-E-E♭-D, then the cadential tail B♭-C-D before falling back onto G. Exactly five measures, which will be repeated eleven times without a single note of variation — the passus duriusculus of the Baroque theorists, the emblem of the lament.

sections.label: Measures 15-19
sections.titre: Ground 2: the voice enters, out of phase
sections.texte: The voice enters over that same ground, but Purcell deliberately writes it out of phase: the vocal phrase does not trace the five measures of the bass, so that the cadence of the singing and that of the ground almost never fall together. The lament floats above a wheel turning at its own speed.

sections.label: Measures 20-34
sections.titre: Grounds 3 to 5: the reharmonisation
sections.chiffrage: … V7 – i6 (D7 → G minor, bass B♭) …
sections.texte: The bass does not change a single note, but its clothing changes at every statement: chains of 7-6 and 4-3 suspensions that shift along the chromatic descent. One precise functional gesture returns at least twice, identically (here in m. 23, then again in m. 38): each time the ground tips from its 4th note to its 5th (D → B♭, the octave dropping), the harmony forms a D7 (V7 of G minor) that resolves onto a G minor in first inversion (i6, bass B♭) — the only strict functional regularity in the midst of an otherwise ever-changing reharmonisation.

sections.label: Measures 35-39
sections.titre: Ground 6: “Remember me”
sections.chiffrage: i … V7 – i6 (il canto ben marcato, m. 38)
sections.texte: The expressive summit of the piece: the voice insists on a single repeated note (D5) while the bass, for its part, pursues its descent implacably — the stillness of the singing against the obstinate motion of the ground, the simplest and most devastating contrast in the piece. Purcell himself marks the vocal part “il canto ben marcato” in m. 38: the performance instruction falls exactly on the second D7–i6 verified in this analysis.

sections.label: Measures 40-59
sections.titre: Grounds 7 to 10: the lament continues
sections.texte: Four further statements of the same ground, each reharmonised differently again — the lament goes on unfolding without the bass ever yielding a single semitone of its trajectory.

sections.label: Measures 60-65
sections.titre: Final ground: ritornello and cadence
sections.chiffrage: i … V – i (bare fifth, no third)
sections.texte: The last ground adds descending chromatic countermelodies that spread to the upper voices — as if the bass had finally drawn the whole edifice into its own descent. The piece ends on a G that is not even frankly minor: the final chord (G-D-G-G) contains no third at all, an open fifth, without the slightest ray of light.

synthese.titre: The suspension, laboratory of the prepared dissonance
synthese.texte: Over a bass that never moves, all the expressive work is lodged in the upper voices: chains of suspensions (7-6, 4-3) whose frictions shift along the chromatic descent. It is the most canonical example in the repertoire for making audible what a prepared and then resolved non-chord tone is — the very subject of this lesson.

synthese.titre: Fixed bass, mobile harmony
synthese.texte: Purcell's ground shares its principle with Bach's Chaconne BWV 1004 already studied in lesson 9 (one repeated bass carrying changing harmonies) — except that here the bass itself never varies by a single note across eleven statements: the entirety of the invention is lodged in the clothing, not in the motif.

synthese.titre: 1689: the common source of the corpus
synthese.texte: The descending chromatic tetrachord of this ground (G-F♯-F-E-E♭-D) is, a hundred and fifty years earlier, exactly the same shape as the lament bass of Chopin's Prelude op. 28 no. 20 (lesson 24). The oldest piece in the corpus turns out to be the common source of several of its running threads: the chromatic descent, the prepared suspension, and the ostinato bass under a changing harmony.

cours39.title: Seventh Chords on Each Degree
cours39.subtitle: Beyond V7: the seventh chord on every scale degree — its quality, its preparation, its resolution, its inversions, and the chain of sevenths.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered the quality, preparation, and resolution of seventh chords.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few points to consolidate (inversions, chain of sevenths).
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — review the quality of each seventh and the downward resolution before starting again.

narrative.maitreAnecdote: Arcangelo Corelli, master of the Roman violin and father of the Baroque sonata, set the handling of dissonance for entire generations. His Sonatas and Concerti grossi overflow with long chains of sevenths that are prepared, struck, and resolved with clockwork regularity — the famous "Corelli cadence." Each seventh is announced as a consonance before becoming a dissonance, then falls by a step: a model of voice leading that Bach, and every treatise after him, would take up without question.
narrative.maitreLesson: A seventh is never a gratuitous effect: it is prepared, it is struck, then it descends to resolve. This discipline is what makes dissonance musical.
narrative.degIntro: Until now, the only seventh studied was the V7, the dominant seventh chord. But by stacking three thirds on any degree of the scale, we obtain a seventh chord. There are therefore seven of them (I7 to VII7), and they do not all have the same quality: it all depends on the intervals the scale makes available.
narrative.degInfoBox: Seventh chords on each degree are all the seventh chords other than the V7. Each belongs to an interval species (major seventh, minor seventh, half-diminished seventh, diminished seventh) according to the degree on which it is built.
narrative.degClickHint: Click a degree to hear it and read its quality.
narrative.degMineurBox: In minor mode: the qualities change. The VII of the harmonic scale (with leading tone) gives a diminished seventh (VII°7) — a stack of three minor thirds, a color of intense tension — instead of the half-diminished seventh of major. The second degree becomes half-diminished (IIø7), and the VI a major seventh. Always check the quality against the scale of the actual key.
narrative.ecrSectionTitle: Writing sevenths: preparation, resolution, inversions, the chain
narrative.ecrIntro: Every seventh is a dissonance: it therefore obeys precise rules of writing. In strict harmony, it is prepared, it is resolved downward, and its figuring is known in each inversion. Chained together, these sevenths form the famous chain of sevenths.
narrative.ecrPrepText: Preparing the seventh means sounding the note that will become dissonant first as a consonant note, in the same voice, in the preceding chord. The dissonance is thus "announced" to the ear before it strikes. Only the V7 is an exception: its dominant function allows its seventh to enter without preparation.
narrative.ecrResolBox: Resolution: the seventh almost always resolves by descending one step. It "falls" onto the lower neighbor note, which belongs to the following chord. Typical example: in V7 → I (C major), the seventh F descends to E, while the leading tone B rises to C.
narrative.ecrResolListenBtn: ▶ Listen to V7 → I (the seventh F descends to E)
narrative.ecrInvText: A seventh chord contains four notes: it therefore admits four positions. Each inversion corresponds to a classical figuring, inherited from the figured bass. In the third inversion, it is the dissonant seventh itself that lies in the bass — it will then have to descend in order to resolve.
narrative.ecrSensibleNote: Reminder — the leading tone changes the figuring. This table gives the BARE figuring, for species sevenths without the leading tone (I, II, III, IV, VI). On the 5th degree (V7) and the 7th (viiø7/vii°7) — the only two chords that contain the key's leading tone — a "+" is added before the figure where it sits: root position +7, 1st inversion +6/5, 2nd inversion +6 or +4, 3rd inversion +4 or +2 depending on the leading tone's exact position.
narrative.ecrMarcheText: The chain of sevenths is a progression in which each chord is a seventh and the roots descend by fifths (descending circle of fifths). The seventh of one chord prepares the seventh of the next: it is a mechanism of linked preparations and resolutions, a model of writing par excellence.
narrative.ecrMarcheBox: Circle of fifths: I7 – IV7 – VII7 – III7 – VI7 – II7 – V7 – I. To lead the voices without errors, one alternates complete chords (4 notes) and incomplete ones (without the fifth): in this way the seventh of each chord is always prepared by a consonance of the preceding chord.
narrative.ecrMarcheListenBtn: ▶ Listen to a chain of sevenths (descending fifths)
narrative.ecrVoixBox: Voice leading: never double the seventh nor let it rise. Each seventh descends, each leading tone rises. It is the alternation of complete / incomplete chords that avoids parallel fifths in the chain — a rule already observed in Corelli and Bach.
narrative.quizFeedbackExcellent: Perfect! You have mastered the quality, preparation, and resolution of seventh chords.
narrative.quizFeedbackGood: Very good! A few points to consolidate (inversions, chain of sevenths).
narrative.quizFeedbackKeepGoing: Keep going — review the quality of each seventh and the downward resolution before starting again.

conservatoire.intuition: The diminished seventh is the chameleon of tonal harmony — a single chord, symmetrical in minor thirds, that can be reinterpreted and resolve towards four different tonics.

reference.citation: The diminished seventh chord, because of its symmetrical structure, is the most useful chord for enharmonic modulation.

voix: vii°7 (the diminished seventh on the leading tone) resolves to the tonic by stepwise motion in both outer voices
Its symmetry (a stack of equal minor thirds) allows 4 enharmonic respellings, hence 4 possible resolutions towards different keys
vii°7 can be built on ANY degree as a secondary dominant (vii°7/V, vii°7/IV...), not only on the tonic

pieges.erreur: Recognising the diminished seventh only in root position, on the tonic
pieges.correction: vii°7 appears just as readily as a secondary dominant (vii°7/V, vii°7/IV) as it does as an enharmonic pivot — it is the same chord, reinterpreted

resume: vii°7 = a stack of equal minor thirds, symmetrical, resolving by stepwise motion to the tonic
That symmetry allows 4 enharmonic respellings: one and the same chord can modulate towards 4 different keys
Grave introduction of the Pathétique (Beethoven): vii°7 takes on, in turn, the roles of secondary dominant, principal dominant and enharmonic pivot

analyseNarrative.tonalite: C minor (key signature of three flats). A passing shift towards E♭ major (the relative major) in mm. 4-5, by way of a headlong dominant (B♭7), before a return to the minor through a single enharmonic pivot (m. 6).
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4 (the C symbol). Grave, very slow (30 to the quarter note), with further slowings at the densest passages.
analyseNarrative.forme: 10 measures = the complete Grave introduction of the first movement, linked attacca to the Allegro di molto e con brio. The whole introduction is a single deferred cadence: statement of the problem (mm. 1-3), crisis and headlong modulation (m. 4), false light and enharmonic pivot (mm. 5-6), great chromatic ascent broken off by a deceptive cadence (mm. 7-9), and the cadence finally achieved but suspended on the dominant (m. 10).

sections.label: Measures 1-3
sections.titre: Statement of the problem
sections.fonctions: i – D – D | D – i6 | D – D
sections.texte: Measure 1 sets down the world in embryo: a complete tonic chord fp in the low register, the characteristic dotted rhythm, then a vii°7/V (F♯-A-C-E♭) resolving onto the dominant — tonic, tension, dominant, in four beats. Measure 2 shifts the same device onto vii°4/2 (B-D-F over an A♭ bass): the bass descends A♭-G-F towards E♭ while the upper voices still hold the chord — a resolution deferred to i6 on the following beat. Measure 3 transposes the whole thing a third higher (the seventh in the bass, E♭-D-C) and immediately relaunches the figure: the harmonic rhythm accelerates.

sections.label: Measure 4
sections.titre: The crisis and the escape
sections.fonctions: D – D – SD – SD – D (in E♭)
sections.texte: On an sf, the harmony accelerates brutally: vii°7/V, V6, then two chords foreign to the circuit of C minor — C7/B♭ (V4/2 of F minor) and F minor/A♭ (iv6), three eighth notes, three functions. Then everything halts on a suspended A♭, and a cascade written out note for note (down to the nonuplets) unfolds B♭7: the dominant of the relative major. The modulation is not prepared; it is precipitated by the crisis.

sections.label: Measures 5-6
sections.titre: The false light and the pivot
sections.chiffrage: E♭ (I) – A♭/E♭ (IV6/4) – B°7 (vii°6/5, in C) – Fm/C (iv6/4) | B°7 (vii°7) – B♭7 (V7/III) – C♯°7 (enh. pivot) – A7 (V7/(V/V))
sections.fonctions: T (E♭) then D (return to C) | D – D – (pivot) – D
sections.texte: E♭ major, p, a fresh texture: repeated chords, an ascending melody taking up the dotted cell again. This clearing lasts no more than two and a half beats: a sudden ff, and the home-key vii°7 (B-D-F-A♭) breaks into the major, while the bass begins a chromatic descent — D, C, B (vii°7 in root position), B♭ (the same aggregate slips a semitone and becomes B♭7, V7 of E♭)… then, over that very B♭ in the bass, C♯-E-G rises up: C♯°7, the enharmonic pivot. In a single chord, the orbit of E♭ is abandoned for that of D: A7 closes the measure, dominant of a dominant as yet unheard of.

sections.label: Measures 7-9
sections.titre: The great ascent, then the deceptive cadence
sections.chiffrage: D/F♯ (V6/V) – D/F♮ (dissolving into a diminished chord) – B°6 (vii°6) | B°7 (vii°7) → G7 (V7) – Fm/A♭ (iv6) | G7 (V7) → A♭ (VI, deceptive cadence)
sections.texte: D major in first inversion (V6/V) — the most remote harmony of the introduction — launches the final ascent. The melody climbs in octaves, then the D chord comes undone beneath it (F♯ becomes F♮, A becomes A♭: the major dissolves into a diminished chord), and the climb continues, fully chromatic, each degree harmonised by a rotation of the same vii°7/dominant stock, up to the V7 at last in root position (m. 8) — a full chromatic sixth, stretched across three measures. Measure 9 ought to resolve: sfp on G7, fragmentation into dry staccatos — and a deceptive cadence: V7 → A♭ major (VI). After eight measures of construction, the resolution is refused. Silence.

sections.label: Measure 10
sections.titre: The cadence, at last — and suspended
sections.texte: The refused tonic arrives first bare, in the melody alone — a voice resuming after the interruption. Then the textbook cadential formula unfolds, drawn out: iiø6/5 (D-F-A♭-C, beneath obstinate staccato A♭s), a cadential i6/4 under which a great descending chromatic run of two octaves and a third pours down (a magnified mirror of the preceding ascent), and finally V7 with a minor ninth — G-B-D-F-A♭, the ♭9 struck sf under a fermata. Last note: the leading tone, B, as a sixty-fourth note. Double bar, attacca: the resolution onto C minor belongs to the Allegro.

synthese.titre: One chord, every function
synthese.texte: vii°7 appears in almost all its possible guises within these 10 measures: secondary dominant (vii°7/V), principal dominant (vii°7 plain and simple), and enharmonic pivot (C♯°7). A single chord type, declined from beginning to end.

synthese.titre: The symmetry of vii°7, engine of modulation
synthese.texte: Because it stacks three equal minor thirds, the diminished seventh chord can be respelled enharmonically in four ways and resolve towards four different tonics — exactly what makes it possible, in m. 6, to leave the orbit of E♭ major for that of D in a single chord.

synthese.titre: Textbook harmony, staged
synthese.texte: Technically, this Grave invents nothing: appoggiaturas, diminished chords, deceptive cadence, cadential six-four — it is all in the treatises. What is new is the dramatic regime imposed on that vocabulary: dynamics like electric shocks, silences that cut the discourse short, resolutions systematically deferred — textbook harmony handled as theatrical material.

cours40.title: The Two-Voice Invention
cours40.subtitle: Subject, imitation at the octave, countersubject, episodes and tonal plan — writing the invention in Bach's style, toward the DEM counterpoint.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You've mastered the subject, imitation at the octave and the tonal plan of the invention.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few points to consolidate (motivic devices, episodes in sequence).
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — review the role of the subject, the imitation and the episodes before trying again.

narrative.maitreAnecdote: In 1723, Johann Sebastian Bach gathered fifteen short pieces (BWV 772–786) which he called “Inventions” for the use of his pupils — foremost among them his son Wilhelm Friedemann. In the preface he set a twofold aim: to learn to play cleanly in two voices, but above all to “have good ideas (inventiones) and to develop them.” Each invention grows from a single motive: a cell of a few notes that Bach imitates, inverts, fragments and carries through the neighbouring keys. The whole art lies in this economy — to bring forth an entire piece from a tiny idea.
narrative.maitreLesson: An invention is a motive brought to life: you state it, imitate it at the octave, develop it in episodes, and bring it back to the tonic. A single well-chosen subject is enough to build the whole piece.
narrative.structSectionTitle: The subject, the imitation and the countersubject
narrative.structIntro: A two-voice invention is a contrapuntal piece in which two independent voices converse from a single motive, the subject. It is the direct ancestor of the fugue and the first step toward the Bach counterpoint required at the DEM.
narrative.structInfoBox: The principle: all the material of the piece — melody, accompaniment, transitions — derives from a single motive. Nothing is gratuitous: every figure is a transformation of the subject or its countersubject.
narrative.structSujetText: The subject is the opening melodic motive. Its head-motive (incipit) — its first notes, its rhythm and its characteristic contour — gives the piece its recognisable identity. A good subject is short and memorable.
narrative.structImitText: The second voice repeats the subject after a short delay. Most often the imitation is at the octave (sometimes at the fifth). It is the imitation that creates the two-voice dialogue.
narrative.structImitBox: At the octave: the answer faithfully reproduces the subject, an octave lower (or higher). At the fifth, we approach the subject/answer principle of the fugue, but the invention most often stays at the octave.
narrative.structImitListenBtn: ▶ Listen to subject + imitation at the octave
narrative.structCsText: While the 2nd voice states the imitated subject, the 1st voice continues with a countersubject — a recurring melodic figure that accompanies the subject — or with a free voice. The two voices must remain genuinely independent (counterpoint).
narrative.structCsBox: Independence of the voices: the countersubject must not merely double the subject in chords. It converses with it: complementary rhythms, contrary motion, staggered entries. Therein lies the whole difficulty of two-voice counterpoint.
narrative.devSectionTitle: Episodes, motivic devices, tonal plan and method
narrative.devIntro: Once the subject has been stated and imitated, the invention unfolds: episodes provide the links and the modulations, while the motive is constantly developed through a series of devices. The whole follows a precise tonal plan.
narrative.devEpisodesText: The episodes (or divertimenti) are linking passages based on fragments of the motive. They are often treated as a sequence: a fragment is repeated at successive pitches, which causes modulation and leads from one key to the next.
narrative.devProcedesClickHint: Click on a device to hear it (motive then its transformation).
narrative.devStretteBox: The stretto: a very close imitation in which the 2nd voice enters before the 1st has finished stating the subject. The entries overlap, tightening the texture. In an invention one mostly encounters light strettos; it becomes systematic in the fugue.
narrative.devPlanText: An invention is not a free succession: it follows a tonal course. In major: exposition in the tonic, modulation to the dominant, development through the neighbouring keys, then return to the tonic to conclude.
narrative.devPlanMineurBox: In the minor mode: after the exposition, the modulation most often goes to the relative major (key of the third degree), sometimes to the minor dominant — the equivalent of the tonic → dominant move in major.
narrative.devMethodeTitle: Method: composing a short invention (8 to 16 bars)
narrative.devMethodeIntro: Four steps to build a complete invention from scratch:
narrative.devMethodeStep1: Invent a short, characteristic subject (a few notes with a recognisable contour and rhythm).
narrative.devMethodeStep2: Imitate it at the octave in the second voice, accompanying the imitated subject with a countersubject (or a free voice).
narrative.devMethodeStep3: Build episodes in sequence on fragments of the motive, modulating to the dominant and then to the neighbouring keys.
narrative.devMethodeStep4: Bring the subject back to the tonic and conclude with a perfect cadence (concluding cadence; intermediate cadences punctuate the tonal articulations).
narrative.devGedalgeBox: Toward the DEM: the rigour of motivic work — subject, countersubject, entries, sequences — is codified by André Gédalge in his Traité de la fugue (1901). Mastering the two-voice invention prepares directly for the DEM counterpoint test in Bach's style.
narrative.quizFeedbackExcellent: Perfect! You've mastered the subject, imitation at the octave and the tonal plan of the invention.
narrative.quizFeedbackGood: Very good! A few points to consolidate (motivic devices, episodes in sequence).
narrative.quizFeedbackKeepGoing: Keep going — review the role of the subject, the imitation and the episodes before trying again.

conservatoire.intuition: The subject of an invention can contain, in its melodic range alone, the chord that will structure the whole piece — line and verticality are never anything but two ways of hearing the same tension.

reference.badge: Bach · at the head of his Inventions
reference.citation: An honest method… of learning to play cleanly in two voices, but also, as one progresses further, of handling three obbligato parts correctly and well.
reference.auteur: J.S. Bach, preface to the Inventions and Sinfonias (1723)

voix: A subject can trace melodically the same interval as a fundamental chord of the key — here, the range of the subject (C♯-B♭) traces exactly a diminished seventh, the chord that will return later stacked vertically.

A written-out trill (genuinely alternating notes, not a mere ornament sign) can function as a pedal point: the voice that seems motionless is in fact the one vibrating most, while the other voice unfolds all the harmonic movement.
A piece entirely in the minor can refuse to decide right to the end: closing on a bare octave, without a third, leaves the major/minor question open at the very last chord.

repertoire.titre: Invention No. 4 in D minor, BWV 775

pieges.erreur: Looking for written chords in order to analyse the harmony of this invention
pieges.correction: There are none: the two voices are strictly melodic from beginning to end. The harmony must be deduced from the vertical meeting of the two lines at every instant, never read directly off the score.

pieges.erreur: Mistaking the written-out trill of mm. 19-21 and 29-33 for mere decorative ornamentation without structural consequence
pieges.correction: These trills function as genuine harmonic pedal points: the note that seems to repeat motionlessly in fact carries the whole tension (a tonic pedal in mm. 19-21, the ♭6→5 of the dominant in mm. 29-33), while the other voice supplies the movement.

pieges.erreur: Analysing the descending scale in the bass of m. 39 as a mere melodic line unconnected to the harmony
pieges.correction: It is a diminished seventh chord (vii°7 of G minor) entirely spread out as a line — the 4 notes of the chord (F♯-A-C-E♭) are all present in the descending scale, surrounded by 2 passing tones.

resume: The subject of Invention No. 4 (Bach, BWV 775) traces a diminished seventh melodically (range C♯-B♭) — the very chord that will return stacked vertically in m. 50, just before the final cadence.

Two written-out trills (D-C, then F-E, for up to 5 measures on end) function as genuine harmonic pedal points: the seemingly motionless voice carries the tension while the other voice supplies all the movement.
The piece ends on a bare octave (D-D), without a third — after fifty-two measures of harmonic minor, the last chord refuses to decide between major and minor.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: D minor — with a detour through the relative major (F major, mm. 9-18), then through the minor dominant (A minor, mm. 27-37) before the final return.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 3/8, with no tempo marking. Two strictly independent voices from beginning to end (no harmony is ever written as chords: it arises entirely from the meeting of the two lines).
analyseNarrative.forme: Exposition (mm. 1-8), sequence towards the relative major (mm. 9-18), first trill-pedal (mm. 19-21), modulating sequence towards the minor dominant (mm. 22-27), second trill-pedal (mm. 29-33), cadence and return (mm. 34-43), recapitulation and closing cadences (mm. 44-52).

sections.label: Measures 1-8
sections.titre: The subject: a melodic diminished seventh
sections.texte: The subject states itself alone: a D minor scale rising from D to B♭ (m. 1), then descending from C♯ (m. 2) — the exact range of these two measures, from C♯ to B♭, is a diminished seventh, the leading tone and the lowered sixth degree of the harmonic minor bounding the line. The left hand imitates at the octave (mm. 3-4) beneath a counterpoint spelling out i-V6/5, then the subject returns in the upper register (mm. 5-6, i-V4/3). The harmony arises entirely from the meeting of the two voices — no chord is ever written as such.

sections.label: Measures 9-21
sections.titre: Towards the relative major, then the first trill-pedal
sections.texte: Moving bass lines carry the music towards the relative major, F, in paired sequences, up to a cadence (mm. 17-18). Then the right hand holds a written-out trill (D-C) for three whole measures while the bass unfolds scales beneath it: an ornamental pedal, where the note that does not move is also the one vibrating most.

sections.label: Measures 22-33
sections.titre: Modulating sequence and the second trill
sections.chiffrage: … → V of A m … i (trill, LH)
sections.texte: Three leading tones light up in turn within a modulating sequence, and the music reaches the minor dominant of D: A minor. Then the structural summit of the piece — the left hand holds five whole measures of written-out trill (F-E) beneath the right hand's sequences: over the dominant of A minor, this is the chromatic motion from the lowered sixth degree to the fifth, literally trilled as a continuous ornament.

sections.label: Measures 34-43
sections.titre: Cadence and return
sections.chiffrage: i (A m) … vii°7 of G m … V7
sections.texte: A cadence closes the episode in A minor. The way back passes through G minor, with a diminished seventh chord entirely spread out as a descending scale in the bass — the diminished chord turned back into a line, as at the very beginning of the subject. An A7 rekindles D.

sections.label: Measures 44-52
sections.titre: Recapitulation and the bare final octave
sections.texte: The subject returns in both voices, in the upper register and then in the bass. Measure 50 offers the aggregate in broad daylight: the complete diminished seventh chord, this time stacked vertically rather than spread out as a line, just before the dominant and the conclusion — a bare octave, D-D, neither major nor minor third, after fifty-two measures of harmonic minor.

synthese.titre: The diminished chord, line and verticality
synthese.texte: The same sonority (the diminished seventh chord) runs through the whole piece in two forms: horizontal from the subject onwards (the C♯-B♭ range of the melodic line), then vertical on two occasions (m. 39, spread out as a scale in the bass; m. 50, stacked up in broad daylight). One and the same tension, heard in turn as melody and as chord.

synthese.titre: The trilled sigh: the oldest cell, transformed
synthese.texte: The motion from the lowered sixth degree to the fifth (♭6→5) — the “sigh” that runs through this corpus from the Baroque laments to Romanticism — becomes here, under Bach's fingers, a continuous ornament five measures long: the oldest expressive cell transformed into a pure object of texture, without ever losing its original expressive charge.

synthese.titre: The bare octave: a family of endings
synthese.texte: Ending on an octave without a third, after a piece written entirely in the minor mode, is a choice that refuses to decide between major and minor at the very last instant — the same gesture of stripping-away as an open fifth or a unison at the close of far later works, here in the service of a perfectly simple Baroque ending.

cours41.title: Stylistic Writing
cours41.subtitle: Pastiching the Classical, the Romantic and the early 20th century — the stylistic-writing discipline of the DEM (specialised cycle / CPES): identify the signatures of a style, then reproduce them.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You unhesitatingly identify the signatures of the Classical, the Romantic and the early 20th century.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few stylistic traits still need refining (Romantic altered chords, Debussyan planing).
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — review the signatures of each style before attempting the pastiche.

narrative.maitreAnecdote: At the Paris Conservatoire, Maurice Ravel was the most subtle pasticheur of his generation: his Menuet sur le nom d'Haydn or his À la manière de… (Borodin, Chabrier) reveal a composer able to adopt another's writing down to its smallest harmonic mannerisms. To reproduce a style is not to copy it: it is to have taken apart its mechanisms — harmonic language, rhythm, texture, voice leading — to the point of being able to write fresh “Mozart” or “Brahms”. That is exactly what the DEM's stylistic-writing unit demands.
narrative.maitreLesson: To write in a style is first to analyse it: you spot the signatures of a model (harmony, harmonic rhythm, texture, voice leading, cadences), then reproduce them — without ever committing an anachronism.
narrative.stylesIntro: Stylistic writing — pastiche — is a central discipline of the DEM in writing (specialised cycle / CPES, e.g. at the CRR of Lyon). You are asked to harmonise a given melody or to complete a page in the language of a precise era. Each style has its signatures: a recognisable way of treating harmony, rhythm, texture and voice leading.
narrative.stylesInfoBox: The principle: you can only pastiche well what you have analysed. Before writing, you identify the characteristic traits of the target style; you then reproduce them faithfully, without mixing in devices from another era.
narrative.stylesClickHint: Click a style to expand its description and its signatures.
narrative.style_classique_desc: The Classical style aims for clarity. A given melody is readily harmonised for string quartet, in homophonic texture: a clear melody supported by a transparent accompaniment (often an Alberti bass). The harmony is diatonic, the cadences clear-cut.
narrative.style_classique_sig1: Clear homophonic texture (string quartet: 2 violins, viola, cello).
narrative.style_classique_sig3: Regular harmonic rhythm (chord change per beat or per bar).
narrative.style_romantique_desc: Romanticism intensifies expression. Chromaticism becomes pervasive, the harmony grows richer (ninths, modal borrowings, augmented sixths, altered chords). The voice leading thickens, tonality becomes ambiguous, and the phrasing calls for rubato.
narrative.style_xxe_desc: At the turn of the century, colour prevails over function. Composers turn to modality, to parallel chords (planing), to unresolved 9ths and 11ths, to the whole-tone scale and to pedals. A chord counts for its harmonic timbre more than for its tension.
narrative.stylesPiegeBox: The trap to avoid — harmonic anachronism: each device belongs to an era. A “Brahms-style” augmented sixth in a Mozart pastiche, or Debussyan planing on a Classical page, immediately “break” the style. It is the error most severely penalised at the DEM.
narrative.methodeSectionTitle: Pastiche method and annotated worked answers
narrative.methodeIntro: Pastiching is not improvising: it is a methodical process. You analyse a model, extract its signatures, then write by reproducing them faithfully. Here is the procedure.
narrative.methodeStepsTitle: The four steps of the pastiche
narrative.methodeStep1: Analyse a model from the target era: spot its harmonic language, its harmonic rhythm, its texture and its voice leading before writing a single note.
narrative.methodeStep2: List the signatures: which chords, which cadences, which texture, which devices characterise this style and set it apart from the others?
narrative.methodeStep3: Write by reproducing these signatures: harmonise the given melody (or complete the page) drawing only on the resources of the chosen language.
narrative.methodeStep4: Reread hunting for anachronisms: check that no device foreign to the era has slipped into the writing.
narrative.methodeAnachroBox: Harmonic anachronism, once again: it is the no. 1 trap of the pastiche. Reproducing a style requires a negative discipline — forbidding yourself everything that does not belong to the era (no whole-tone scale in Mozart, no Alberti bass in Debussy).
narrative.corrigesTitle: Annotated worked answers — one example per style
narrative.corrigesIntro: On one and the same given melody, here is how the chosen language shapes the realisation. Each worked answer highlights the signatures to reproduce.
narrative.corrige_classique_text: The given melody is harmonised for string quartet in homophonic texture. Diatonic harmony, regular harmonic rhythm (one chord per strong beat), accompaniment in Alberti bass in the second violin and viola. The phrase closes on a perfect cadence, prepared by a II–V–I or a half cadence at the midpoint. No superfluous chromaticism: clarity prevails.
narrative.corrige_romantique_text: The same melody is coloured with chromaticism: ninth chords, borrowings from the minor mode, an augmented sixth leading to the dominant. The voice leading becomes dense, with expressive inner lines; a resolution is delayed to create tonal ambiguity. The phrasing, ample, implies rubato.
narrative.corrige_xxe_text: Here harmony becomes colour: one uses parallel chords (planing) of ninths, a coloured pedal in the bass, modal inflections (e.g. Dorian or Mixolydian) and, occasionally, the whole-tone scale. The dissonances do not resolve: they sound for themselves. Tonal function fades in favour of sensation.
narrative.methodeDemBox: Towards the DEM: the stylistic-writing unit (DEM / CPES cursus, e.g. CRR of Lyon) assesses precisely this ability to write “in the style of”. Practising the three languages — Classical, Romantic, early 20th century — and banishing anachronism is the key to the exam.
narrative.quizFeedbackExcellent: Perfect! You unhesitatingly identify the signatures of the Classical, the Romantic and the early 20th century.
narrative.quizFeedbackGood: Very good! A few stylistic traits still need refining (Romantic altered chords, Debussyan planing).
narrative.quizFeedbackKeepGoing: Keep going — review the signatures of each style before attempting the pastiche.

satb.noError: No errors in the notes placed so far.
satb.complete: Progression complete — no harmonic errors found.

errors.missing_accidental: {voice}: {note} natural — without a key signature, use {expected} (bar {from})
errors.wrong_chord: Bar {from}: this is not the requested chord

parallel_fifth.quoi: Two voices a perfect fifth apart moving in the same direction while keeping that fifth. Example: bass C and tenor G (a fifth) rising together to bass D and tenor A — two perfect fifths in a row.
parallel_fifth.pourquoi: The perfect fifth is so consonant that, repeated in parallel, it fuses the two voices: we no longer hear them as two distinct lines but as a single, thickened one. The independence of the four voices — the whole point of four-part writing — is lost.
parallel_fifth.comment: Prefer contrary motion: one voice rises while the other falls. Or route one of them through a different chord tone, so the interval is no longer a fifth. Swapping two notes between voices is often enough.

parallel_octave.quoi: Two voices an octave (or unison) apart moving in the same direction while keeping that spacing. Example: soprano C doubled at the octave by tenor C, then both moving to D — the octave D–D slides in parallel.
parallel_octave.pourquoi: At the octave, one voice merely doubles the other: if they move together, four real voices become three. An octave reinforcement is superb when held, but in motion it erases a voice and thins the polyphony.
parallel_octave.comment: Contrary motion for preference. Change the doubling: double a different chord tone instead of this one. A held common note is never flagged — keeping one voice still while the other moves solves it.

hidden_fifth.quoi: The soprano and bass reach a fifth together by similar motion, the soprano arriving by a leap. Example: the soprano leaps from E to A while the bass rises from C to D — the two outer voices land on the fifth D–A.
hidden_fifth.pourquoi: The ear anticipates the fifth filled in by the parallel motion: the hidden fifth suggests a parallel fifth sketched out, and on the two outer voices, the most exposed, it can be heard. It is only a warning, not a serious fault.
hidden_fifth.comment: Approach the fifth by contrary or oblique motion. Above all, avoid the soprano leaping into it: a soprano moving by step is not flagged. Or place the fifth in an inner voice.

hidden_octave.quoi: The soprano and bass reach an octave by similar motion, the soprano by a leap. Example: the soprano leaps from G to D while the bass rises from C to D — arriving on the octave D–D, reached too head-on.
hidden_octave.pourquoi: As with the hidden fifth, an octave reached in the same direction and by leap sounds like a parallel octave begun. On the outer voices, well to the fore in the texture, the effect is audible; the independence of the two lines blurs.
hidden_octave.comment: Approach the octave by contrary or oblique motion. Let the soprano move by step rather than by leap. Or double a different chord tone so as not to aim for that octave.

leading_tone.quoi: At a dominant → tonic (or degree VI) progression, the leading note — the 7th degree, a semitone below the tonic — must resolve to it. Example: in C major, the B of the G chord must rise to C; if it goes elsewhere, it is flagged.
leading_tone.pourquoi: The leading note creates a tension the ear expects to see resolved a semitone higher. Leaving it hanging frustrates that expectation and weakens the cadence. In the outer voices (soprano, bass) it is an error; in an inner voice, only a warning.
leading_tone.comment: Move the leading note up a semitone to the tonic, especially in the soprano and bass. In an inner voice, its fall of a third to the dominant (to complete the chord) is tolerated. So is the bass of a V6 descending to VI.

doubled_leading_tone.quoi: In a dominant-function chord, the leading note (7th degree) appears in two voices at once. Example: in C major, the B of the G chord present in both the tenor and the soprano.
doubled_leading_tone.pourquoi: The leading note wants to rise to the tonic. If it is doubled, both voices would rise together — producing parallel octaves on the tonic — or one would have to give up its natural resolution. So we prefer to state it only once.
doubled_leading_tone.comment: Double the leading note only once. Rather double the root or the fifth of the chord, which move freely. Replace one of the two leading notes with another chord tone by swapping notes between voices.

seventh.quoi: The seventh of a chord is a dissonance that must fall by step, or be held if it belongs to the next chord. Example: in G7 (G–B–D–F), the F must fall to E in the C chord.
seventh.pourquoi: The seventh introduces a dissonance the ear expects to see resolved downward, gently. Making it leap or rise leaves the tension unresolved: the seventh chord loses its sense of preparation and resolution.
seventh.comment: Let the seventh fall by a semitone or a tone (F→E). Or hold it if the note stays in the arriving chord. You can also prepare it — presenting it as a consonance just before — so its resolution feels natural.

spacing.quoi: Between soprano and alto, and between alto and tenor, the gap must not exceed an octave. Example: soprano G and alto G an octave apart is the limit; if the alto drops to E, the gap with the soprano exceeds an octave and is flagged.
spacing.pourquoi: Too wide a gap between the three upper voices makes the chord hollow, poorly blended, top-heavy. Between tenor and bass, on the other hand, a wide gap is natural (that is how the harmonic series resonates): this pair is not checked.
spacing.comment: Tighten the upper voices: raise the alto or the tenor by an octave. Redistribute the chord to fill the gap. Double a closer note to keep the three upper voices within an octave.

crossing.quoi: A voice moves above the one that should sit over it. Example: the tenor rises to D4 while the alto stays on C4 — the tenor ends up higher than the alto, breaking the soprano ≥ alto ≥ tenor ≥ bass order.
crossing.pourquoi: The listener follows each voice by its pitch. When two voices cross, the ear loses the thread: it no longer knows which is which, and the clarity of the polyphonic fabric blurs for the duration of the crossing.
crossing.comment: Keep the order of pitches in every bar. Swap the two notes between the voices concerned to restore the hierarchy. Or rewrite the offending note an octave lower, within its voice's range.

range.quoi: Each voice has a comfortable range: bass E2–C4, tenor C3–G4, alto G3–C5, soprano C4–G5. A note beyond it is flagged. Example: a soprano written on A5 exceeds G5, its upper limit.
range.pourquoi: Beyond its range a voice strains, becomes inaudible or loses its tone: the writing stops being singable. Yet four-part singing remains the reference — what a human voice cannot sustain sounds wrong, even on paper.
range.comment: Transpose the note by an octave to bring it back within range. Give it to the neighbouring voice, whose range covers it better. Or redistribute the chord so each voice stays at home.

cross_relation.quoi: The same note appears in two forms (two different accidentals) in two different voices, from one chord to the next. Example: F natural in the tenor, then F sharp in the soprano in the following bar. Chromaticism carried within one and the same voice, however, remains allowed.
cross_relation.pourquoi: The clash of the two versions can surprise the ear — but it is often perfectly defensible, notably in the minor with its melodic movement. That is why Harmonia flags it without counting it in the mark: it is a pointer, not a fault.
cross_relation.comment: If you would rather soften it, keep the chromatic step within a single voice (F→F sharp in the same part). Otherwise, embrace it when the minor context justifies it: it is part of the language.

missing_accidental.quoi: Without a key signature, the accidentals of the key must be written by hand on each note concerned. Example: in D major, every F must be F sharp and every C a C sharp; an F natural is then flagged.
missing_accidental.pourquoi: Without its accidental, the note no longer belongs to the key and the harmony becomes wrong. This is not a matter of taste but a reminder about pitch: hence the mere warning, until the correct pitch is restored.
missing_accidental.comment: Add the required accidental (sharp or flat) shown in the message. Review each note against the key signature. When in doubt, compare with the reference scale of the piece.

wrong_chord.titre: This is not the requested chord
wrong_chord.quoi: The notes in the bar do not form the chord the exercise expects. Example: the exercise asks for C major (C–E–G) and your four voices give C–E–G–B — that B makes it another chord.
wrong_chord.pourquoi: The chord is the harmonic frame of the exercise: the wrong chord changes the meaning of the progression. The good news: only the nature of the chord (its notes) and its bass count. The layout is free — octaves, doublings and distribution among the voices are yours to choose.
wrong_chord.comment: Check the chord's expected notes. Keep only those (root, third, fifth…). Then distribute them freely among soprano, alto, tenor and bass: it is your choice of layout, not the octave, that gives the colour.

wrong_bass.quoi: The chord's notes are right, but the wrong one is in the bass — the inversion is wrong. Example: the chord C–E–G is correct, but the exercise wants C in the bass (root position) and you have placed E (first inversion).
wrong_bass.pourquoi: The bass sets the inversion, which changes the chord's stability and function. Only the bass note is judged here: the three upper voices remain free in octave and distribution. Fix the bass, the rest is up to you.
wrong_bass.comment: Place the requested note in the bass (often the root). Swap the current bass for the right one. Once the bass is correct, arrange the upper voices freely: their octave does not count.

squelette.sousTitre: Lay out a chord progression over 8 bars, see it realised in four voices, listen to it, then flesh it out in the workshop.
squelette.banqueAide: Pick a slot, then click a chord to place it there.
squelette.vide: Place chords from the bank to see the realisation.
squelette.conduiteOk: Voice leading correct — no mistakes detected.
squelette.infoOuvrir: Understanding the functions and the chords
squelette.infoIntro: A harmonic progression tells a story in three moments: rest, preparation, and the tension that leads back to it.

infoTonique.texte: Rest. The I chord (i in minor) and its close relatives (vi, iii): where a phrase begins and ends, the tonality's anchor point.

infoPredominante.texte: Preparation. IV, ii, ii6: they announce the dominant and build motion toward it, without yet reaching maximum tension.

infoDominante.texte: Tension. V, V7, vii° and their inversions: the leading tone they contain pulls the ear toward the tonic — this is the chord that wants to resolve.

infoChromatisme.texte: Colors borrowed without changing key: secondary dominants (they briefly tonicize a degree), leading-tone chords on a degree, and borrowings from the parallel mode.

infoRenversements.texte: The same chord can appear several times in the bank: root position (I), third in the bass (I6, first inversion), fifth in the bass (I6/4, second inversion), and the equivalent figures for seventh chords (6/5, 4/3, 2). The inversion changes the bass and the color, not the function.

cours42.title: Keyboard Harmonization & Figured Bass
cours42.subtitle: Reading and realizing a Baroque continuo in four parts, then at the keyboard — figures, inversions, cadential six-four, suspensions and sequences. The first licence-level course.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You read and realize a figured bass without hesitation.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few figures still to consolidate (7th inversions, cadential six-four, suspensions).
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — review the table of figures and replay the examples before trying again.

conservatoire.intuition: A harmonic scheme can belong to everyone and to no one — La Folia has crossed five centuries of composers, each of whom realised it in his own way, without any one of them ever owning it.

reference.citation: La Folia is perhaps the oldest melody to have survived to our own day in Western Europe in a continuously recognisable form.
reference.auteur: Musicological tradition on the Iberian origin of La Folia

voix: A fixed harmonic scheme can carry, without ever changing, centuries of different realisations — the very principle of figured bass: one and the same framework, an infinity of ways of clothing it.
The major subtonic (VII, a major chord built on the 7th degree of a minor key) is a modal imprint older than fully codified tonality — it survives in formulas far more recent.

A false relation (two voices striking almost together the same note at chromatically adjacent pitches, e.g. C natural against C♯) is a genuine compositional technique of the 16th and 17th centuries, not simply a harmonic error.

pieges.erreur: Labelling the chord of measure 4 (C major, in D minor) as a mistake or as a modulation
pieges.correction: It is the VII of the scheme — the major subtonic, a modal colour characteristic of La Folia (and of many popular formulas older than codified tonality), neither an accident nor a change of key.

pieges.erreur: Taking the C natural against the C♯ (m. 6 and m. 14) for a writing error to be corrected
pieges.correction: It is a deliberate false relation (cross-relation), an authentic technique of early writing — the leading tone and the subtonic heard almost simultaneously, not a voice-leading mistake.

pieges.erreur: Looking for a single composer or a single source for “the” Folia
pieges.correction: The scheme is anonymous and older than any modern notion of authorship — Corelli, Vivaldi, Marais, C. P. E. Bach, Liszt and Rachmaninov each realised it separately, each in his own manner, without any one of them having invented it or owned it.

resume: La Folia is a fixed 16-measure harmonic cycle (i-V-i-VII-III-VII-iv6-V, twice over), anonymous and of Iberian origin — the oldest and the most frequently reused of all Western harmonic schemes.
Two signatures characterise the formula: the major subtonic (VII), a modal imprint older than codified tonality, and the iv6-V cadence carried by a lowered sixth degree descending to the dominant.

A harmonic scheme shared by generations of composers without any one of them owning it is exactly the principle of a jazz standard — a progression everyone knows and that each musician crosses in his own way.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: D minor, never with a Picardy third — the most fixed and most frequently reused formula in the whole history of Western music.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 3/4, in sustained chords (a simplified sarabande) — one chord per measure, sixteen measures, twice eight.
analyseNarrative.forme: One and the same scheme of 8 chords, played twice: the first statement closing on the dominant (m. 8), the second on the tonic (m. 16).

sections.label: Measures 1-8
sections.titre: The scheme, first hemistich
sections.chiffrage: i – V – i – VII – III – VII – iv6 – V
sections.fonctions: T – D – T – ? – T – ? – SD – D
sections.texte: Eight chords, eight measures: the Folia formula lays itself out in full. Two features sign it among a thousand possible minor progressions — the major subtonic (VII, C major in a D minor context), the imprint of a modal world older than codified tonality; and the iv6-V cadence, which brings the bass down by step (B♭ to A) exactly as any lowered sixth degree resolving to the dominant will do centuries later. In measure 6, one detail: the right hand holds C natural while the bass is already descending to C♯ — a deliberate false relation, leading tone and subtonic heard almost together.

sections.label: Measures 9-16
sections.titre: The scheme, second hemistich: the real cadence
sections.chiffrage: i – V – i – VII – III – VII – iv6 – V … i
sections.fonctions: T – D – T – ? – T – ? – SD – D … T
sections.texte: The same course, note for note, is played through again — the false relation returns unchanged (m. 14) — but this time the formula does not stop on the dominant: it closes on the tonic, bare D minor, with no Picardy third. The complete loop, in the barest form imaginable.

synthese.titre: The scheme as common property
synthese.texte: La Folia is a fixed, anonymous harmonic cycle that generations of composers — Corelli, Vivaldi, Marais, C. P. E. Bach, Liszt, Rachmaninov — have each clothed in variations of their own, without any one of them owning it. It is, term for term, the principle of the jazz standard: a progression that everyone knows, that no one owns, and that each musician crosses in his own way.

synthese.titre: The modal imprint within an already tonal syntax
synthese.texte: The major subtonic (VII) that structures the formula belongs to a harmonic world older than fully codified functional tonality — the same ♭VII found centuries later in Debussy's modal harmony or in certain film-music formulas. A 16th-century scheme already carries, in its very framework, a colour that theory will not name until much later.

synthese.titre: From the Baroque ground to the jazz standard
synthese.texte: The principle of a fixed bass or a fixed scheme over which a melody or an improvisation unfolds freely runs through the whole history of Western music — from the obstinate ground of Baroque laments (Purcell) to the chorus of a jazz standard (Autumn Leaves), La Folia is one of its very first documented examples, and one of the most durable: the formula has crossed five centuries without ever ceasing to be reused.

cours43.title: Renaissance Modal Counterpoint
cours43.subtitle: The Palestrina style (prima pratica): church modes, the melodic line, consonant two-voice counterpoint, strict dissonance (suspensions, nota cambiata) and modal cadences in 3-4 voices. Extends courses 13 and 10.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! You have mastered Palestrina's modal counterpoint — lines, regulated dissonance and cadences.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few points still to consolidate (dissonance treatment, modal clausulae).
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — review the melodic rules and the handling of suspensions, then replay the examples.

conservatoire.intuition: Before dissonance became an event, a drama or a colour one inhabits, it was a simple rule of traffic between the voices — an accident so rare that it can be counted on the fingers of one hand across fifty-six measures in four parts.

reference.citation: For the Council of Trent, Palestrina's style became the very model of church music.
reference.auteur: Musicological tradition on the reception of Palestrina

voix: A classical point of imitation has each voice born from the previous one at a regulated interval (the fifth, the octave) — here confirmed note for note: soprano, then alto a fifth lower, then tenor at the octave of the soprano.

In strict modal counterpoint, dissonance belongs to two categories only: the passing note (on a weak beat) and the suspension (prepared as a consonance, struck on a strong beat, resolved downwards by step) — never a free object.
A modal piece can close without a dominant and without any V-I polarity: the final then imposes itself by the weight and the frequency of its clausulae, not by a functional attraction.

pieges.erreur: Labelling this piece with functional Roman numerals (I, IV, V) as though it were a classical tonal work
pieges.correction: That would be anachronistic: in 1570 codified functional tonality does not yet exist. The analysis must proceed by CLAUSULAE (cadential points of repose) — the final imposes itself by the weight of its clausulae, not by a dominant-tonic polarity.

pieges.erreur: Looking for numerous chromatic accidentals in a Renaissance piece
pieges.correction: It is the opposite: this piece contains just ONE SINGLE accidental in its 56 measures for four voices (an A natural, musica ficta, m. 45) — the regime of dissonance here has a severity that later tonal music will never know again.

pieges.erreur: Treating every dissonance encountered as an expressive event to be interpreted individually
pieges.correction: In this style, dissonance is a simple rule of traffic between the voices (passing note on a weak beat, or suspension prepared-struck-resolved) — a matter of regulated circulation, not an isolated expressive object to be commented on case by case.

resume: Palestrina's style (Missa Brevis, 1570) treats dissonance as a strict rule of traffic between the voices — passing note on a weak beat, or suspension prepared-struck-resolved — never as a free event.

A classical point of imitation brings each voice in at a regulated interval from the previous one: here soprano, then alto a fifth lower, then tenor at the octave of the soprano, confirmed note for note.

With no concluding dominant, the modal final establishes itself by the weight and frequency of the clausulae rather than by a V-I polarity — a mechanism of tonal attraction entirely different from that of the functional music that came after.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: Mode transposed onto E♭ (edition with three flats) — no functional key in the classical sense: the final imposes itself by the frequency and the weight of the clausulae, not by a dominant-tonic polarity.
analyseNarrative.metrique: Cut-common 4/4 (modern alla breve). Moderate tempo, with neither acceleration nor slowing.
analyseNarrative.forme: A single point of imitation in four voices (mm. 1-9), then a continuous weaving of recurring cadential modules, punctuated by clausulae on the successive degrees of the mode, up to the final plagal cadence.

sections.label: Measures 1-9
sections.titre: The point of imitation: the four-voice exposition
sections.texte: The subject — a stepwise descent from B♭, the pleading curve of the Agnus — enters alone in the soprano, then answers in the alto on E♭ (a fifth lower, confirmed note for note), then in the tenor on B♭ (an octave below the soprano, confirmed), then in the bass: the classic exposition of the Palestrina style, each voice born from the one before it.

sections.label: Measures 10-44
sections.titre: The economy of modules: suspensions, clausulae, varied repetition
sections.chiffrage: successive clausulae on E♭, G minor, B♭…
sections.texte: The movement is built on a small number of cadential modules — in particular a double-suspension formula (two voices suspended in parallel, resolving together) that returns, unchanged or varied, at regular intervals. The invention lies not in the material but in the stitching: the clausulae mark out the course (E♭ as the principal point of repose, a colouristic detour through G minor) without any one of them functioning as a dominant in the classical sense — attraction here is a matter of stepwise motion and cadential convention, not of fifths.

sections.label: Measures 45-46
sections.titre: The only accidental in the whole piece
sections.texte: Out of the 503 sounding events in the piece, exactly one falls outside the diatonic scale of the key signature: an A natural in the soprano, the musica ficta that manufactures the leading tone of the clausula on B♭. All the rest — every dissonance in these 56 measures — belongs to two strictly regulated categories: passing notes on weak beats, and suspensions, prepared as consonances, struck on the strong beat, resolved downwards by step, without exception.

sections.label: Measures 47-56
sections.titre: The final plagal cadence
sections.texte: The last period superimposes the cadential modules already heard before closing on a plagal cadence: the A♭ chord (IV), adorned with a descending neighbour-note figure in the alto, then the final E♭ chord — a complete triad, with its third. No concluding dominant: the final imposes itself by the weight of its clausulae and the gravity of its bass, not by a V-I polarity that does not yet exist in this language.

synthese.titre: The zero regime of dissonance
synthese.texte: One single accidental in 56 measures for four voices, and every dissonance rigorously sorted into two categories (passing note, suspension): this is the world before any dramatisation of dissonance. Here it is not yet an event, nor a drama, nor a colour one deliberately inhabits — it is a rule of traffic between the voices, a matter of circulation, never an object in itself. The Council of Trent made this discipline the very model of the church style.

synthese.titre: The economy of the module: invention in the stitching
synthese.texte: Palestrina builds this entire movement on a small number of recurring cadential formulas rather than on a profusion of new ideas — the same principle that underlies, centuries later, a fixed harmonic scheme such as La Folia or a jazz standard: limited material, but an inexhaustible combinatorics.

synthese.titre: The final by weight, not by the dominant
synthese.texte: With no concluding dominant and no V-I polarity, the final of this piece imposes itself by the repetition and the gravity of its clausulae — a mechanism of tonal attraction entirely different from the one functional music would develop afterwards, and a reminder that the very notion of “tonality” covers several historically distinct systems, not one single universal principle.
