conservatoire.intuition: The same theme, reharmonized six times towards six different destinations, reveals that a melody has no single harmonic meaning — it has as many meanings as there are possible harmonizations, and each one tells a different story.

reference.citation: These are reminiscences of a grown-up for grown-ups, and not scenes intended for children.
reference.auteur: Robert Schumann, on the Kinderszenen (letter to Clara Wieck, 1838)

voix: One and the same melodic phrase can be harmonized towards a different tonal destination at every return — dream-form, where you always set out from the same threshold and never wake up in the same place.
A diminished seventh chord can work as a simple modulating pivot, with no dramatic intent — a hinge that turns without creaking, modulation as the pure association of ideas.
A fermata can be promoted to a structural event in its own right: a dominant ninth chord held for its own sake, savoured before it even resolves.

pieges.erreur: Analysing the six returns of the theme as mere repetition, without difference
pieges.correction: Every return of the theme is reharmonized towards a different tonal destination (I, V, ii, IV with a detour through vi, then I) — only strophes 1 and 5 are rigorously identical (verified note for note).

pieges.erreur: Taking the fermata in m. 22 for a simple pause with no harmonic function
pieges.correction: It is a genuine chord (G9, the dominant of the dominant), held and savoured for its own sake — the expressive summit of the whole piece, neither a silence nor a mere prolongation.

pieges.erreur: Looking for a dramatic function (Beethoven-style) or a suspensive one (Wagner-style) in the diminished seventh chords of this piece
pieges.correction: Here the diminished seventh works as a discreet modulating pivot — a hinge that turns without creaking, modulation as an association of ideas rather than as drama or sustained tension.

resume: The same theme (the C upbeat, the climb towards F) returns six times in Träumerei, each time reharmonized towards a different destination — I, V, ii, IV (with a detour through vi), then I: the complete family circle of F major.
Two diminished seventh chords work as silent revolving doors, swinging the phrase into new regions without ever dramatizing the transition.
The fermata in m. 22 (a held G9, the dominant of the dominant) is promoted to a structural event in its own right — the reverie held in the hand, before the tiptoe awakening by way of a complete V9.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: F major from beginning to end — every strophe sets out from the same tonic, but visits a different region before returning to it or moving away from it.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4, Moderato (quarter note = 90). One and the same phrase, breathed six times, with an upbeat.
analyseNarrative.forme: Six four-measure strophes on a single theme: I (mm. 0-4) — V (mm. 5-8) — ii (mm. 9-12) — IV, with vi in passing (mm. 13-16) — I, exact reprise (mm. 17-20) — I, with fermata and final cadence (mm. 21-24).

sections.label: Strophes 1 and 5 (mm. 0-4, mm. 17-20)
sections.titre: The exposition, home — and its exact return
sections.texte: The theme rises from the C upbeat to its summit, F5, before a I6/4-V7 half cadence. Strophe 5 takes up that same phrase note for note, identical down to onset and pitch — verified exhaustively — the return to reality after the journey of the intervening strophes.

sections.label: Strophe 2 (mm. 5-8)
sections.titre: The first revolving door
sections.texte: The same departure, but the phrase slips towards vi (D minor), then pivots on a diminished seventh chord (F#-A-C-E♭, confirmed exactly) that tips it towards the dominant of the dominant, then towards C major: the dream has drifted a whole fifth without ever forcing the door.

sections.label: Strophe 3 (mm. 9-12)
sections.titre: The darkest detour
sections.chiffrage: I → C minor (borrowed) → D7♭9 → G minor (ii)
sections.texte: Departure in F, but the minor mode surfaces very quickly (the borrowed E♭), the phrase takes on a D7 with a minor ninth, and finally settles on G minor — the darkest point of the whole piece, reached mezzo forte.

sections.label: Strophe 4 (mm. 13-16)
sections.titre: The masterstroke: the theme in B♭
sections.texte: The theme itself, heard until now as a melody over an F chord, is restated in B♭ major (IV) — and here reaches the absolute summit of the whole piece, B♭5. A second revolving door (a diminished seventh chord on C#) slides towards D minor (vi), before a C7 prepares the return.

sections.label: Strophe 6 (mm. 21-24)
sections.titre: The fermata and the awakening
sections.texte: The theme sets out one last time, but instead of continuing on its way the phrase comes to a standstill: a G9 chord (G-B-D-F-A, confirmed exactly) is held under a fermata, the melody suspended on A5 — the reverie held in the hand, outside time. Then one last crossing (I6/4-V7), and the final cadence, pianissimo: ii, then a complete V9 in which the D and the E sound together (confirmed), before the F chord under a second fermata — the tiptoe awakening.

synthese.titre: The diminished seventh as a silent hinge
synthese.texte: The two revolving doors of the piece (strophes 2 and 4) use the very aggregate that, elsewhere in this corpus, dramatizes (Beethoven) or suspends indefinitely (Wagner): here the diminished seventh does neither — it pivots without a sound, modulation as the pure association of ideas rather than as an event.

synthese.titre: The fermata promoted to a structural event
synthese.texte: The held G9 of m. 22 is not a simple pause: it is the expressive summit of the piece, a chord suspended for its own sake, savoured before it even resolves — twenty-one years before Tristan, the same idea of a tension held for itself, but one that here always ends up going back to bed.

synthese.titre: A lesson in reharmonization avant la lettre
synthese.texte: The same melodic material, harmonized six times towards six different destinations (I, V, ii, IV, vi in passing, then I): Träumerei is the clearest reharmonization exercise in the repertoire, a theme everyone knows, seen in six lights by a single author.

cours47.title: Orchestration and Score Reading
cours47.subtitle: Reading a full score — page architecture, C clefs, transposing instruments with written/sounding listening, verticality of a tutti, piano reduction and orchestral balance. Second course of the DNSPM track.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! Full score, clefs, transpositions, verticality: the orchestra holds no more secrets on paper — now hear it.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few transpositions to consolidate — reread THE table of section 3 and replay the written/sounding pairs.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — go back over the transposing-instruments table and the C-clef lines (Fa3–La3–Do4–Mi4–Sol4) before trying again.

conservatoire.intuition: An orchestral texture is not always a stack of chords struck together: most of the time it is a melodic line carried by sustained pedals — and knowing how to tell a sustained pedal from a real tutti attacked together is already knowing how to read an orchestral score.

reference.citation: Orchestration is part of the very soul of the work itself.
reference.auteur: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, Principles of Orchestration (posthumous treatise, ed. Steinberg, 1913)

voix: A string accompaniment can support a melody without ever forming a chord that is really struck together — “verticality” is sometimes nothing but a sustained pedal, not an attacked chord.

Telling a real tutti (all parts attacking together, in the same rhythm) from a merely sustained pedal calls for checking the actual onsets, not just the pitches that happen to sound together at a given instant.
Pizz./arco markings are not mere nuances of playing: they redistribute the roles of the sections between carriers of melody and carriers of implied harmony.

repertoire.titre: Scheherazade, 3rd movement “The Young Prince and the Young Princess” (excerpt, condensed version)

pieges.erreur: Believing that an arrangement in 5 instrumental parts forms a complete chord at every instant
pieges.correction: Here a single line (violin) carries the melody almost throughout while the other 4 parts hold a pedal — the rare tuttis (5 parts attacking together, same rhythm) are concentrated at the articulations of the form, and the chord of the very last measure is by far the densest in the piece.

pieges.erreur: Looking for a chord grid that can be figured measure by measure in every orchestral arrangement
pieges.correction: An essentially melodic arrangement (like this one, or the first Boléro file / course 19) carries no harmonic progression to be figured — the harmony stays implicit, and the analysis then bears on line and texture rather than on scale degrees.

pieges.erreur: Treating the “oriental” chromatic ornament (the Princess's C#) as a real modulation or a functional borrowing
pieges.correction: It is pure sonic decoration, never resolved, colouring the melody without ever entering a harmonic syntax — an ornamented augmented fourth, not an altered chord.

resume: This movement is a diptych: the Prince (G major, pure diatonicism, mm. 1-42) against the Princess (G minor adorned with an “oriental” C#, mm. 43-58), before a return of the Prince and then a coda (mm. 75-80).

The accompaniment is almost always a pedal sustained beneath the melody; the rare tuttis (5 parts together, same rhythm) mark the articulations of the form, and the chord of the very last measure — where the viola even adds its own E-C-A arpeggio on top of the G major triad of the other parts — is by far the densest of them.

The Princess's descending tetrachord (D-C-B♭-A-G) and her never-resolved chromatic ornament link this movement to a whole lineage within the corpus (Folia, Purcell, Sibelius, Boléro, Morricone) — Rimsky-Korsakov is its Russian source, handed on to Stravinsky, his pupil.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: G major for the Prince (one-sharp key signature); an adorned G minor for the Princess (two-flat key signature, mm. 43-58); return to G major for the reprise and the coda.
analyseNarrative.metrique: 6/8, a diptych of two melody-worlds over the same rocking pulse, without a single real break of metre.
analyseNarrative.forme: Prince (mm. 1-42, with an inner pizzicato episode, mm. 24-30) — Princess (mm. 43-58) — return of the Prince, varied da capo (mm. 59-74) — coda (mm. 75-80).

sections.label: The Prince (mm. 1-9)
sections.titre: Suavity as a calculated absence of accidentals
sections.texte: The violin states its upbeat alone, then the four other strings come in on a pedal (G-B-D, held for two measures on end) while the line pursues its curve: B-C, D-E, the falling-back G-A-B. Not a single accidental before the closed period of m. 9 — perfect diatonicism, elegance without event.

sections.label: The pizzicato episode (mm. 24-30)
sections.titre: Harmony reduced to a skeleton
sections.texte: A dialogue of pizzicato basses, A and B alternating beneath a held F#: the dominant is suggested, never struck as a complete chord. This is accompaniment at its most frugal — three notes sketching a function without ever gathering into a chord attacked together.

sections.label: The Princess (mm. 43-58)
sections.titre: The exact negative: the ornament as decoration
sections.chiffrage: i (G minor), with a C# foreign to the mode
sections.texte: The C#-D acciaccatura, repeated like a tambourine, embroiders an augmented fourth that belongs to no scale in the passage and never resolves — a purely “oriental” ornament, colour without function. Then the line coils into a descent D-C-B♭-A-G, the same chromatic-melodic tetrachord that frames the Folia, Purcell's ground and Sibelius's Andalusian descent, here as dance finery rather than as a harmonic foundation.

sections.label: Return of the Prince (mm. 59-74)
sections.titre: The varied da capo
sections.texte: The Prince's theme comes back, reworked but recognizable, in G major — the tonic recovered after the Princess's modal detour, preparing the coda.

sections.label: The coda (mm. 75-80)
sections.titre: The storyteller's signature, and the one tutti
sections.chiffrage: I — the only chord really ATTACKED together by all 5 parts
sections.texte: Chromatic slides (A#-B-C, E♭-F#-G) evoke the arabesque of Scheherazade's own violin, which prowls through the whole cycle. Then, in the very last measure, the five parts articulate TOGETHER, in the same rhythm, the densest tutti of the entire movement: G-D-B in the violins and the double bass, but the viola superimposes its own pizzicato arpeggio (E-C-A) — a final stroke of colour that enriches the triad rather than a plain bare G major chord. Everywhere else, “verticality” was only a pedal sustained beneath a line that keeps moving, with rare flashes of ensemble at the articulations of the form alone; here, to finish, it is the richest collective gesture of the piece, and even this gesture keeps one voice that steps aside from it with a light flourish.

synthese.titre: Sustained verticality versus struck verticality
synthese.texte: The note-by-note survey distinguishes two textures that the eye easily confuses on a score: a string pedal SUSTAINED beneath a melody that keeps moving (the case almost everywhere in this movement) is not the same thing as a chord really ATTACKED together by all the parts, in the same rhythm (rare, and concentrated at the articulations of the form — end of the Prince, end of the Princess, end of the return, coda). The final chord (m. 80) is not the only one of those moments, but it is by far the densest. Checking the actual onsets, not just the pitches that sound together at a given instant, is the only reliable way to decide between a sustained pedal and a real tutti.

synthese.titre: The descending tetrachord and the “oriental” ornament, two Russian exports
synthese.texte: The Princess's chromatic tetrachord (D-C-B♭-A-G) links this movement to the Folia, to Purcell's ground and to Sibelius's Andalusian descent; and the recipe of the ornamented augmented fourth, never resolved, as pure sonic decoration, is exactly the one that the B theme of the Boléro (1928) and Morricone (1966) would later industrialize — here at its Russian source, with the master whose orientalism supplied the lexicon to three generations.

synthese.titre: 1888, the year with two faces
synthese.texte: The same year as Satie's First Gymnopédie: in Paris harmony loses its function; in Saint Petersburg, Rimsky-Korsakov brings the opposite art to perfection, colour WITHIN function — chromaticism as costume, modality as perfume, the whole thing prudently moored to tonality. And the thread is direct: Rimsky-Korsakov was Stravinsky's teacher, and Stravinsky's Augurs of Spring (course 21) turn this workshop against itself.

cours48.title: Harmonic Dictation Methodology
cours48.subtitle: The methodological companion to the /releve tool — bass first, functions before chords, inversions by ear, the discipline of the 6 listenings. Last course of the DNSPM track and of the catalogue.

quiz.perfect: Perfect! Bass, functions, inversions, the 6 listenings: the method is mastered — now practise it in /releve.
quiz.veryGood: Very good! A few reflexes to consolidate — reread the reflex card and redo the V/V7 examples of section 4.
quiz.keepGoing: Keep going — go back over the golden rule (key → cadence → bass → figures) and the reflex card before trying again.

conservatoire.intuition: A “literal reprise” announced in a score is never verified at first glance from the rhythm or the touch — it is verified in the bass, by following the one line that carries the actual progression, stripped of everything that varies around it.

reference.citation: To shiver, frozen, amid the icy snows, at the harsh breath of a horrid wind.
reference.auteur: Sonnet accompanying the original edition of The Four Seasons (1725), attributed to Vivaldi himself

voix: The bass first, always: it is by following the bass line alone, independently of a figuration that changes completely, that one identifies a harmonic sequence as a genuine repetition.

One and the same sonority can change STATUS according to its context — a sustained texture with no functional motion, or a precise function within a cadence — and the survey must first establish WHAT THE CHORD DOES before naming it.
Verifying a claim of “literally identical” requires comparing the right landmarks: a discrepancy of a single measure in the alignment can lead to the wrong conclusion that a reprise is not exact.

repertoire.titre: “Winter” (L'inverno), 1st movement of The Four Seasons (expanded piano arrangement)

pieges.erreur: Confusing a chord HELD as texture (which is not yet functioning) with a functional chord preparing a specific cadence
pieges.correction: The same chord (G-B♭-D♭-F, a half-diminished seventh) opens the movement as pure texture — the cold, physically represented — and closes it, fifty measures later, as a cadential linchpin (iiø6/5–V–i): two thoroughly distinct statuses for one and the same sonority.

pieges.erreur: Verifying a “literal reprise” by comparing measures in the order in which they are mentioned, without checking the actual alignment
pieges.correction: The circle of fifths at m. 111 does NOT take up the one at m. 44 measure for measure, but the one at m. 45 — a one-station shift within the circle that a naive alignment would have missed.

pieges.erreur: Assembling a chord from several partial readings without checking the order of the arguments (pitch, accidental, octave)
pieges.correction: An error of shifted arguments (already encountered in the Folia file, course 42) can silently turn a correct chord into a wrong one — reread yourself systematically rather than trusting a first draft.

resume: The opening of the movement (mm. 1-22) builds a half-diminished seventh (G-B♭-D♭-F) by accumulation, note after note, as pure texture representing the cold — ten measures of frozen dissonance before the first resolution in F minor.

The complete circle of fifths (C-F-B♭-E♭-A♭-D♭-G-C, mm. 44-51) returns literally — same bass sequence — at m. 111, but in an entirely different figuration: the bass first is the only reliable way to verify it.

The great final cadence (mm. 111-124) closes the loop: the very chord of the initial freeze (G-B♭-D♭-F) comes back there as iiø6/5, a perfectly functional cadential linchpin — the two lives of one chord, fifty measures apart, in the most orthodox Baroque writing.

analyseNarrative.tonalite: F minor from beginning to end (four-flat key signature), with a detour to the relative major (A♭ major) under the più Vivace (m. 77).
analyseNarrative.metrique: 4/4, Allegretto, sempre pedale, with written-in accelerations (the tempo climbs in tiny notches throughout) and a più Vivace at m. 77.
analyseNarrative.forme: The frozen opening (mm. 1-22) — the episodes in C, the wind (mm. 23-51, with the complete circle of fifths at the end) — the chromatic clusters (mm. 52-66) — più Vivace and preparation (mm. 67-110) — the great cadence, restatement and double life of the chord (mm. 111-124).

sections.label: The frozen opening (mm. 1-22)
sections.titre: Programmatic dissonance: ten measures of freezing before the first resolution
sections.texte: The voices enter one by one and freeze on the spot: F alone, then +G +B♭, then +D♭ — the chord thus built by accumulation, held in repeated eighth notes, is G-B♭-D♭-F, the half-diminished seventh. It is not yet functioning: it REPRESENTS, physically, through texture, the cold taking hold. The F♭ (enharmonic of E) sharpens it into vii°7; the resolution in F minor arrives only at m. 11, after ten measures of frozen dissonance. Then a ladder of secondary dominants (F7, G7, A°7) raises the tension a notch at each level — the chattering of teeth intensifies.

sections.label: The episodes in C, the wind (mm. 23-51)
sections.titre: The Baroque engine at full throttle
sections.chiffrage: v (gusts), then complete circle of fifths
sections.texte: Gusts of ascending and descending scales, hammered chords: the wind, the feet stamping the ground. Then the circle of fifths settles in at full throttle — the bass descends C-F-B♭-E♭-A♭-D♭-G-C, a seventh at every station, the dominant of the dominant of the dominant… as far as a half-diminished chord on G that closes the loop. The same framework as the cadence of K. 545 (Mozart, course 28) and the chord grid of Autumn Leaves (course 15) — sixty years before the one, two centuries before the other.

sections.label: The chromatic clusters (mm. 52-66)
sections.titre: Textural dissonance, once again
sections.chiffrage: aggregates of seconds over a C pedal
sections.texte: E-F-G-A♭ stacked in seconds: the biting wind, in clusters. Then maximal chromaticism — as far as an E double flat — and the frictions F♭/F over a C pedal held below. Vivaldi is not writing chords that function: he is writing textures that represent, exactly as at the start of the movement, but here pushed to the chromatic extreme.

sections.label: Più Vivace and the preparation (mm. 67-110)
sections.titre: The freezing procedure, a second time
sections.chiffrage: i (tutti), then accumulation in the relative major, chain of dominants
sections.texte: A brief return to the tutti on the tonic, then the più Vivace relaunches the accumulation degree by degree (E♭, +F, +A♭, +B♭) — the same procedure as at the opening, transposed to the relative major. A chain-ladder of dominants (F major–G major–C) and chromatic descents prepare the great final cadence.

sections.label: The great cadence (mm. 111-124)
sections.titre: The two lives of the chord, fifty measures apart
sections.chiffrage: circle of fifths restated, then C7 — iiø6/5 – V – i, twice
sections.texte: The circle of fifths returns, literally identical station for station to the one at m. 45 (same bass sequence, F-B♭-E♭-A♭-D♭-G) but in a hammered figuration, different from the first time. Then C7 (V7) introduces the cadential formula iiø6/5–V–i, repeated twice, hammered down into the depths of the keyboard — the B♭0, the lowest note in the whole file, falls exactly on the 2nd occurrence of the linchpin chord. And that linchpin chord, G-B♭-D♭-F, is EXACTLY the one of the initial freeze: the piece opens by building the half-diminished as texture, and closes by striking it as function. Conclusion in F minor, without a Picardy third: winter remains winter.

synthese.titre: One chord, two statuses, a single movement
synthese.texte: The same sonority (G-B♭-D♭-F) opens the movement as pure TEXTURE — held, repeated, with no functional motion, representing the cold — and closes it as pure FUNCTION — an inversion (ø6/5) preparing the dominant in a textbook cadence. Here, a century before Berlioz and two before the Rite of Spring, Vivaldi invents programmatic dissonance and textural dissonance as poetic licences inside the most orthodox functional system.

synthese.titre: A calling card across four centuries
synthese.texte: The half-diminished chord of this corpus now has six documented statuses: texture of the cold and cadential linchpin in Vivaldi (1725), workhorse in Bach, drama in Beethoven (the Pathétique, course 39), enigma in Wagner (Tristan, course 25), timbre in Debussy (The Sunken Cathedral, course 29), a word of the language in Evans (My Funny Valentine, course 16). Nothing is born, everything is promoted — the history of this chord is a change of status, not an invention.

synthese.titre: Method of the survey: the bass first, always
synthese.texte: It is by following the bass line alone — not the upper voices, radically different in figuration — that one identifies the circle of fifths at m. 111 as IDENTICAL to the one at m. 45: same sequence of degrees, same order, only the texture changes. A “literal reprise” announced in a score is verified in the bass, never at first glance from the rhythm or the touch.

releve.sousTitre: Listen to a four-voice textbook progression, then transcribe it in stages: the bass, the figures, the full SATB.

consignes.basse: Write down the bass you hear, measure by measure — any octave is accepted. Select the Bass voice in the editor.
consignes.chiffrage: The correct bass is given. For each measure, choose the figure you hear among the chips.
consignes.satb: Write the four voices you hear. The full school-style checking applies (conformity, resolutions).

releve.modeExamenAide: {n} listens of the full progression, no chord-by-chord replay.
releve.ecoutesEpuisees: No listens left — write down what you remember.
